en: The Seventh Chapter.
Here, first of all, the sequence of the establishment of defects (*doṣa*), merits (*guṇa*), styles (*rīti*), and ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) in poetry has been shown.
Now, in response to the inquiry as to what these are, he states the nature of the defects, which have reached their turn according to the order of enumeration:
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ka) Here, indeed, the meaning is that first, in the first chapter, the sequence of the abiding of the defects (*doṣa*) and the manner of their abiding have been shown.
Those are the defects.
By the statement, "Its defects are those which cause its depreciation," the manner in which defects function as causes of depreciation is shown.
[And it is said: "Qualities, ornaments, and styles are declared to be the causes of excellence."
By this statement, the manner in which qualities (*guṇas*) and so forth exist as enhancing factors is shown.
Furthermore, in this context, the reading *rītyalaṅkārāṇām* appears to be the result of a scribal error transmitted through successive generations, as it violates the order of the enumeration;
for that very reason, the phrase *uddeśakramaprāptānām* (of those obtained according to the order of enumeration) was stated.
Locanā:
Having defined the nature of poetry (*kāvyasvarūpa*), [the author], desiring to define its defects (*doṣa*), shows the introduction to that topic with the words "For here... (*iha hi*).
"Svarūpa" means one's own unique form, a property that distinguishes it from others.
"Defects" (doṣas) are those which detract from the aesthetic flavor (rasa);
the meaning of this has already been made clear previously.
He states its specific details:
"Vijñapriyā: (vi, kha) It has already been made clear."

Defects such as *śrutiduṣṭa* (offensive to the ear) and so forth [are defects] by way of the word; defects such as *apuṣṭārtha* (insufficient meaning) and so forth are [defects] by way of the meaning.

The meaning is that the state of being denotable by words such as "transitory emotions" (vyabhicāribhāva) and so forth directly detracts from the aesthetic flavor (rasa); this point has already been made clear previously. "Its specific varieties" refers to the specific varieties of defects (doṣa).
"Those, moreover," refers to those defects (*doṣa*). Locanā explains:
"Tasteless" means that which detracts from the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), being the cause of the destruction of its savor.
"Even earlier"—that is, previously in the first chapter.

Furthermore, those [defects] are considered to be fivefold, as they occur in the word (*pada*), its constituent part (*tadaṃśa*), the sentence (*vākya*), the meaning (*artha*), and even in the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). (VisSd 7.1)
Locanā:

"Furthermore, those"—meaning those defects residing in the fivefold group beginning with the word (*pada*) and its parts (*tadaṃśa*), etc.—are of five kinds because they are the causes of the diminution of aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*), which constitutes the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*).
They are: being unpleasant to hear (*duḥśrava*), the three types of vulgarity (*aślīla*), and the employment of an inappropriate meaning (*anucitārtha*).
Vulgarity, unintelligibility, ambiguity, indirectness of meaning, and tautology; // VisSd_7.2 //
Inexpressiveness, obscurity, the production of a contradictory cognition, and the state of having an undistinguished predicate-component belong to words and sentences. (VisSd 7.3)
Certain defects may occur even within a word-part or in subsequent words: namely, meaninglessness, lack of semantic coherence, and corruption of grammatical formation. (VisSd 7.4)
Vijñapriyā: (vi,

ga) Regarding the passage beginning with "difficult to hear" (*duḥśrava*), in the phrase "the state of being unapplied" (*aprayuktatā*), because the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) following the *dvandva* compound is connected to each member individually, "difficult to hear-ness" (*duḥśravatva*) and so forth are themselves the faults.
The meaning is that these thirteen defects, beginning with *avimṛṣṭavidheyāṃśa* and ending with *bhāvānta*, occur both in words and in sentences;
that is to say, some among them may also occur in a portion of a word (*padāṃśa*). "In the word, however" [is said] because...

The meaning is that the three defects—meaninglessness (*nirarthakatva*), lack of capacity (*asamarthatva*), and corruption of grammatical refinement (*cyutasaṃskāratā*)—belong exclusively to the word (*pada*) alone and not to the sentence (*vākya*).
We shall explain the basis for this when discussing each of those respective defects.
—*Locanā*—
(Lo, ī) To the question, "What are the defects there, and what are they based on? he says: *duḥśrava* and so forth. The suffix *-tva* is connected to each of the terms beginning with *duḥśrava*.
*Sandigdha* means doubt (*sandeha*).
Now, it might be defiled; that is, a compound word whose constituent parts are not clearly discerned and which produces a contradictory understanding.
All such defects belong to words and sentences.
Among these, such as "difficult to hear" (duḥśravādi) and so forth—within these [categories]—it may be defiled.
*Duḥśravatva* (unpleasantness to hear) is the quality of causing pain to the ear due to harsh phonemes,
as in the following example from the *Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, gha) Regarding that, he states the characteristic of being unpleasant to hear: "harsh," etc.
It should be understood that this applies with the exception of the heroic (*vīra*), the loathsome (*bībhatsa*), and the furious (*raudra*) sentiments, for it is precisely appropriate to those.
Thus, this fault occurs only when [the word] is partial;
however, when it pervades the entire word, one must understand that there is instead the fault of "discordant phonemes" (*pratikūlavarṇatva*), and so forth—as in:
“When will the slender-limbed woman come under the power of the bodiless god? (*kārttarthyaṃ yātu tanvaṅgī kadānaṅgavaśaṃvadā*).
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ṅa) "The state of having accomplished one's purpose" is clear.
A syllable joined with the letter *ra* causes pain to the ears;
*Locanā*:
(*lo*, *u*) a harsh syllable is one with harsh phonemes.
*Kārttārthya* means the state of having accomplished one's purpose—the condition of being one whose aim is achieved.
*Aślīlatva* (indecoracy) is threefold, because it manifests shame, disgust, or inauspiciousness.
*Vijñapriyā*: [End of commentary].
(Vi, ca) "Because of being shameful, disgusting, and inauspicious.
This means because these three are the causes.
Causality consists of both being an indicator (*jñāpakatva*) and being a producer (*kārakatva*).
In this context, it should be understood that shame (*vrīḍā*) and disgust (*jugupsā*) function as causes (*kāraka*), while auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) functions as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
The examples follow in order:
"O King, you who are satisfied with victory over your enemies..."
"Your means of accomplishment is very great.
Regarding "Vijñapriyā":

(vi, cha) the word *sādhana* signifies both an army and a proof (*artha*), because it has multiple meanings and the context is primary. Thus, the expressed meaning (*vācya*) of the word *sādhana* is twofold.
However, the meaning in the form of the male organ is what is suggested (*vyaṅgya*), which causes shame in the listeners;
it is not, however, the suggester of shame (*vrīḍāvyañjaka*), because that [shame] is not perceived [from the words themselves].
For example: "O slender one, at your destruction, the wind then slowly spread forth."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ja) "prasasāra" means that after the period of separation, having regained the hero, this is the hero's speech:
"O slender one (tanvi), when you were lost to my sight—that is, in your disappearance—the wind blew gently and slowly to produce suffering for me. This is the meaning.

In this context, the suggested meaning of the word *vināśa*, which possesses multiple senses, is death; as such, it suggests inauspiciousness. The word *vāyu*, however, through its suggestion of the downward breath (*apānavāyu*), generates disgust in the form of loathing, because at a time of suffering, the downward breath is perceived as having slowly issued forth.
"Unsuitability of meaning" (*anucitārthatvam*) means that the essence [of this fault] is the capacity to suggest censure regarding something that is not to be censured.
*Locanā*:
(lo, ū) Regarding "haughty" (*dṛpta*), here the word *sādhana* is employed in the sense of equipment such as elephants and horses, yet it refers to the male organ (*puṃdhvaja*).
The word *vāyu* (wind) signifies mere air, yet it suggests the specific downward wind (*apāna-vāyu*);

the word *vināśa* (destruction) signifies disappearance, yet it evokes death. Because they thus successively suggest shame and other such emotions, the words *sādhana*, *vāyu*, and *vināśa* are indecorous (*aślīla*) in this context.

“‘The brave attain immortality when they become sacrificial animals in the sacrifice of battle. Here, the state of being a sacrificial animal reveals cowardice; thus, there is the fault of ‘inappropriateness of meaning’ (anucitārthatva).
— *Vijñapriyā*.
(vi, jha) Regarding the word *dṛpta* ("proud"): here, the word *sādhana* is employed in the sense of "means" such as elephants and horses for the male organ;
the word *vāyu* is used in the sense of a "wind-instrument" for a specific downward breath (*apāna*);
and the word *vināśa* is used in the sense of "disappearance" for death. Because they thus remind one [of these things], they sequentially suggest shame and other such emotions.
Locanā:
(lo, ṛ) The word *paśu* is employed in such a conventional sense;
its "non-employment" likewise refers to its being disregarded by poets even though it is well-known.
For example: "The lotus shines in the lake."
In this context, the word *padma* is masculine.
*Vijñapriyā*:
"Even though it is well-known [otherwise]."
The meaning is: "even though it has been stated [by others] in the *Anuśāsana* as having those characteristics.
By the use of the plural "by poets" (*kavibhiḥ*), the sense is "by many ancient poets.
Consequently, even if there were respect for this [work] by many contemporary poets or by a single ancient poet, it would still be nothing but a fault.

And thus, even though there is respect [for the usage] on the part of the ancient poet Nala-kāraka (Śrīharṣa) in the verse, "For in the rainy season, the wagtails [eat] lotuses," this is indeed a fault;
for if that respect were directed toward mere speech outside of poetry, it would not be a fault at all.
Therefore, the authority of grammatical instruction is not absolute.
Vulgarity (*grāmyatva*) is, for example:
"Your hip steals my mind."
In this context, the word *kaṭi* is vulgar (*grāmya*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
"As for 'vulgar'—the meaning is that it is a vulgar word."
Its "suchness" (tathātva) consists in not being employed [by the learned].
Its distinction [from other defects] lies in its not being used because it is disregarded by the learned who are common to both poetry and poets.
"Unintelligibility" (apratītatva) means being established only in a single region.
As it is said:
"One whose latent tendencies have been shattered through yoga."
In this context, within the Yogaśāstra itself, the word *āśaya* has the sense of *vāsanā*. Vijñapriyā: (vi, ṭha) in a single philosophical system.
Locanā: Regarding "in only a single treatise" (*ekaśāstramātre*),
[the word] "intention" (*āśaya*) [is to be supplied].
This is found only in the treatise on yoga, and not in common worldly usage or in the science of material prosperity (*arthaśāstra*).

For instance, the *Pātañjala-sūtra* states: "The Lord (*īśvara*) is a distinct Puruṣa untouched by afflictions (*kleśa*), actions (*karman*), their results (*vipāka*), or their latent impressions (*āśaya*)."
The afflictions are ignorance and karma; their fruit, consisting of evil and good deeds and so forth, is maturation (vipāka);
and the latencies (vāsanā) conforming to those are the dispositions (āśaya).
And since these [qualities] reside in the mind, they are predicated of the person.
Furthermore, in this way, there would be a fault for both the speaker and the listener if they lacked knowledge of the treatise and so forth.
Consequently, it differs because it is not employed [in that manner].
“Place the venerable lineage of preceptors upon your ear and show compassion.
Here, there is a doubt as to whether the word *vandyām* means “one who has been made captive” (*bandībhūtāyām*) or “one who is worthy of worship” (*vandanīyām*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ḍa) "Doubtful" means: what is this word? Thus there is doubt regarding the word itself.
"Having placed upon the ear" means "having heard."
Regarding the phrase "having become a captive" (*vandībhūtāyām*),
it means "the wife of an enemy who has been forcibly taken captive.
Here, there is a doubt concerning the two words *vandī* and *vandyā*.
Locanā:

Regarding the word *vandyām*—there is doubt because it could be interpreted either as having a locative ending (*saptamyanta*) or an accusative ending (*dvitīyānta*), and in the absence of a specific context, there is no decisive factor (*vinigamanābhāva*).

It is not a case of conveying a meaning through etymological derivation (*notyarthatva*), nor is it a figurative indication (*lakṣyārtha-prakāśana*) caused by incapacity, since there is neither conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) nor a specific purpose (*prayojana*).
Vijñapriyā: (vi,

ḍha) "In the case of being of interpretable meaning (*neyārthatva*)," the phrase "caused by incapacity" means it is produced merely by the poet's lack of ability, and not produced by either conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) or a specific purpose (*prayojana*).
Regarding the phrase "kamale": the face is the agent; the striking with the foot is the object.
Regarding the phrase "by the blow of the foot" (*caraṇāghātena*):
the meaning is "by the word *caraṇāghāta*.
Since metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is accepted even within a sentence, "being conquered" is what is indicated.
And thus, the meaning is that he brought about the state of being surpassed by the lotus.
Now, one might ask: why is the excellence of being surpassed not the intended purpose here?
For it has been shown in various places that the excellence of the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) constitutes the purpose. To this we say: no.

In the case of a secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) that is fit for a poet's usage, the cause [of such usage] is not only the cognition of an obstruction to the primary meaning, but also the cognition of a connection with the intended primary meaning. However, the cognition of a connection based on the possession of a single common property—such as being the object of the speaker’s intention—is not a cause, because it lacks the power of exclusion (*avyāvarttakatvāt*). In the present instance, regarding "conquered" (*nirjita*) as the indicated meaning, the intended connection residing in the face is precisely its being produced by beauty; whereas in the primary meaning, "kicking with the foot," since such beauty is absent in the unreal [face], there is no production of that [beauty], and thus no "conquered-ness."
It is simply not perceived.

Consequently, because that [excellence] is not perceived, this definition is known to be unfit for use by poets; thus, due to its lack of credibility, the purpose—which is the excellence of the expressed meaning—is indeed not perceived. This is the intended sense.
For example—
“O lotus-faced one, your face has dealt a kick to the lotus.

Here, by means of the "kick," the state of being conquered is indicated. This is the fault of *nihatārthatva* (obscured meaning), because there is the employment of a word with two meanings in a sense that is not commonly established.
For example:
"Yamunā spread out the sky as Śambara.
The word *śambara* is well-known [in this context] as referring to a Daitya.
But here, in the water, the meaning is "destroyed.
*Vijñapriyā*:
"Destroyed" (*nihatā*).
He spread the water of the Yamunā across the sky—that is, it pervaded the atmosphere; for the lexicon states, "ambu and śambu [mean] water.

Regarding the word *atra*—it should not be argued that because of the specific neuter gender-form, only water is understood [by the word *ambaram*], for such a restriction applies only in cases where the meanings are equally well-known.

In this case, however, by virtue of common usage (*prasiddhi*), even without considering the indicative mark (*liṅga*), one first relies on the mere word for its presentation; yet, because the understanding of the connection and the indicative mark occurs only subsequently, the cognition of water arises later, as in the expression "he lends his ear to songs.
Here, the verbal root *dā* preceded by the prefix *ā-* is not expressive of the sense of "giving" (*dāna*).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ta) "Non-expressive" means being prompted by an error regarding [the word's] expressive power (*śakti*).
It takes up and it gives;
here, since the root *ghas* has multiple meanings, it certainly possesses the capacity for both giving and taking.
However, because the prefix *āṅ* merely obstructs the cognition of "giving," one should not ask how there could be a misconception of capacity regarding that which is [actually] capable.

Because it is cumbersome to assume that a prefix functions as an obstacle by introducing the concept of being the counter-positive of an absence that serves as a causal condition, it is more appropriate to hold that the verbal root *dā* alone— devoid of the prefix *āṅ*— possesses the power (*śakti*) for the act of giving. As for the perception of a general power expressed in the rule "the root *ḍudāñ* [means] giving," that is merely an error regarding its power.
However, in the case of the *neyārtha* [provisional meaning], there is no error because the seed of error is absent; this is the distinction.

Therefore, by including the qualification "provided there is no error regarding the capacity (*śakti*)" in the definition of *neyārtha*, there is no confusion [with *lakṣaṇā*]. Furthermore, in the case of a non-expressive word, since there is an intention toward the intended meaning due to an error regarding its capacity, the indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—which consists in that intention—indeed possesses the capacity to convey the intended meaning.

Therefore, because it brings about the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, this [defect] does not incur the status of a "sentence-meaning defect" (vākyārtha-doṣa), unlike those [defects] such as the meaningless (*nirarthaka*), the unexpressive (*asamartha*), and the corruptly formed (*cyutasaṃskāra*).

This is because the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is produced from a collection of words that have been separated [from their original context], either through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or by way of producing the comprehension of its own sentence-meaning which in turn generates the comprehension of the [intended] sentence-meaning.
However, this secondary indication is not "forced interpretation" (*neyārtha*).
Furthermore, it should be understood that [the fault] is not applicable to the usage of poets.
However, since the triad of faults beginning with the "meaningless" (nirarthaka) cannot possibly be faults of the sentence (*vākya*), they must be excluded [from this category].
— *Locanā* —
In this context, [the prefix] *ava-* does not signify "giving," because its meaning is "grasping";
according to the maxim: "The meaning of a verbal root is forcibly led elsewhere by a prefix."
Or for example:
"When you, O Conqueror, have arrived, even the night shrouded in darkness [is as if] day.
Here, the word *dinam* (day) is non-expressive (*avācaka*) with respect to the sense of "that which consists of light."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, tha) Or as it is said: "When you have arrived, even the night, though shrouded in darkness, is a day for me. The meaning is: "for me," it is full of light.

Regarding the phrase "even though covered by darkness" (*dhvāntacchannāpi*), the particle *api* indicates that what is being made known as the opposite of being covered by darkness is precisely the state of consisting of light (*prakāśamayatva*), and not the state of being day (*dinatva*).
This is because a day covered by clouds does not possess the opposite quality [of darkness].
Furthermore, since a day is generally observed to consist of light even in this case, the delusion regarding its power (*śaktibhrama*) occurs precisely on the basis of that [luminosity].
Locanā: (Lo, Ai) "Day" means until the setting of the sun.

The meaning is that it is specifically a particular period of time delimited by that pleasure which is denoted by the word "day," and not its inseparable concomitant, the state of being composed of light.
The difficulty lies in the fact that the comprehension of the meaning is mediated, as for example:
“Clear [are the waters] that are the birthplace of the inhabitants of the Milk Ocean.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, da) Regarding "affliction" (*kliṣṭatvam*)—and obstruction is of two kinds.

In some cases, when a specific meaning is not perceived due to the force of a connected connection (*anvitānvaya*), there is a temporal intervention (*kālikavyavadhāna*); in other cases, however, there is an intervention consisting of non-proximity (*anāsatti*). Of these, he illustrates the first type as residing within a word with the example: “kṣīrodajāvasatijanmabhuvaḥ.”
The commentary on this is contained within the *vṛtti* itself.
As for the separation consisting of non-proximity (*anāsatti*), he will provide an example under the faults of sentence (*vākya-doṣa*).
Here, "born from the milk-ocean" refers to Lakṣmī; her abode is the lotus; and the waters are the birthplace of that [lotus].
Locanā:
Even the line beginning with "kṣīrodaja" (o lo) is a *pada*,
because it is a compound (*samasta*).
“May the Lord of Bhavānī be for our prosperity.
Here, the word *bhavānīśa* causes a contradictory cognition because it suggests a husband other than Bhavānī. *Vijñapriyā*: [This is an example of the fault of] "causing a contradictory cognition."
(vi, dha) "Contradictory" means that the essence [of this figure] consists in the manifestation of censure toward the person being praised by virtue of its connection with something else. However,
the distinction from "inappropriate meaning" (*anucitārtha*) is that the latter occurs even without such a connection to something else.

Regarding this: because the meaning of the word *pati* (husband) is construed with the meaning of the word *bhavānī*—which is established in the sense of "the wife of Bhava"—there arises the perception of a paramour (*upapati*), just as in the expression "the husband of Caitra’s wife. Thus, there is no censure [of the term].
Locanā:
the word *bhavānī*, in the sense of "the wife of Bhava," ends in the suffix *ān* according to the *nadādi* group.
The state of being subordinate due to the absence of reflection upon the predicate is the defect known as *avimṛṣṭavidheyāṃśatva* (the failure to clearly indicate the predicate).
For example:
"What is the use of these arms, which are vainly swollen from plundering the petty village of heaven?"
In this case, "futility" (*vṛthātva*) is the predicate; however, because it is subordinated within the compound, it causes the impression that it is merely being restated (*anuvādya*).
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, na) Regarding the term *avimṛṣṭa*—its essence is the failure to produce the cognition of something as being the predicate (*vidheya*) due to the specific nature of its co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*). And that [co-occurrence] is witnessed by the cognition itself; it has not already passed away.
For instance, when the predicate falls within another compound—other than a *bahuvrīhi*—without the previously specified predicate being present, [the fault arises].
In the case of a non-compound, however, when the predicate precedes the subject, there is likewise that [defect].
Therein, he provides an example of the lack of clarity regarding the predicate within a *karmadhāraya* compound: "svarga... and so forth.
This is an utterance of despair by Rāvaṇa, whose Laṅkā was surrounded by Rāma’s army.
The meaning is "by way of plundering.

In this context, the swelling of the arms is already established; now, their futility is being asserted. Therefore, with the swelling as the subject (*uddeśya*), futility is the predicate (*vidheya*).

The meaning is that this [quality] remains unconsidered here because it occurs within a *karmadhāraya* compound. However, in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the predicate previously indicated is perceived precisely as a predicate.

For example, in the phrase "the body of Virūpākṣa," the deformity of the eye; in "the lip with its color rubbed away," the state of being rubbed away from the color; and in "Citragu" (the one with brindled cows), the brindling of the cows—all these predicates are universally recognized as being perceived precisely as predicates.
It is true that in a *karmadhāraya* compound, when the predicate (*vidheya*) falls [into the compound], there is no such deliberation; however,
this is so provided that the predicate is connected with the subject (*uddeśya*),
as will be illustrated later.

In the verse "Like the sixth arrow of the five-arrowed one," the quality of being "sixth" (*ṣaṣṭhatva*), which is the predicate (*vidheya*) connected to the subject (*uddeśya*) "arrow," is *avimṛṣṭa* (unconsidered).
However, where the predicate connects with the delimiting property of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), there is no fault, because it is experienced as being perceived precisely as a predicate.

For example, in the phrase "He is extremely learned in these [subjects]," the predicate "extremely" (*atyanta*) connects specifically with "learning" (*pāṇḍitya*), which is the delimiting property of the subject; thus, it is perceived precisely as a predicate.

Likewise, in the phrase “nitāntasundarīkāntā” (beloved of one who is exceedingly beautiful), it is the quality of being "excessive" (*nitāntatva*) that is connected with beauty—just as in the verse: “How can your heart be so hard toward this soft form, which is enjoyed without cruelty? Indeed, its bond is like that of a *śirīṣa* flower.”

"In this case, it is an empirical fact that there is a cognition of 'cruelty'—which is construed with the delimitor of the object of reference (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*, i.e., 'enjoyment')—as being the very thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*).

And so, in the present instance as well, how could there be a lack of clarity (*avimṛṣṭatva*) regarding 'futility' (*vṛthātva*), which is construed with 'swelling' (*ucchūnatva*) as the delimitor of the object of reference? For the futility in respect to the 'swollen arms' has indeed been stated by the word *kiṃ* (what) itself.
As for what was said by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* regarding the first quarter of this very verse: 'nyakkāro hyayameva me yadaham...'"
In this context, he illustrates the fault of "lack of clarity regarding the predicate" (*vidheyāvimarśa*) as it occurs within a sentence.

It has been stated here that in the phrase *caraṇe*, only the swelling (*ucchūnatva*) is the subject of the restatement (*anuvādya*), and not that which is qualified by futility (*vṛthātva*); by this, the fault of lack of clarity regarding the predicate is demonstrated in relation to the predicate itself.

In the context of demonstrating defects in a sentence, it was unnecessary to demonstrate defects occurring within compounds, since examples of such defects were already shown in the passage beginning with “mūrddhāmudvṛttakṛttā.
However, by way of incidental discussion, only the defect of *abhavanmatayoga* (non-connection of intended meaning) has been demonstrated here.
For instance, in the act of plundering heaven, only swelling (*ucchūnatva*) is produced, not futility (*vṛthātva*), nor is there swelling qualified by futility.

Since the state of being "vainly swollen" (*vṛthocchūnatva*) arises precisely from Rāma's siege of Laṅkā, there is no connection between the act of plundering and the "vain swelling" through the relation of being a generator; thus, the fault of *abhavanmatayoga* (non-connection of the intended meaning) has indeed been demonstrated. Now, it might be asked: "Is the fault of *abhavanmatayoga* restricted solely to the sentence as a whole? To this he replied: "How so? [and proceeded to explain].

It should be stated that "its occurrence is in a single compound word," because since a compound possesses both the status of being a word (*pada*) and a sentence (*vākya*), the intended meaning is the absence of its occurrence in non-compounded words.
Thus, since the defect of *avimṛṣṭavidheyāṃśatva* (an undiscerned predicate) does not exist here at all, he provides another example.
Locanā:
(lo, a) "Futility" [is implied] here;
because in a compound, specifically a *tatpuruṣa* compound, [the subordinate element] becomes secondary (*guṇībhāva*).

This is the intended meaning: in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, because the final member alone possesses predominance (*prādhānya*), the fault known as *avimṛṣṭavidheyāṃśa* (an undiscerned predicate) arises, since the preceding member *vṛthā*—which is the element to be predicated—is not indicated with predominance.
For "non-discernment" indeed consists in the failure to indicate [the predicate] with predominance.
Here, the intention of the speaker, the Ten-faced One (*Daśamukha*), is this: "That swelling of my arms which existed formerly has now become useless."
Thus, because the futility (*vṛthātva*) intended to be predicated is subordinated within the compound, it is perceived as a mere restatement (*anuvādyatva*).
Consequently, since the swelling of the arms is not futile in the preceding context, only the inferiority of the arms is understood, and not the excellence of the flinging of the arms.
This should be understood likewise in the subsequent examples as well.
Or, for example:
"Even the *rākṣasas* are unable to stand before my younger brother Rāma.
Here, it should have been stated as "Rāma's" (*rāmasya*).
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
pa) Or, as in the phrase "even the *rākṣasas*," here the meaning is that by the intonation (*kāku*) of shaking one's head, it signifies they are not even able to stand before him.

In this context, since this sense of "I" (ahaṅkāra) arises solely from its connection with Rāma, the connection with Rāma—which is indicated by the genitive case—is omitted in the *tatpuruṣa* compound; consequently, there is a lack of explicit reflection upon the connection with Rāma as the predicate (*vidheya*). However, if the genitive were present, there would be no such fault; thus he says: "In this [context]," etc. (*Locanā*).
(Lo, ā) He shows other examples for the purpose of pervading the entire scope [of the definition] with the words "the Rākṣasas," etc.
This is the speech of Lakṣmaṇa.
"Of Rāma," etc.
Indeed, its primacy does not belong to that [word] alone, but rather to that which is connected with Rāma;
as for example:
"āsamudrakṣitīśānām" (of the lords of the earth as far as the ocean).
In this case, it should be stated as "not reaching the ocean.
Or, for example: "Wherever you fall, O fair-browed one..."
"The side-glance is like a sixth arrow of the five-arrowed one.
Here, "as if it were a sixth" is the poetic fancy (utprekṣā).
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, pha) "Or as in..."—here, there is no clear discernment (*avimarśa*) of the predicate (*vidheya*), namely "extending to the edge of the ocean," within the compound.
He provides an example of the lack of discernment of the predicate conjoined with the subject (*uddeśya*) in a *karmadhāraya* compound: "Or as in... where you... (*yathā vā yatra te*).
That which is to be imagined (*utprekṣyam*) is the predicate by way of poetic fancy (*utprekṣayā*).
Locanā:

Regarding the phrase "the sixth" (*ṣaṣṭha*), the meaning is that it is improper to place the word *ṣaṣṭha*—which is intended here as the object of a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*)—in the first position within a *tatpuruṣa* compound.

The sense is that its status as the predicate (*vidheya*) alone is appropriate; it is not proper to convey it as a subject (*anuvādya*) through the function of a subordinate element (*guṇībhūta*) by means of a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
Or as it is said:
"O Lord, formerly she was not separated from you even for a moment."

Regarding the phrase "not liberated" (*amukta*) here, since the negative particle (*nañ*) functions as a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), it is appropriate that [the state of being liberated] is indeed what is to be enjoined (*vidheya*).
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ba) provides an example even within a *nañ*-compound: "not liberated" (*amukta*).

"Being a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (non-presuppositional negation)" means: having "presupposed" (*prasajya*)—that is, having brought to mind—the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) without using a compound, it is a negation; the meaning is that it is an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). And since, in this case, it is precisely the absence of liberation (*mocana*) that is to be enjoined (*vidheya*), it is appropriate to convey that status [of being a *prasajya-pratiṣedha*] only through a non-compound; thus he says: "It is indeed appropriate that it be the object of injunction. However, in the case of a compound, because there is the cognition of being different from that [the counter-correlative], it is merely an *paryudāsa* (exclusionary negation). For in that case, the negation of the enjoined object is not cognized; such is the sense of the statement "there is no consideration of that."
As they say:
"Where the injunction is subordinate and the negation is primary,
such that the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with the action, that is *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (non-presuppositional negation)."
Locanā: (Lo, ī) To the question, "What is this *prasajya-pratiṣedha*? he says: "It is the lack of predominance.
This refers to cases where there is no predominance of the positive injunction (*vidhi*), as in examples such as "He protected himself, being fearless."

As in the example just mentioned, beginning with "navajaladhara," where negation is predominant—whether by means of a verb explicitly stated or one to be supplied, such as *asti* or *bhavati*—there arises the application of *paryudāsa* (exclusion) due to the attainment of the status and requirements of *paryudāsa*;
for example:
"This is a fresh rain-cloud equipped [for battle], not a haughty night-stalker."

However, in the case of the *tatpuruṣa* compound illustrated above, because the negative particle (*nañ*) functions as a *paryudāsa* (exclusion), there is no apprehension of the negation as that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*), since it has become subordinate (*guṇībhāva*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
Only in the case of a non-compound (*asamāsa*) does the meaning of the negative particle possess primacy in the form of being the object of injunction.

Regarding the fact that the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is subordinate and that in such cases the negative particle (*nañ*) expresses a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (a non-implicative negation), he provides corroboration with the words "aprādhānyam" (subordination).
The meaning is: of the counter-positive, which is the positive entity (*bhāva*).
Due to the absence of a compound, there is predominance (*pradhānatā*) in the negation, which is the meaning of *nañ*.
The ellipsis "it is understood as being subordinate" is to be supplied.

To the question, "What kind of usage constitutes such a state?", he says: "by means of a verb"—for instance, in cases such as *na pacati* ("he does not cook"), there is no compound with the verbal action (*ākhyāta-kriyā*);
by the term "by means of a verb," it is precisely the absence of a compound that is indicated.
And thus, the meaning is that [this occurs] where there is no compound (*asamāsa*) with the negative particle (*nañ*).

For this very reason, although here the negative particle is associated with an independent action (*muktakriyā*), because there is no compound, it does not constitute a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation).
Likewise, in the case of "navajaladhara" (new cloud) as well, even though the negative particle is not associated with an action, because there is no compound, it constitutes a *prasajya-pratiṣedha*.
But regarding the word *amukta*, he states that it does not possess that same character because of its being a compound (*samāsa*), saying: "In the example cited, however...
Since its status as such is not understood due to the force of the compound, it is indeed a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion).
As they say:
“That in which the affirmation is primary and the negation is secondary is to be known as a *paryudāsa* (exclusion), where the negative particle is connected with the following word.”
In the passage beginning with "Vijñapriyā: (vi, ma)," he states the corroboration with the words "yadāhuḥ" (as they say).
Here, "primacy" (*pradhānatva*) refers to being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*), by virtue of it being a *tatpuruṣa* compound in which the final member is predominant.

The meaning is that when there is a negation of an absence that serves as the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), the negative particle (*nañ*) is subordinate; by virtue of the compound, its subordination consists in the fact that its status as something to be enjoined is not perceived.
He shows such a case with the words "where [it occurs] in the subsequent member" (*uttarapade*);
and here, "member" (*pada*) refers to the position [within the compound].

The meaning is that where the negative particle (*nañ*) stands in the position immediately following the word denoting the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), that is to say, when it follows the subsequent member [of a compound], one should understand it as an *apavāda* (exclusion) by way of non-compounding (*asamāsa*).
However, in the case of "he does not cook" (*na pacati*), because the negative particle occurs after the subsequent element, it is not an *apavāda*.

The following point must be noted here: since a compound cannot occur when the negative particle (*nañ*) follows the word denoting the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), the rule "where [the negative] follows," etc., signifies that exclusion by negation (*paryudāsa*) occurs only within a compound.

Otherwise, because the negative particle would be an exclusion even in cases such as *na pacati* ("he does not cook") and *na dṛptaniśācaraḥ* ("not a haughty night-stalker"), where the negative particle has fallen before the other member, the rule "where [the negative] follows," etc., would result in mere nonsense.

Although it is established that even when not occurring within a compound, "ghaṭo na" (there is no jar) is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), whereas that which is not in a compound and connects with a verb is a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), this must nevertheless be understood as a fixed rule.

For even in a compound, that which connects with a verbal action ending in a *kṛt* suffix is an exclusion; thus, the term "not compounded" (*asamasta*) is an adverbial qualifier [of the action], and in a compound, there is only exclusion.
Furthermore, in that case, there is a requirement for expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatā*) following that [exclusion] through a distinction [between the two].
Therefore—“Fearless, he protected himself; free from illness, he practiced dharma;
ungreedy, he acquired wealth; and unattached, he experienced happiness.”

In this case, since the concealment of one's own self and so forth is to be enjoined by restating fearlessness and the like, it is appropriate that the negative particle (*nañ*) functions as a *paryudāsa* (exclusion), thereby becoming subordinate.

[The author] shows an example of the term "Vijñapriyā" (Vi, Ya)— namely, "jugopa"— and explains that when the negative particle is a *paryudāsa*, its meaning is not perceived as being the thing to be enjoined within the compound.

In the phrase "it is joined" (*yukta*), it has been established that there is indeed no consideration of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) as the primary element; [this is] because its non-primary status is evident right here in this very example, just as in cases such as "he protected himself as the primary one" (*jugopātmānam pradhānatvam*). *Locanā*: (Lo, u) Regarding "the state of being primary"—the state of being primary [is absent], just as in examples like "he protected himself as the primary one," where non-primacy is present in this very illustration.
"Here" means "in the first member [of the compound]," such as in *atrastata* and so forth; it does not refer to the second member, but rather to the first member.
Regarding the word *amukta*, the remainder of the sense is that this applies even when the negative particle (*nañ*) subsequently enters into another compound.

If it is argued that, just as in cases such as "a Brāhmaṇa who eats from the hands of one who lacks faith" (*aśrāddhabhojī brāhmaṇaḥ*) or "the king's wives who do not see the sun" (*asūryampaśyā rājadārāḥ*), there is likewise a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation) in the case of "not liberated" (*amuktāḥ*), we say no.
For even here, a term can be said to be an absolute negation only if the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with a component of action, such as eating;
however, that is not the case here. This is because the negative particle is connected with the agent—the primary factor—as the qualifier of that which is to be eaten.
Locanā: (lo, ū) In the aspect of the activity consisting of the sight of food; "by the agent-aspect" means—
Because the suffix *ṇini* is prescribed after a verbal root when the agent (*kartṛ*) is the object denoted by the affix, [the term *aśrāddhabhojī*] is derived from that [agent].

If the negative particle (*nañ*) were connected to the action-component (*kriyāṃśa*), then it would indeed be a prohibitive negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), according to the rule: "Where the negative particle is connected with an action. However, in this case, because the negative particle is connected only with the agent-component—as in "one who is other than a person whose habit is eating at śrāddhas"—it is exclusively an exclusionary negation (*paryudāsa*).

The phrase "for the purpose of not being eaten" (*abhojya-arthena*) should be understood as an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*), implying also "for the purpose of not being seen" (*adarśya-arthena*).
As they say:
"For it is understood that the performer [of the rite] is one whose habit is to eat at a *śrāddha* feast."
But that is not merely a matter of food, according to the injunctions regarding the ritual knife (kartarī).
Thus [it is said].
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ra) one who eats the food of those lacking faith.

In the compound *asūryampaśyāḥ*, even though it is a compound, we observe the cognition of two things: the absence of eating at a *śrāddha* and the absence of seeing the sun, both of which take the form of a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation).

On the basis of that example, one raises the objection—starting with "But surely" (*nanu*)—that in the case of *amuktaḥ* as well, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the negation in the form of the absence of liberation being itself the thing enjoined (*vidheya*).
"If it is argued that [the negative particle] conveys a restriction," [we reply:
the rule that a negation is exclusively a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (non-presuppositional negation) applies only when it is connected with a verb.

If, in the case of these two words *akṣodhra* and *adṛkṣat*, the meaning of the negative particle were connected with the actions of "eating" and "seeing," only then would such a restriction be possible.

He states that there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) between those two in that case with the words "nor is it so. If one asks, "In what case, then, is there concomitance? he replies, "by way of being the qualificand" (*viśeṣyatayā*).

The meaning is that the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with the meaning of the negative particle only together with the aspect of the agent in the form of "one who eats," which is presented by the two *kṛt* suffixes prescribed for the agent.
To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of the suffix *ṇini* [denoting] the agent.
It should be understood that, by way of illustration, the phrase "in the sense of one who eats" (*bhojyārthena*) also implies "by the aspect of being the agent of seeing" (*darśanakartraṃśena*).

Since the agent is presented by the *kṛt* suffix, in the expression "one who eats at a *śrāddha*" (*śrāddhabhojī*), only the agent of eating is perceived; regarding this, he provides corroboration by citing what they say: "In the case of 'eating at a *śrāddha*,' etc."

It should also be understood that here, by the very suffix of the *kṛt* participle, even the king’s wives are perceived as the agents of seeing. Thus, the meaning is that for those two [the king’s wives and the Śūdra] as well, there is the state of being distinct from both the Śrāddha-eaters and the non-seers of the sun; in this way, only a *paryudāsa* (exclusion) is perceived. Furthermore, having in mind that the *paryudāsa* nature of the negative particle (*nañ*) within a compound is established by the example of "not seen" (*adṛṣṭa*) in the compound, one should consider that in the word "unreleased" (*amukta*), there is only a slight difference from the word "eater" (*bhojī*).
He demonstrates the distinction [from other systems].
Locanā:
Regarding this point, he cites the consensus of the masters (*ācāryasammati*), saying "as they say."
In this context, regarding the phrase "one who eats at an aśrāddha," it refers merely to that act of eating;
"merely eating at an aśrāddha" is the intended meaning.
The word "connection" (sambandha) is followed by the understood term "is intended" (abhimata).

In this case, however, even if one accepts the meaning of *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation) with respect to the requirement for connection with an action, based on the view of the author of the Bhāṣya and others,

a compound is simply not possible in examples such as *amukta* because of the primacy of the action alone. Furthermore, in the case of *amuktā*, since there is a connection only with the action, it remains a defect.
Vijñapriyā:
Regarding the phrase "amukta" [in the verse], the word "tu" (but) applies here;
however, in the case of "abhojī," the connection with the agent occurs within the compound.
In the case of *amukta* (unreleased), however, the distinction is merely that the connection occurs with the action itself as situated within the compound;

the point is that in both instances, there is indeed a *paryudāsa* (exclusion). Even though the agent is presented in the connection "he does not cook" (*na pacati*) or "he does not sleep" (*na nidrāti*), the connection is only with the actions of sleeping and cooking. Thus, even in the absence of a formal rule, by virtue of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) connects specifically with the agent in those cases.
If this is argued, we say no;
for such an intention (tātparya) is simply absent there.

However, in the case of the cognition "one who does not habitually eat at a *śrāddha* ceremony" (*śrāddhābhojanaśīla*) when applied to a lineage where one habitually eats at a *śrāddha*, even a person who does eat is never perceived [as being excluded]. Therefore, this was stated by the author of the treatise merely through oversight.
A resolution has been made.

We, however, on the basis of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), hold that the word *śrāddha* refers solely to the *śrāddha* rite itself, and it is with respect to that very thing that the negation (*nañ*) is construed.
And likewise, when the sense "one who eats only at a *śrāddha*" is obtained, we say that by the force of the word *mātra*, the meaning "one whose habit is eating at a *śrāddha*" is obtained.
Furthermore, these defects such as being *kliṣṭa* (obscured) and so forth are indeed compound-word (*samāsa*) defects residing within the individual words.
— *Vijñapriyā* —

"And these" means that there are three [types of defects] characterized by being contrary to defilement (*kliṣṭatva*), causing a contradictory understanding (*viruddhamatikṛt*), and having an undiscerned predicate portion (*avimṛṣṭavidheyāṃśa*).
"Only those occurring within a compound" means that these are defects of the word (*pada*) only when they occur in a compound, and not even when they occur outside of a compound.
This is because the defect of being "obscured" (*kliṣṭatva*) due to dependence on the connection of a subsequent element cannot exist within a single word (*pada*) without a compound;
and as for the defect of being "obscured" due to lack of proximity (*anāsatti*), since a compound itself would be impossible in that case, it cannot reside in a word.

Furthermore, a word that causes a contradictory cognition is defective precisely because of its connection with another word-meaning, and a word with an "unclarified predicate-part" (*avimṛṣṭavidheyāṃśa*) consists of two words—one expressing the subject and one the predicate—so it too cannot be a word without a compound.
Regarding the harshness of sound (*duḥśravatva*) in a sentence— as in *Vijñapriyā* (vi,
śa): having demonstrated that these thirteen [faults] reside in individual words (*padagatatva*), he now begins to demonstrate those residing in sentences (*vākyagata*).
Regarding the phrase "as there is unpleasantry in a sentence":
thus, by depending on two words within a single sentence, it constitutes a fault of the sentence (*vākya-doṣa*). *Locanā*.

In the phrase "being afflicted" (*kliṣṭatva*) and so forth, the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) includes "causing a contradictory cognition" (*viruddhamatikṛttva*) and "the state of having an unclarified predicate portion" (*avimṛṣṭavidheyāṃśatva*).

Therefore, although harshness of sound (*śrutikaṭutva*) and other such defects may reside in a single word-part in some instances, they should be understood as belonging to the sentence as a whole because of their wide prevalence.
Example: *"O [beloved], blinded by the pain of passion for you, when shall I attain fulfillment in your absence?"* (Smara-ārtty-andhaḥ kadā lapsye kārttārthyaṃ virahe tava).
Vijñapriyā:
Regarding "by the affliction of love" (*smarārttyā*)—the meaning is "I am blinded by the affliction of love.
Here, because the word *ārttyā* connects with both [the preceding and following] words, namely *ārttyā* and *kārttārthyam*, it constitutes a syntactical fault (*vākyadoṣa*).
A poet who applies his efforts toward another's purpose eats what has already been vomited.
Locanā: (lo, ḷ) activity, endurance.
And the voiding of excrement;
"vomited" means that which has been spat out, and "eaten" means that which has been regurgitated.

Herein lies the indecorousness (*aślīlatā*) that manifests disgust (*jugupsā*). *Vijñapriyā* (vi, sa) states: "The indecorousness of disgust is expressed by the phrase 'having commenced [the act]' (*kṛtapravṛttiḥ*)."
"Regarding another meaning" means regarding a meaning composed by another poet.
Here, there is disgust because the word *pravṛtti* suggests excrement and the word *vānta* denotes that which has been vomited.
In the phrase "by means of a condiment" (*vyañjanena*), the meaning is "by means of producing" (*jananena*).
[For example: "The body is adorned by curved [eyebrows] possessing the redness of rising lotuses."
In this context, the redness of the *kalala* [embryonic stage] is the ruby (*padmarāga*),
and "crooked" refers to those who are perverse;
thus, there is a figurative interpretation (*neyārtha*).
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ha) Having disregarded other faults for the sake of brevity, he states the fault of the *neyārtha* (interpretable meaning) regarding the sentence, beginning with "udyat": by means of the rising, that is, the glowing, redness of the lotuses—which function as rubies (*padmarāga-maṇi*).
The meaning is that [the body] is adorned with women who are crooked and beautiful, serving as ornaments for the body.
Regarding the word "here" (*atra*):
since the literal sense of "body-ornament" is sublated by the redness of the lotus, the word *padmāraga* (ruby) is indicated here as having a meaning equivalent to its synonyms.

The meaning is that by the word *lakṣita* (indicated), the ruby (*padmarāgamaṇi*) is expressed. Nor should it be argued: "Since suffixes convey their own meanings as being connected with the sense of the verbal root (*kṛtyartha*), how can instrumentality (*karaṇatā*) toward the ruby be conveyed here by the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*)? For in such instances, it is accepted that [the suffix] conveys that [instrumentality] even with respect to the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*).
And in the phrase "by those who are crooked" (*vakrābhiḥ*), there is metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the word *vāmā*;
by that [indication], the meaning "woman" is presented.

However, in reality, since there exists the seed of a confusion regarding the expressive power (*śakti*)—namely, the observation of the identity of synonymy between the words *vāmā* and *avakrā*—it is more appropriate here to maintain that [the word] is simply non-expressive (*avācaka*).

“Upon beholding the beauty of Dhammilla’s hair— [the beauty] of that fawn-eyed maiden— whose mind would not take great delight, since it possesses an understanding of a hitherto unprecedented arrangement?”

In this case, the connection— "Whose mind is not captivated upon beholding the beauty of the *dhammilla*?"— is considered *kliṣṭa* (obscure). *Vijñapriyā* explains its obscurity with the words "of the *dhammilla*."
“*Dhammilla* refers to hair tied up; another [scholar] says it is so called because it ‘delights exceedingly’ (*atiśayena rajyati*). The etymology of *bandha* is the arrangement of the hair.
The rest has already been explained in the commentary on the verse.”
"In this [verse], 'For this alone is my humiliation—
that there are enemies,' the intention is that 'this alone' is the predicate (vidheya) of 'humiliation.
However, due to the inversion of word-order, that [predicate] has become subordinate."
Furthermore, the composition of the two words is inverted; this is a fault of the sentence (*vākya-doṣa*).
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, kha) states that the status of the predicate (*vidheya*) has not been clearly discerned, saying: "In the word *nyakkāraḥ*..."
"Arrangement of words" (śabdaracanā) means that the word expressing the predicate (vidheya) is mentioned prior to the word expressing the subject (uddeśya);
the sense is that this follows the rule: "One should not utter the predicate without having first stated the subject."
For this very reason, the expression "the mountain possesses fire" (*vahnimān parvata*) is not employed.

Now, one might object: "If there is a fault due to the placement of the word denoting the predicate (*vidheya*) first, it is more appropriate that this be considered a 'word-fault' (*pada-doṣa*"; to this, [the author] says: "and the composition," as noted in the *Locanā*.
Regarding the term *nyakkāra* (insult): this is the intended meaning.

According to the principle that a property (*dharma*) is enjoined with reference to a subject (*dharmī*), it is proper to first restate the subject and subsequently specify the property to be enjoined; thus, *nyakkāra* should have been mentioned last.
When the order is reversed, it constitutes the fault known as *avimṛṣṭavidheyāṃśa* (an indistinctly expressed predicate).

For this very reason, they say that when one ought to say "sound is impermanent" (*śabdo 'nityaḥ*), the statement "impermanence is sound" (*anityaḥ śabdaḥ*) constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
To explain how there is a fault in the sentence here, he says: "by the arrangement" (*racanā*).

This is because, having first pointed out the word *padadvayasya* (of the two words), the word *viparītatāyām* (in the case of reversal) follows; and subsequently, the word *nyakkāraḥ* (defeat) is mentioned before the word that was intended to follow it.
Furthermore, because this defect is so widespread, it is considered a defect of the sentence (*vākya-doṣa*).

In this case, however, the defect follows strictly the presence and absence of the single word "ājaghne" alone; since the defect remains even when other words are substituted, it is indeed a word-level defect (*padadoṣa*).
Thus, as in this instance, even if the middle-voice ending (*ātmanepada*) were changed, there would be no word-level defect.
Likewise, this applies to the verbal root *han* as well; thus, there is no fault regarding a portion of a word.
Locanā:
In the case of *ājaghne*, it is not the entire word that is incapable of being substituted.

Its conformity with positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), however, is established because there is no fault in using the words *ājaghāna* ("struck") and *prajahāra* ("seized") as synonyms for that [meaning].

Having thus demonstrated how the middle voice following the root *han* conforms to the conditions that render it defective, [the author] states— beginning with "Just as here," etc.— that the root *han* preceding that middle voice is likewise [defective], in order to prevent the objection that this constitutes a defect of the entire word (*pada*).
Because it constitutes a fault through the combination of base and suffix, it is indeed a word-fault (*padadoṣa*), not a partial-word-fault (*padāṃśadoṣa*); this is the meaning.

This is what must be noted here:

for if, according to the aforementioned principle, it is stated that even multiple defects such as *aprayuktatva* (unconventionality) are defects belonging solely to the word, then how is it that in examples such as *smārārttyandhaḥ*, those [defects] are cited as being located within the sentence (*vākyagata*)?
Or how is it that meaninglessness (*nirarthakatva*), loss of grammatical refinement (*cyutasaṃskṛtatva*), and lack of capacity (*asamarthatva*) alone are excluded from the defects of a sentence?
For it would be equally appropriate to exclude unidiomatic usage (*aprayuktatva*), non-expressiveness (*avācakatva*), and so forth, as well.

If you argue that these are cited as defects of a sentence because they depend upon multiple words situated within a single sentence, then the statement of the principle shown [by you] regarding what constitutes a defect of a word alone would be nothing more than the idle chatter of a drunkard.
Furthermore, it is impossible for the three [defects]—meaninglessness and so forth—to depend upon a single word situated within a single sentence, as in: "He goes along the beautiful path;
may Hari purify you."
Regarding the phrase "it kills" (*hanti*) in another sense— as in "the righteous man now kills the Gaṅgā"—
therefore, because a collection of words composed of such terms characterized by these three defects does not produce verbal cognition, its status as a sentence (*vākyatva*) is impossible.

As for the reason why these three are excluded from the defects of a sentence, that cause should be understood as we have shown it in the course of explaining the defect of non-expressiveness (*avācakatva*).
Locanā:
(lo, ai) "Prākṛta, etc."— here, "refinement" (*saṃskāra*) is characterized solely by the grammatical analysis of the aphorisms (*sūtra*),
based on the etymological derivation that "it is refined by this."
The phrase from the verse beginning with "Some [faults] are... connects, by way of the *kākākṣi-golaka* (crow's eye) maxim, with the sentence beginning with "meaningless" (*nirarthaka*).

Thus, the meaninglessness is as follows: in the example "A flow of waters like that of the *surasindhu*," since the intended sense is already conveyed by the word *surasindhoḥ* alone, the suffix *-aṇ* is meaningless.
Thus, since the meaning is already conveyed by the form *vanakariṇām* alone, the suffix *ya* is employed in *vanyakariṇām*.
Similarly, in the phrase "tadīyamātaṅgaghaṭāvighaṭṭitaiḥ," the suffix *iya* is used;

In the phrase *padaparam*, the word *param* serves to exclude the mere sentence [as the locus of the defect].

Now, one might object: in the example "the slender-waisted woman strikes the bower" (*kuñjaṃ hanti kṛśodarī*), since the verbal root *han* itself cannot tolerate the transposition [of its elements], the defect resides only in a part of the word (*padāṃśa*); how then can it be said to reside in the word (*pada*)?

To this it is replied: because a separate status of residing in the word is generally not observed for the state of being semantically incompetent (*asamarthatva*). For the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) convey their respective meanings.

Thus, disregarding the view that a word must be employed as a complete, integrated unit (*samuditam padam*), and adhering instead to the opinion that [meaning] resides in the individual word, it was stated that in the case of *hanti*, the defect resides in the word itself.

For this very reason, the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* also said: "Setting aside those defects of corrupted grammar (*cyutasaṃskāra*), semantic incompetence (*asamartha*), and meaninglessness (*nirarthaka*), these same defects exist in a sentence (*vākya*) as well, and some of them even in a portion of a word (*padasyāṃśe*)."
Thus, this sūtra was stated under the heading of examples of defects in parts of words (*padāṃśa-doṣa*), even though it concerns incapacity (*asamarthatva*).

Although words such as *dina* (day) and *śoṇita* (blood) can tolerate substitution (*parivṛtti-sahatva*), because the expressive forms and the expressed meanings that convey the primary nature of the substratum (*dharmī*) lack such a quality, [defects] such as non-expressiveness (*avācakatva*) are said to reside in the word (*pada-gata*).
For this very reason, in the *Alaṅkāra*: "O fair-eyed one!"... [etc.]
Although there is no tautology in the phrase "nayane vidhehi," *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration) has been mentioned [there].
Here, however, when words are not used at all, it is "incapacity" (*asamarthatva*); when they are used rarely, it is "obscured meaning" (*nihatārthatva*).
The state of having a redundant meaning (*nihatārthatva*) pertains to words that possess multiple meanings.

*Vijñapriyā* (vi, da): Now, even though the mutual distinctions among the aforementioned defects are possible by following the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) already shown, he states another distinction with the words "of words" (*iva śabdānām*).
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that there is a mutual distinction between words, such as those that are "incapable" (*asamartha*) and so forth.
In the phrase "of words," the meaning is "of defective words.
Regarding the expression "in every respect there is an absence of usage," the ellipsis (*śeṣa*) is that this occurs "without" the specific auxiliary factor residing in the term *jaṅghāpaddhati*.

"Viraleti"—it refers to a state where multiple meanings, both well-known and obscure, are the object [of the word]. The meaning is that the fault of *nihatārthatva* (obscure meaning) occurs when there is sparse usage. —Locanā.
In every respect, there is an absence of usage; for this very reason, it is not counted among the defects of a sentence.
Since such a lapse is extremely rare even when occurring occasionally, it constitutes the defect of "obscured meaning" (*nihatārthatva*) in the case of rare usage.
Therefore, they say: "The unused (*aprayukta*) and the obscured (*nihatārtha*) are not defective in cases such as *śleṣa* (punning)."

Unpopularity (*apratītatva*), however, is the absence of universal usage even for a word that has a single meaning; it pertains to a word whose meaning is already established but which is not employed [in common practice]. *Vijñapriyā*: [This is the definition of unpopularity.]
(vi, dha) He states the distinction between that which is incapable and that which is not employed: "the state of being unemployed.
Regarding the phrase "a word with multiple meanings," here "word" refers to a verbal root (*dhātu*).
Incapacity refers to the domain of words with multiple meanings.

In cases of incapacity, even verbs such as *han* (to kill) are recorded as having the sense of "going," while verbs such as *div* (to play) have the sense of "shining" and so forth when they are incapable [of their primary meaning].

the first meaning is exclusively technical (*śāstrīya*) because its cause is unestablished,
whereas the second, though possible, is merely worldly (*laukika*).
Likewise, even a worldly meaning that is inappropriate [for the context] is not distinct from that [fault], because words such as *apaśu* (non-cow) are applied through superimposition (*āropita*).
Thus, the faults of the sentence that belong to the same class as the faults of the word have been stated;
now, those belonging to a different class are being stated:

Since whatever defect exists in a word (*pada*) is also present in a sentence, there is a similarity of kind (*sajātīyatā*) between them.
"Because it does not reside in that, it is of a different genus from it.
Locanā:
(lo, a) Now he states the verse which demonstrates the distinction of the sentence faults about to be discussed from those immediately preceding—namely, "In this way," etc.

The faults of words (*padadoṣas*), such as harshness of sound (*śrutikaṭutva*) and the like, belong to both [word and sentence] because they reside in both; thus they pertain to the sentence alone, and not—like harshness of sound and so on—to the word, its parts, and the sentence. "The discordance of phonemes, the elision of *visarga*, and its improper placement..."

"Excessive words," "deficient words," and "repeated words" refer to three defects.

There are another three defects: non-occurrence of the *ma* sound (*abhavan-ma-sambandhatā*), lack of sequence (*akramatā*), and having an unintended secondary meaning (*amataparārthatā*).
Finally, there are two defects: the misplaced insertion of words (*padasamāsayoḥ*) and their placement in an improper position (*asthāne nyāsaḥ*).
Incompatibility (*pratikūlatva*) refers to the discordance between the colors (*varṇa*) and the sentiments (*rasa*).

She releases [tears], she does not laugh, she gazes at him in her heart,

She rolls about, turning face downwards;

She delights us with her agitated heart; she falls away from shame and breaks her steadfastness.

That in which the *visargas* have been struck and have attained the state of *otva* (the sound *o*),

"In some places" (*kvacit*) means in certain instances;

And this has been refuted by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*. He says:

“Vṛkodara spoke these words to the king”; “Kautsa, having set out, addressed these words”; “The daughter of the mountain king uttered this speech. “It was said by the elephant among ascetics.”

The justification for this is as follows: the production of speech is twofold—namely, the striking together of the throat, palate, and so forth, and the verbal expression produced by that, which is the meaning.
In that context, when used in the sense of the verbal expression itself, the form *vācam* is not employed.
However, when the root is used in the sense of striking the throat, palate, and so forth, the employment of *vācam* as its object is indeed appropriate.
Furthermore, the objection that the word *vācam* is redundant is also valid;
for if the verbal root *vac* has the meaning of "speaking," then *vācam* would be a mere repetition.
For the state of being a tautology itself entails the fault of superfluous words (*adhikapadatva*), as in the example: "red in the form of a sprout" (*pallavākṛtiraktā*). — *Locanā* —
(Lo, ī) [The word] *sadāśiva* does not convey any further specific meaning beyond what has already been understood;

[As it is said: "If my gaze is fixed upon me, then what is the use of my being Indra?"

The soldiers—the people assembled in the army—whose lances were held aloft, ate (jakṣuḥ) lotus stalks (visaṃ); that is, they consumed them.
Here, it is implied that there is the fault of "repetition of a word" (*kathitapadatva*) regarding the word *bisa*.

*Hatavṛtta*— even if it follows the formal definition, it is unpleasant to hear (*aśravya*), discordant with the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), and lacks a heavy syllable at the end where a light syllable is required.
In sequence, for example:
"Alas! The enraged God of Love constantly pierces his heart. "O proud one, toward me!"
"Do not harbor pride.

(vi, va) Having categorized the types of "killed" (hata) word-meanings, he describes the threefold "killed" meter with the words "hatavṛttam.

Nevertheless, there is indeed adherence to the metrical characteristics of the *gāhā* verse, namely "paḍhamaṃ vāradamatta."
He states the meter that is not concordant with the rasa: "ayi mayi mānini" (O proud one toward me).
This meter means the meter named *dodhaka*, which is a specific *chandas* (prosodic pattern). — *Locanā*.
"Hanta" means "alas, [of this woman] constantly.

thus, [the word] "idam" [is used].

This is why it was stated that even a short syllable at the end of a foot acquires the status of a long one.
This applies everywhere to the scope of the second and fourth quarters [of a verse],

In this case, there is no occurrence of the substitution of a heavy syllable for a light syllable at the end of a quarter-verse (pādānta). He shows the scope for the substitution of a heavy syllable for a light syllable at the end of a quarter-verse by saying "at the end of a quarter-verse," meaning only in cases such as the Vasantatilakā meter.

he refines the reading with the word "here"—"pramuditam" means an object of joy.

such that when this youth is seen, weapons fall from the palms of the hands of enemies whose minds are deluded, and garments fall from the hips of women whose minds are deluded—this is the meaning.
The two adjectives beginning with "śrīmat" are qualifiers for both [the youth and the provisions].

it is the earthly portion consisting of the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of clay.
Here, due to the fact that the letter *ca* is pronounced with very slight effort, there is looseness of articulation (*bandhaśaithilya*).
However, if the reading is "vastrāṇyapi," there is no fault, as it implies firmness.
The author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* states: "This [verse] has a heavy syllable at the end that has not yet attained its status as heavy.
In reality, others maintain that even if one follows the formal definition, it remains unpleasant to the ear (*aśravya*).
Vijñapriyā:

Regarding this, he states "here" (*atra*) because the light syllable at the end of the fourth foot causes looseness in the binding, and thus lacks the capacity to produce firmness in the binding of the work; hence, there is the fault of an unmelodious meter (*aśravyavṛtta*).
[The author] says that there is no fault in the case of "firmness of binding" (*bandhadārḍhya*).
The meaning is that there is no fault because the *takha* (the *kha* of *takha*) has been removed.

According to the view of the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, both [cases] are indeed instances of the fault of *apahatavṛtta*, where the final syllable has not attained the status of being heavy (*guru*). Thus he says: "This too...
According to other views, however:
He says "In reality, however" to show that this [verse] is indeed one whose metrical form is ruined by being unmelodious (*aśravya*).
Here, those who follow his own view are indicated by the phrase "others.
— *Locanā*:

(lo, ṝ) Even when following the [metrical] definition (*lakṣaṇānusaraṇa*), the meaning here is that the short syllable at the end of the second and fourth quarters has not attained the status of a heavy syllable (*agurubhāva*).
Locanā: "Possessing a mass of mane on his powerful thighs, with flames of intensely blazing fire."
May Narakesarin protect you— he whose magnificent mane of manes rests upon his neck, and who has cast down the lords of the earth with a mere breath.
In this instance, the excellence of alliteration has fallen away in succession.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ha) states regarding "falling excellence": "May Narakesarin protect you," beginning with the words "projjvalat" and so forth.
Of what sort is he?
He is one whose mass of mane on his chest possesses a fierce yet beautiful luster, like the flames of a blazing fire;
he is one by whom the great mountain ranges, the principal mountains, have been cast down and toppled by his breath.
Deficiency occurs at the beginning:
"O lady of stainless limbs, these two eyes of yours are like crushed blue lotuses.
Such a disjunction of the *sandhi* (euphonic junction) is a fault only when employed repeatedly.
Locanā:
(lo, e) Because such a lack of aesthetic relish arises from using [the conjunction] even once when it should be used repeatedly;
for while the violation of euphonic combination (*sandhi*) occurs even once out of a mere fear of breaking the meter by transgressing the rules of instruction, [the aforementioned flaw does not].
For example:
"The moon shines at the face of the eastern quarter like a drop of sandalwood paste.
— Locanā.
In the two instances "bhāti induḥ" and so forth, no *sandhi* was performed because they have reached the end of their metrical feet (*vṛtta*);
however, that is contrary to the convention of great poets.
The meaning is: [this applies] only to those occurring at the beginning and the end [of a sentence].

Regarding the phrase “calaṇḍāmaraceṣṭitaḥ,” here, at the juncture [of the words], there is indecorousness (*aślīlatva*) that suggests disgust (*jugupsā*). As for the example: “urvyasāvatra tarvālīmarvante cārvavasthitiḥ.”
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ka) He speaks of the hiatus-sandhi (*viśleṣasandhi*)—in the phrase "dalite" and so forth. That is to say, when [the word] has been "shattered," i.e., drawn away from its stem, in such a manner that the sandhi is prohibited by grammar.
The direction of Vāsava is the eastern quarter (aindrī dik).
He states an instance of an indecorous euphonic junction (*sandhi*): "calaṇḍāmaraceṣṭitā" (of impudent and violent actions).

In this *sandhi*, because the word *laṇḍā* arises [from the corruption of *laṇḍa*], there is disgust due to the implication of long-lasting excrement, which is the meaning of the corrupt form *laṇḍā*.
The word *mauli* means "rows.
The meaning is that she is one whose beautiful arrangement (*avasthiti*) is such [a series].
In this context, the phonemes produced by the junctions (*sandhi*) are the "spines" (*kaṭavaḥ*).
Locanā:

(lo, o) The connection is that "he" (*asau*) [is] "the earth" (*urvo*) at the end of "maru" and at the end of "anta. In this case, there is harshness (*kaṣṭatva*) in the euphonic combination (*sandhi*).
“The moon shines, whitening the world with rays as white as camphor; O slender-limbed one, do not show pride toward your beloved who has prostrated at your feet.”
In this case, it would have been more appropriate to read "jagat" (the world) in the first half-verse:
"Destroying the thick darkness, tormenting those separated from their lovers,
and illuminating the surface of the earth, the rays of the moon fall."
In this case, the fourth quarter of the verse is repeated even after the sentence has been completed.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, kha) states that this constitutes "repetition after completion": "nāśayanta" (destroying).
Regarding this:

although the sentence-meaning is completed in the third quarter through the connection of the qualifier with the action, there is here the fault of "repetition" (āvṛtti), in that the qualifier is employed for the sake of connecting a qualification that was not required.
For in this case, since the illumination of the earth's surface is already achieved by the mere destruction of darkness, that further qualification is unnecessary.
However, where an expectancy for a qualifier persists, this fault does not arise.

For example, in the verse: "Even now, the breath produces a throbbing in the breasts; it exceeds [its] measure," there is an expectancy regarding the breath’s exceeding of its measure, because the production of a throbbing in the breasts by the breath under discussion would not occur without the qualifier of exceeding its measure.
Similarly, in cases such as "ua ṇiccala" and so forth, there is an expectation for the sake of attaining excellence in the form of the figure of speech known as *upamāna* (simile).
This same principle should be investigated in other instances as well. An example of "unintended connection" (*abhavanmatasambandha*) is as follows:
“That glory of victory belonging to the Mind, by whom the world was adorned—that fawn-eyed woman, without whom my life-breaths are now fruitless; where is she today?”

In this context, because the sentences indicated by the word *yat* are mutually independent, it is simply not tenable that the poet’s intended connection of the word *eṇākṣī*—which falls within the scope of one of them—with the others [is valid].
*Vijñapriyā*:
[This refers to the phrase] "they did not exist."

The meaning is: "wherein the intended connection of the poet is impossible" (*asambhavī*), because it is impossible due to a lack of linguistic proficiency (*śābdavyutpatti*). This will be demonstrated in the example.

Regarding the phrase "yā jayaśrīḥ" (she who is the glory of victory): here, the poet intends an agreement (*anvaya*) in which "the fawn-eyed one" (*eṇākṣī*) is the substantive—either as "she who is the fawn-eyed one" or "by that fawn-eyed one"—yet such an agreement is not possible.
This is because [the relative pronoun] *yā* refers to the meaning of a word ending in the second case (*dvitīyānta*).

To demonstrate that the referents of the words *yayā* (instrumental) and *yā* (nominative)—which stand in the first and third cases respectively—arise as coreferential (*viśeṣya*) through identity (*abheda*), he says: "In this case" (*atre*). Now, one might object: there is no coreferential connection between *yā* and *yayā* with the word *eṇākṣyām* (the fawn-eyed woman); rather, there is a mutual coreferential connection only between *yā* and *yayā*. To this, he replies: "Of those indicated by the word *yat*."
Because it is independent, because it possesses a common substratum (anvayi), and because it is free from expectancy (nirākāṅkṣa), its status as such [a compound] should be understood.

And thus, since there is expectancy only with respect to "the fawn-eyed one" (eṇākṣyām), the coreferential connection (arthānvaya) intended by the poet between the two words "yā" and "yayā" must have that very [woman] as its qualificand; yet that [connection] is not possible, as he states: "because it falls exclusively [within the scope of the former]."

Regarding the phrase "yāṃ vineti": the meaning is that by the word *eṇākṣī*, which falls within that single word (*yatpadam*) and is connected to its meaning—that is, by the referent of the word *eṇākṣī*.
As for the other [words], such as *yā* and *yayā*, the plural number is used because a plurality is superimposed upon both of these referents of the pronoun *ya-* here.

Nor should it be argued that here the word *eṇākṣīm* connects with *yā* and *yayā* through a transposition of case endings; for a transposition is only understood when there has first been a connection without transposition. In this instance, however, the connection of *yām* occurs only later, without any transposition.
Locanā:
(lo, au) She provides an example of the "resumption after completion" (*samāptapunarāttatva*): "It occurred;
it was thought."
The desired [meaning] is that wherein there is a *yoga*, that is, a connection, of the poet;
