because of their mutual independence, they stand as objects of restatement (*anuvādya*), and since the sentence expressing the predicate (*vidheya*) indicated by the pronoun is subordinate, they do not coalesce due to such equality.

As for what they have said: "Because qualities exist for the sake of another, there would be no connection [between them] because of their plurality"—this refers to those statements falling within a single sentence, such as:
"Without her, these breaths of mine are in vain; where is that fawn-eyed woman now?"
Thus, even though [the word] is included within a sentence indicated by the pronoun *tat*, its connection with sentences indicated by the relative pronoun *yat* is possible.

However, if the word *eṇākṣī* (the fawn-eyed one) is employed as the substantive for the referent of *tat*, then there is no fault; so he says: "Without whom my [life] is in vain. (Vijñapriyā, vi, gha)
The usage "sā eṇākṣī" (she, the deer-eyed one) occurs precisely as a case where that word [eṇākṣī] functions as the qualificand. Regarding the phrase "by all [grammarians]":
even so, it should not be asked how there can be a coreferential relation of non-difference between the referents of the pronouns *yad* and *tad*, which possess different case endings.
This is because there is no rule requiring identical case endings when a subject qualified by the referent of *tat* is construed with the referent of *yat*;

for example, in the statement "The place where there is smoke is possessed of fire," the place—which is the referent of the nominative-ending term qualified by the referent of *tat*—is construed with the referent of the locative-ending *yat*. (Locanā)
Regarding how that is established, he says:
"Without which," and so forth.
The sentence indicated by the word "that" (*tat*) is what is to be understood.
The meaning is that there is a connection with the word "deer-eyed" (eṇākṣī).
Or, for example:
"When you look [at me] with a sidelong glance, then the mind-born god becomes an archer."
In this context, the connection between the word *yat* and the word *tadā* is not tenable;
rather, the reading *īkṣase cet* is appropriate.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ṅa) Here, even for one who accepts the transposition [of the words], he states another counter-example: "īkṣase yat" ("that which you look upon").
The meaning is "for which reason.
Regarding the word "atra" (here): by the word "yat," there is the presentation of the side-long glance (*kaṭākṣekṣaṇa*).

The meaning is that, because the word *tadā* (then) brings about the presence of time, there can be no syntactic connection of identity (*abhedānvaya*) between those two [the glance and the time], as they do not present a single referent.
As for "if you look":
the sense is that if you look with a sidelong glance, then by that very glance, the Mind-born (Cupid) becomes an archer.
Or, for example:
“The moon, the king of the royal swans in the lake of the sky, shines forth— the moonlight is its mass of foam, the stars are its lotuses, and the water is its flood.”
In this case, because the word *vyomakāsāra* has become subordinate (*guṇībhāva*) within the compound, its meaning is not connected with all [the other words].

Having thus shown the possibility of non-differentiated connection (*abhedānvaya*), [the author] states the impossibility of differentiated connection (*bhedānvaya*) with the words "jyotsnācaya" and so forth.
*Kāsāra* means a lake.
In this case, which has the nature of space (*vyomarūpa*), the meaning is that there are floods of water in the form of masses of moonlight and so forth.

Regarding the word *atra*: in a *tatpuruṣa* compound such as "the royal swan in the lake" (*kāsāre rājahaṃsaḥ*), because the meaning of the final member (*uttarapadārtha*) is the primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the meaning of the word *kāsāra* (lake) necessarily occupies the status of a subordinate qualifier (*guṇībhāva*).
Furthermore, for such a subordinate element (guṇībhūta), its subordination even with respect to another qualificand is unestablished because of a lack of expectancy;
thus, the meaning is that its connection as a qualifier with "the flood of milk" and so forth is impossible.
However, when such a qualifier is connected elsewhere due to the absence of a [suitable] qualificand, there is indeed a lack of expectancy.

For this very reason, in the expression "Caitra’s servant’s wife," the word *bhāryā* (wife) possesses expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatā*) when it is construed with its qualifier *dāsa* (servant), because of the absence of a connection with the qualificand *caitra*.
Locanā:
[This refers to] all things such as milk, fullness, and so forth.
In the case of *vidheyāvimarśa* (non-apprehension of the predicate), that which is not clearly apprehended as the predicate is itself the defect.

Here, however, because the primary referent of the word *kāsāra* (lake) is not perceived as the principal element, the entire meaning of the words such as *payaḥpūra* (flood of water) and so forth is not perceived as subordinate to it; thus, there is an appearance of contradiction with the entire sentence-meaning.
This is the distinction between the two.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, cha) He states the distinction between *abhavanmatayoga* and *vidheyāvimarśa* with the words "vidheyāvimarśa.
In the case of *vidheyāvimarśa*, the comprehension of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) certainly does arise.
However, the meaning is that because the predicated element (vidheya) is not perceived as being predicated, that very predicated element which remains unconsidered is what is defective.

Nor should it be argued that this would result in the defect belonging to the sentence itself; for since the predicated nature is not perceived in relation to the subject (uddeśya), and because the sentence is composed of the subject, the defect belongs to the sentence through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), whereas the word expressing the predicated element alone is what is defective. This is the meaning.

In the present case, however, because connection is impossible due to the lack of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*), he states "But here... that the entire compound [of words] whose correlate for connection (*anvayapratiyogin*) is defective is indeed faulty.

"Of the principal" (*pradhānasya*) means "of that which is the principal by virtue of being connected with the entire compound," such as *payaḥ-pūra* and so forth. "By way of predominance" (*prādhānyena*) means "by way of being connected with the entire compound."
"By being a part of that" means by being connected with that; "concealment" means the impossibility of cognition.
Locanā:
(lo, i) That very falsity which consists in such things as swelling and so forth is indeed defective;
however, it does not entail the disappearance of all sentences.
Thus, in expressions such as "trees produced by the aeon" (*kalpopapadā drumāḥ*),

where the quality of being produced by the aeon belongs to the tree itself and not to the object denoted by the word "tree," one should understand that there is a lack of connection between the intended meaning and the construction (*abhavanmatayoga*).
“O Bhārgava, this sword, which was bound in rivalry with this beast that has now severed your mother’s throat, feels ashamed before me.”

Regarding this, the ancients hold that "the connection of the axe with the act of cutting the throat of [Paraśurāma’s] mother—which was employed as a reproach against Bhārgava—is not appropriate. The moderns, however, maintain that "through the medium of the reproach directed at Nanda, the axe itself illuminates the poet's ingenuity in intensifying the reproach against Bhārgava. Vijñapriyā: The ancients argue that the axe cannot logically be connected to the act of severing the throat of the mother, as that act was performed by Paraśurāma. The moderns counter that the mention of the axe serves to highlight the poet's cleverness in magnifying the insult toward Paraśurāma by means of the insult toward Nanda. This is because the axe is the instrument of the very act of severing the throat; thus, its presence here suggests that the poet intends to emphasize the severity of the reproach against Paraśurāma by implying that even his own weapon is being used against him. This is an instance of *parivṛtti* (exchange) or *vyājastuti* (disguised praise), where the literal meaning is subverted to reveal a deeper intention. The phrase "by means of the reproach toward Nanda" (*nandāmukhena*) indicates that the primary focus remains the censure of Paraśurāma, while the mention of the axe acts as a catalyst for that censure. Thus, the moderns find no fault in the construction.

(Vi, Ja) To refute the opinion of the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*—that this fault occurs in some cases even when the intended connection with the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) is impossible within the literal meaning (*vācyārtha*)—he says: "By this... The syntactic connection is:
"by [me], while cutting the throat of your mother... and "my sword... is the other connection.
The Easterners, such as the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* and others, offer this criticism:
"By the word 'para' (the other), the excessive censure of Bhārgava highlights the superior cleverness of the speaker (*kartṛ*). This is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*).
Just as at the very moment [the autumn] arrives, it seems to proclaim to embodied beings its power over the ignorant,
for the harsh cries of the swans in autumn cause the peacocks to lose their desire for their own melodic calls.
In this context, the use of the word "immediately" (eva) is appropriate after the sentence being referred to,
but not after the word "praṇigadanta.
Thus—
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, jha) "In succession" (*akramataḥ*) means that for a word which intends to refer to that [object], the fact that another [word] follows it is for the purpose of referring to that very object, by way of its immediate occurrence following it as a rule.
"Only in convention" (*samaya eva*).
In such a manner that the peacocks—whose notes had become harsh and unpleasant to hear—were rendered so, the cries of the swans attained beauty in the autumn.
How so? They were as if proclaiming: "It is Time alone that determines the strength and weakness of embodied beings.

For although the cries of the swans are inferior to those of the peacocks, because Time renders the swans' notes harsh in autumn, it thereby establishes the relative strength and weakness of the notes; and through this, even embodied beings attain their own respective strengths and weaknesses.
Such is the sense.
Here—the phrase "the relative strength and weakness" (*balābala*) refers to the sentence being referred to.

Furthermore, it should be understood that there is also a strained construction (*kliṣṭatā*) in the analysis [of the compound] as "the relative strength and weakness even of embodied beings" (*śarīriṇām api balābala*).
Locanā:
(lo, ī) "But [the word] 'praṇigadantaḥ'..."— immediately after this,
the meaning is that since such is the case, there is the suspicion that the word *praṇigadantaḥ* itself might enter into the scope of the sentence being restated (*anuvādya-vākya*).
“Now two things have become objects of lamentation due to their longing for union with the Skull-Bearer:
that radiant digit of the Moon, and you, who are the moonlight for the eyes of this world.”
In this context, the particle *ca* would have been more appropriate immediately after the word *tvam*. [Vijñapriyā] (vi, ña):
"She has now reached a state of lamentability"—this is a statement of self-reproach by Śiva, who is in the form of a matted-haired ascetic, directed toward Pārvatī as she performs penance.
Previously, it was only the digit of the moon (*candrakalā*) that was to be pitied; now, however, because you too are in such a state, there are two.
The description of her being like a skull-cup is for the purpose of inducing sleep, and the prayer for the digit [of the moon] is to be inferred from her union with him.
An example of the "unintended benefit to another" (*amataparārthatā*) is as follows:
“‘Struck by the arrow of Rāma’s love’ and so forth.
Here, the second meaning, which suggests the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), is undesirable because it is opposed to the primary sentiment [of the context].
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, ṭa) *Amata*—the meaning is: a sentence where that which is intended for another purpose (*parārtha*), being of a nature not relevant to the context (*aprakṛtārtha*), is considered "unaccepted" (*amata*) because it is improper due to its manifestation of a sentiment (*rasa*) that contradicts the primary sentiment (*prakṛtarasa*).

*Rāmamanmatha*—that night-stalking female demon (*rākṣasī*), Tāḍakā herself, acting as a woman going to meet her lover (*abhisārikā*), was struck in the heart by the unbearable arrow of Rāma—who is himself the god of love (*manmatha*, *kandarpa*)—and thus became like blood mixed with foul-smelling substances, resembling red sandalwood paste infused with fragrant materials.
"Ukṣitā" means she has gone to the abode of the Lord of Life, namely Yama, the Lord of Life (the master of her breath) and her guide.

Here—the second meaning being suggested, such as that of a woman going to meet her lover—is undesirable and inappropriate, because it would manifest the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), which is incompatible with the intended sentiment of disgust (*vibhatsa*).
—Locanā.
(Locative, Upameya: The Lord of Life is Yama, and the primary sentiment (*rasa*) is the loathsome (*bībhatsa*).
An example of the non-expression of the literal meaning (*vācya*) is as follows:
"O fair-eyed one, seeing what slight transgression of mine do you become angry?"
In this context, it was not stated that even a minute transgression (*vyatikramalava*) must necessarily be mentioned.

*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ṭha): "The non-expression of what ought to be expressed" (*vācyasyānabhidhānam*)—the meaning is that there is a failure to express that which must necessarily be said, whether by its explicit utterance or by implication (*adhyāhāra*).
Regarding the case of missing words (*nyūnapada*), it will be explained later that there is a distinction in that the meaning is expressed through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*).
"Even a mere fraction of transgression" (*vyatikramalavam*) means even a slight degree of transgression regarding the action that causes pleasure.
Here, the word "fraction" (*lava*) is used to indicate that one does not perceive a general transgression—whether gross or subtle—and thus it should be stated as "even in some way" (*kathamapi*).

In this case, however, even by supplying the particle *api* [to read as] "even a minute fraction of transgression" (*vyatikramalavam api*), the intended meaning is not established. This is because, through the compound *vyatikramasya* itself, provided that the genitive case is present, it is possible to understand a gross portion related to the transgression; it does not, however, yield the understanding "even a minute fraction of transgression. For if it were a compound, the cognition that would arise would be "even a minute fraction of transgression is another distinct object" (*padārthāntara*). Therefore, in this instance, whether by explicit utterance or by ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), there is necessarily a failure to express what ought to be expressed.

In the case of "deficiency of words" (*nyūnapada*), the deficiency intended is that of the expressive word itself; however, this is not the case for the particle *api*. This is the distinction between these two.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, ḍa) He states the distinction of this [fallacy] due to its deficiency in words: "deficiency" (*nyūna*), etc. The meaning is that there is a deficiency of expressive words (*vācaka-pada*) itself, and not even a deficiency resulting from ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). The intention is that in that case, ellipsis is possible; however, here, such ellipsis is not possible.
The same applies elsewhere as well; for example:
"O slender one, whose beauty is bowed by her feet..."
Nevertheless, you still harbor anger."
In this context, it should have been stated as "caraṇānatakāntāsī" (you whose beloved has bowed at her feet).
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ḍha): Regarding "caraṇanatā"—O passionate woman (*caṇḍi*)!
"O wrathful one!
Even though you have a beloved who bows at your feet, you still feel anger"—this is the meaning.
Here, by virtue of the interrogative intonation (*kāku*), the sense is: "How can there be anger?"
In this context, by the phrase "tathāpi" (nevertheless), the word "yadyapi" (even though) is required;
for while "yadyapi" remains syntactically complete in itself, its connection with "tathāpi" is only logically possible when the latter occurs within a second sentence.
Thus, even here, there is no possibility of supplying [the missing term] through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*).
Locanā:

(lo, ū) In the case of *nyūnapadatva* (deficiency of words), there is no fault merely by the presence of a deficient word; however, here, the distinction between these two lies in the fact that, having discarded a word ending in the genitive (*ṅas*), the word *asi* has been inserted.
Broken sequence (*bhagnaprakramatā*) is as follows:
"Thus addressed by the chief ministers, Rāvaṇa replied.
Here, since the root *vac* was employed at the outset, it would have been more appropriate to use that very same root for the reply as well.
Therefore, the reading "Rāvaṇaḥ pratyavocata" (Rāvaṇa replied) is appropriate;
and this being the case, there is no fault of repeating a word (*kathitapadatva*), because that [fault] applies only to cases other than those involving the subject of the statement (*uddeśya*).
For here, in the case of a statement and its reply, there is the relationship of the subject and its subsequent specification.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ṇa):
"Broken sequence" (*bhagnaprakrama*)—the essence of this is the non-utterance in the same form of that which was expected by the form initially introduced.
"Thus it was said"—this is clear.

Here, by using the root *vac* for both the subject of the statement and the response, he shows that there is still an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) [for further specification], as indicated by the phrase "he replied.

And thus, he dispels the fault of *kathitapadatva* (repetition of the same word) by means of the word "thus" (*evam*). The phrase "of that subject" (*tasyoddeśye*) indicates that the subject is to be restated (*pratinirdeśyatā*).
In various ways, there is a restatement of that very dharma which was previously indicated as the subject to be enjoined (*vidheya*), now being required again as the object of an injunction.
For example, in this very verse, there is a restatement as an injunction by way of a reply to the speech of Rāvaṇa, which had been indicated as the subject to be enjoined.
Or, for instance: "The sun rises copper-red, and it sets copper-red."
In prosperity as well as in adversity, the great remain uniform in their character.

In this instance, because of the statement of a single form (*ekarūpatā*), there is a reference back to the "copperiness" (*tāmratva*)—which was previously specified as the predicate (*vidheya*) in the case of the rising sun—as a predicate again in the case of the setting sun.
(2) Another [type] consists of a reference back to a predicate, which was previously the subject (*uddeśya*) under a single subject, now as a subject under another predicate.
For example: "Control of the senses is the cause of discipline; excellence of virtues is obtained from discipline."

In this instance, because the state of being the cause of discipline (*vinaya*), which is to be enjoined through the quality of having conquered the senses, has entered into the body [of the subject], there is a reference back (*pratinirdeśa*) to the discipline itself—which was the object of the injunction—as the object of a further injunction regarding the excellence of its qualities.
(3) Another type is: "the reference back as the object of yet another thing to be enjoined of that which was already indicated as the object during one injunction.
For example: *te himālayamāmantrya punaḥ prekṣya ca śūlinam*... [and so forth].
"Having reported the accomplished matter to him, they departed through the sky, dismissed by him.

Here, in this instance of the rule for reporting an accomplished matter (*siddhārthanivedana*), there is another type [of *punarukta*] consisting of the re-specification as the subject (*uddeśyatā*) of that which was already indicated as the subject in the very same context where it was to be enjoined.
And an example of this will be shown later in the passage beginning with "to acquire fame" (*yaśo 'dhigantum*).
And I shall demonstrate that very point right there.
Locanā:
(lo, ṝ) It is proper to express it by that [root] alone, and not by the verbal root *bhāṣ*.
Because that which has its word already stated must have as its object something distinct from both the subject of reference (*uddeśya*) and the subsequent reference (*pratinirdeśya*).

This is the intended meaning: whatever is the subject of reference is precisely what is intended to be subsequently referred to. That [subsequent referent] must be referred to either by means of a word previously used as the subject of reference or by means of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*).
He confirms this very point by showing an illustration:
"The sun rises copper-red, and it sets copper-red as well."
For in this case, if that very same meaning is expressed by another word, then, appearing as if it were a different meaning, it obstructs the comprehension.
*Vijñapriyā* (Vi, Ta):
Having thus cited "ittham evam uktaḥ" as an example of a breach of uniformity (*prakramabhanga*), he now provides an example of the absence of such a breach (*prakramābhanga*).
For example: "it rises.

According to the view that there is no cognition of the substrate (*nāmin*) as such [without qualifiers], the appearance of difference arises from the distinction between the two qualifying attributes—namely, the words *tāmra* (copper) and *rakta* (red)—just as if there were two separate objects.
This refers to the cognition, namely, the cognition of non-difference.
Locanā:
"It rises" (*udeti*) means it obstructs comprehension;
and such being the case, the sense is that there is an impediment to the experience of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
Or as it is said:

"Having taken leave of Himālaya and having looked again upon the Wielder of the Trident (Śūlin), and having reported the matter accomplished to him, they, being dismissed by him, ascended into the sky."

In this context, the reference to that which has been introduced by the word "asmai" (to him) should properly be made by that same pronoun, or by the two words "etad" (this), which are identical to it in form, and not by the word "tat" (that).

Regarding the rule for a single type [of pronoun], the author provides an example of a breach of uniformity (*prakramabhaṅga*) when there is a re-reference as the subject (*uddeśya*) even after another predicate (*vidheya*) has been stated— namely, "te himālayam" (they [went] to the Himalaya).

Those seven seers [attained] their accomplished purpose, which consisted of the arrangement of Pārvatī’s marriage; they were dispatched by the Wielder of the Trident (Śūlin), who was himself sent by Him whose purpose is identical to theirs.
Nor should it be argued that the appearance of difference arises from the difference between words having the same meaning;
for a pronoun refers only to that which is qualified by the name mentioned first, and not to that which is unqualified.
Nor should it be argued that there is no fault because the pronoun *tat* likewise refers in the same manner; [for that is not the case].
The meaning is this: here, by the word "this" (*idam*), Mahādeva is referred to as being present before the mind;
however, because the word "that" (*tat*) refers to something remote, it is impossible to refer to him with it.
Or, for example:
“The earth is bounded by the ocean, and that lord of waters [extends] for a hundred *yojanas*.
In this case, the correct reading is: “The earth is measured by the lord of waters, and he, the lord of waters [extends] for a hundred *yojanas*.
(Vijñapriyā)

(vi, da) Because it manifests a distinction between the substrata (*dharmin*), there is an appearance of difference; thus, even when one thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*) is restated in the form of another substratum for the sake of a single subject, he cites that fault as follows: "The earth is bounded by the ocean, and he [the ocean] is the lord of waters, extending over a hundred *yojanas*. This is the ellipsis. Here, with respect to the earth as the subject (*uddeśya*), "being bounded by the ocean" is the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), and the ocean itself is also a thing to be enjoined.
The fault is that, in the act of measuring out its extent of a hundred *yojanas*, the term "Lord of Waters" (*apāmpati*) is used as a designation for the object of the measurement.
He remedies this fault with an alternative reading: "measured by the Lord of Earth" (*bhūpati*).
The meaning is that it was measured and delimited by the Lord of Earth.
Thus:

"Success, as if longing for them, comes into the lap of those who are free from worldly desire yet devoted to effort, whether they seek fame, the desire for pleasure, or to transcend the ranks of ordinary men."
In this context, "to seek happiness" (*sukham īhitum*) would have been appropriate.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, dha):

It provides an example of the violation of sequence regarding the meaning of the suffix, where that which was indicated as the object of an injunction is subsequently referred back as the subject of that very injunction—namely, "to attain fame" (*yaśo 'dhigantum*).
This is Yudhiṣṭhira’s speech directed toward Draupadī, who was agitated by the prospect of fighting:

"Into the lap of those who, though desirous of attaining glory, obtaining happiness, and rising above the ranks of men— transcending the number of humanity— are yet free from longing because they are indifferent to such desires, and who instead engage in exertion in the form of efforts favorable to those goals."
The meaning is that accomplishment approaches as if eager or longing.

Here, there is a reference back (pratinirdeśa) to the desire specified in the injunction regarding the absence of eagerness (*nirutsukatva*), by treating it as the object of that very injunction on the absence of eagerness.
And the sequence [of the elements] is broken because the statement of the subject matter is made through the distinct suffix *tumun*.
Here, in the first two cases, there is a breach of uniformity regarding the base (*prakṛti*);
in the third, it concerns the synonym (*paryāya*);
and in the fourth, it concerns the suffix (*pratyaya*).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, na) The elision (*ati*) occurs here in the first two instances;
that is to say, in the passage "Thus addressed by the chief ministers" and in the passage "Having taken leave of the Himālaya."
In the third [verse], "bounded by the ocean," and in the fourth, "in order to attain glory";
likewise in other cases as well.
An example of the renunciation of what is well-known is as follows:
“The roar of the water-releasing clouds is terrible.
In this case, only the thundering of the clouds is well-known;
as they say:

“In the case of anklets and the like, it is primarily *raṇati*; among birds, it is *kūjita* and so forth; in sexual union, it is *stanita*, *maṇita*, and so on; and in the case of clouds and the like, it is *garjita* and so forth.”
And so forth.
*Vijñapriyā*:
"It is well-known" means...
The definition [of *dhvani*] is the non-employment of a word whose meaning is well-established in reference to a specific relation with respect to such a related object.

Regarding the term "ghora," the author provides corroboration from the statement of the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*—namely, that specific words are employed only with respect to specific relations—in the passage beginning "in anklets (*mañjīra*) and so forth.
This means: with respect to related objects such as anklets.
The same applies in subsequent cases as well.
An example of misplaced words (*asthānasthapadatā*) is as follows:
"While crossing the Ganges upstream at his sacred bathing place by means of a bridge formed by elephants..."
The swans, with their wings fluttering as they soared through the sky, became effortless fans for him.

In this context, it is appropriate to read the word "Gaṅgām" before "tadīya-pādāt. Regarding the term *asthānastha* (placed in the wrong position): its defining characteristic is being situated in a location other than that specific place where, by its very nature, a particular word possesses the capacity to convey meaning.

Regarding the distinction between the verse "tvamasya lokasya ca" and the present one: in the former, the fixed word (*niyatapada*) is read later [in the sequence], whereas here, the word is not subject to such a restriction.

As for the phrase "at his sacred ford" (*tīrthe tadīye*): because of this king’s construction of a bridge with elephants, the Ganges flows upstream; at that sacred ford belonging to the Ganges (*gāṅgīye tīrthe*), situated to the north, the swans—whose wings are eager to soar into the sky—have flown off toward the north.

The sense is that, due to the rise in water levels from the bridge construction, the swans have taken flight toward the north in the belief that it is the rainy season, intending to go to Lake Mānasa.
In this context,
[the word] "here" refers to the Ganges;
for it is possible to refer to that [Ganges] by means of that word within the first cognition.
Locanā:
(Lo, e) It is more appropriate for the reading "Gaṅgām" to precede "tadīya";
for it is proper to speak [of the latter] immediately after the reference by the pronoun "tat".
Thus:
"He who does not listen to what is beneficial—how can he be a master?"

In this case, the placement of the negative particle (*nañ*) before the word "saṃśṛṇuta" would have been appropriate. Furthermore, even when a single word is placed in an improper position, the entire sentence becomes sluggish in conveying the intended meaning; thus, it constitutes a fault of the sentence (*vākyadoṣa*).
The same applies elsewhere as well.
In this regard, some say: “By the word ‘term’ (pada), that which is expressive (vācaka) is generally meant;
however, the negative particle (nañ) is not expressive, because it lacks the capacity to convey a meaning independently, a point free from dispute.”
Just as in the verse beginning with “The two have gone,” there is a lack of sequential order because the word *ca* is not employed immediately after *tvam*, so it is here as well.
*Vijñapriyā*:
“Not from a beneficial person”—that is, from a person who is helpful.
In some places, the reading is *hitam*.
Regarding the word *atra*—it is because it is more appropriate for the negative particle (*nañ*) connected with the action to be read in close proximity to that action.
Here, he demonstrates why this constitutes a syntactical fault (*vākyadoṣa*).
Regarding the phrase "and here"—*mantharam* means "incapable.
He shows the opinion of some that *hitān na yaḥ* is an example of the fault of "lack of sequence" (*akrama-doṣa*) with the words "here some [say]...
and "by the word *pada*."

In the expression *apadasthapada*, the meaning is "by the second word. It is indeed expressive; however, because it is not employed without connection to another word—just as one does not say "five-word" or "three-word" [without specifying what they are]—the negative particle (*nañ*) likewise lacks expressiveness in that context, since it is not used without connection to a word denoting its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).

The meaning is that the status of being a word (*padatva*) is beyond dispute in the case of fixed words [such as *niyata*]. However, since words like "jar" (*ghaṭa*) are used independently, their status as words is beyond dispute there; this is why it was stated "for the most part," because the Naiyāyikas apply the conventional term "word" to mere phonemes that possess expressive power (*śaktimat*).
The phrase "as in 'dvayam' and so forth" means that in each such case, there is precisely the fault of lack of sequential order (*akramatva*).
Thus, the example for the fault of misplaced words (*asthānasthapadatva*) is precisely "tīrthe tadīye," and so on. This is the meaning.

An example of the *asthānasthasamāsa* (misplaced compound) is as follows: "Even now, this pride (*māna*)—red as if with rage, having cursed itself for desiring to dwell in the hearts of women, which are difficult to traverse like fortresses of mountain-breasts—seizes, at that very moment, the sword-like rows of bees emerging from the blossoming buds of the night-lotuses, as the moon stretches forth its rays far away. In this verse, the compound *prodyaddūrataraprasāritakaraḥ* ("stretching forth his rays far away") is misplaced; it should have been placed after *karṣatyasau*, not before it. Thus, it is an instance of a misplaced compound.
In this instance, no compound was formed in the statement of the fool, whereas it was formed in the statement of the poet.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, bha) Regarding "inappropriate place" (*asthāna*): this refers to the occurrence of a compound that expresses a particular rasa in a location other than the one appropriate for expressing that specific rasa.
Regarding "even now": this is a description of rows of bees emerging from the buds of night-lotuses at the time of twilight.
Regarding "even now" and so forth: this moon, rising red with anger as previously described, emerges as if from a scabbard—the very form of a sword-sheath—consisting of blooming night-lotus buds.
The hand was extended so far that it was like a ray of light—a hand whose palm was spread out at a great distance like a row of bees emerging from a sword.
Being such [as described], even while pulling [the sword] at that very moment, the hand remained extended far away.
He states the seed of his anger with the words "even now."
"Let the pride of women remain for now, taking refuge in the inaccessible fortress of their breasts;
even today, even upon my rise, it persists—shame on me! This is the anger [of the Moon].
Here, the compound *kopinaḥ* (of the angry one) refers to the Moon (*candra*), and it is a long compound (*dīrghasamāsa*).
Locanā:
(lo, ai) A "sheath" (koṣa) is a bud and the scabbard of a sword.
Interfusion (saṅkīrṇatva) consists in the intrusion of words belonging to one sentence into another sentence.
For example:
"O fawn-eyed one, leave the moon;
O lady, look at the sky full of pride."
In this case, it is appropriate to say, "O lady, look at the moon in the sky; abandon your pride.
This is distinct from [the fault of] *kliṣṭatva* (obscuration), which pertains to a single sentence.
*Garbhitatā* (embarrassment) consists in the intrusion of one sentence into another.
For example:
"O friend, now that my lover’s foot is inclined toward prostration at its edge, I say this:"
Therefore, it is never appropriate for you to give way to anger.”
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ma) He speaks of the mixture [of the two]— beginning with "vākyāntara" and ending with "muñca mānam."
The connection of this [term] is clear in the commentary itself.
He states its distinction when it is "defiled" (kliṣṭa) with the words "its very defilement.
He states its "embarrassment" (garbhitatva) with the words "in another sentence."

Regarding "in the act of love" (*ramaṇe*): here, within the sentence "Now that he has fallen at the edge of your feet during our lovemaking, anger is not appropriate," the sentence "O friend, I tell you the truth" has been interpolated.
He states the faults of meaning (*arthadoṣa*):
lack of nourishment (*apuṣṭatā*), harshness (*duṣkamatā*), vulgarity (*grāmyatā*), contradiction (*vyāhatatā*), indecorousness (*aślīlatā*), and difficulty (*kaṣṭatā*).
The unqualified, the causeless, the revealed, and the contradictory. // VisSd_7.9 //
Doubtful repetition, contradiction with common knowledge or established science, expectancy, deviation from the natural order of association, and lack of propriety in placement. (VisSd 7.10)

Where there is no distinction, there is a distinction; likewise, where there is no rule, there is a rule. There are also their reversals, as well as the improper application of injunction and restatement. (VisSd 7.11)
The defects of meaning (*arthadoṣa*) are proclaimed to be those [qualities] such as being devoid of *nū* and *ru*.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ya) Now he states the twenty-three defects of meaning with the words "the defects of meaning."
Regarding the term "renowned" (*khyāta*):
it refers to two faults, namely, contradiction with what is renowned and contradiction with valid knowledge (*vidyā*). Their opposites are the two [virtues].
The meaning is as follows: when there is no distinction, the statement of a distinction; when there is a distinction, the statement of no distinction;
when there is no restriction, the statement of a restriction; and when there is a restriction, the statement of no restriction—these constitute the reversals [of the intended meaning].
Furthermore, there are two defects: the improper formulation of an injunction and the improper formulation of a restatement.
Locanā:
(lo, o) [The letters] *la* and *o* [indicate] those that have not been mentioned as faults of meaning (*arthadoṣa*).
Each of [the faults] such as "insufficiency" (*apuṣṭa*) is to be construed with the suffix *-tva*.
The opposite of that [is]: lack of distinction where there is distinction, and lack of restriction where there is restriction. Here, "insufficiency" means not being primarily contributive.
For example:
“O beloved, seeing the moon in the vast sky, abandon your anger.
Here, the word *vitata* (vast) does not contribute anything toward the relinquishing of the anger.
In the case of *adhikapada* (redundancy), the perception of contradiction arises at the very same time as the comprehension of the syntactic connection (*padārthānvaya*) of the words.
But here, the distinction is that it occurs "later.
Vijñapriyā:
"Principal" means having the nature of the predicate (*vidheya*).
The rest is clear.
He states the distinction of this [type] from *adhikapada* (redundant word) as follows: "Excessive," etc.

The meaning is that in the phrase "her lips are red, having the form of sprouts" (*pallavākṛtiraktoṣṭhī*), the sublation (*bādha*) consisting in the uselessness of the word *ākṛti* manifests at the very same time as the comprehension of the sentence-meaning (*anvayabodha*).
Locanā: (lo,
au) The primary subject to be explained here is that the manifestation of cognition occurs in this way at the very same time [as its object].
For this very reason, it is a fault of the sentence;
since it occurs immediately after the comprehension of the meaning,
for that same reason it is a fault of the meaning.
A "vivara" (opening), a "chidra" (hole), or the "strīvarāṅga" (female organ) is indecorous (*aślīla*),
because they call to mind the male organ (*puṃdhvaja*). An example of improper sequence (*duṣkramatā*) is as follows:
“Give me a horse, O King, or an elephant lord languid with rut.
In this case, it would have been more appropriate to request the elephant lord first.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, la) He states the difficulty of the sequence with the words "dehi" (give).
Here—meaning, when an object of high value is being offered, it is appropriate to request a lower price precisely because of the possibility that [the seller] might not agree to it.
“Sleep near me; I too am now sleeping, my dear.
Herein, the meaning is vulgar (*grāmya*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, va) "Sleep"—this is a statement by the heroine to the hero.
O beloved, here I am sleeping; you too should sleep nearby—this is the meaning.
The term "vulgar" (grāmya) means stated due to a lack of cleverness or refinement.
"Contradiction" (vyāhatatva) consists in first stating the excellence or deficiency of something, and subsequently establishing its opposite.
For example: "The crescent of the new moon and such do not steal the hearts of the young."
"By whomsoever this slender maiden, the moonlight for the eyes of the world, is beheld."
In this case, the attribution of "moonlight" to the slender lady is for the sake of the joy of those very people for whom the digit of the moon is not a cause of joy.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi,
śa) states the definition of contradiction (*vyāhata*)— namely, "of someone"— where "its being otherwise" means its becoming otherwise in terms of excellence, that is, inferiority.

The meaning is that "inferiority" (*apakarṣa*) is a state of being otherwise, which is to say, the demonstration of that [inferiority]. Regarding this, he provides an example of "prior inferiority" (*pragapakarṣa*): "They carry away..."—the sense is that the young men do not carry away their hearts with the new crescent moon and so forth; here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), even the moonlight is disparaged. This slender girl, beautiful as moonlight to the eyes of the world, whom these youths gaze upon—their hearts are not carried away by the new moon’s digit and the like. Here, by the word "and so forth," even the moonlight is censured.
In that case, excellence is established through its attribution to a slender woman; thus he says: "here.
But as for excellence [attributed] previously, it is as follows: "O slender one, by your ear-ornament, the moon in the sky is eclipsed."
Thus it is said:
"For one who is intent on killing, arrogant, and seeking an opening,
the fall occurs as quickly as it does, but such a rise again never happens."
In this case, the meaning is indecorous; Vijñapriyā [comments]:
"It means precisely for the sake of killing."

This is a description of a man engaged in battle without any resolve. For one who is arrogant and does not distinguish between good and evil, there is merely a desire for the enemy's vulnerability—that is, his weakness—but no actual engagement, because of his arrogance; he has no regard for it. Here, the gender of the person is understood through the grammatical mark (liṅga).
"The Lord of Day rains on this day, yet not as a cloud pours down clear water from his abode; truly, she is the daughter of Savitṛ, like the flood of the celestial river.
Who does not trust the words of Vyāsa? And who has no faith in the Veda? Yet even so, the foolish doe perceives water in the rays of the sun."
Vijñapriyā:
Even in the absence of being afflicted (*saṃkliṣṭa*) and so forth, the reality (*tattva*) consists in the meaning being difficult to comprehend.
"It rains"—this is an expression of longing by a certain amorous woman addressed to the messengers of her beloved, under the guise of speaking of something else. Day.
The Lord Sūrya rains down this visible water situated in his own rays— that which stands in his abode— but the cloud does not rain it,
because the cloud is like the hand of Sūrya.
Likewise, she by whom the flood— the current— of the celestial river Gaṅgā was inundated is, in truth, the daughter of Savitṛ, the Sun, namely Yamunā.

To the question, "How is this certain? he says: "Of Vyāsa..."—namely, that the fact of the Yamunā and the rain originating from the Sun was certainly not stated by anyone who was untrustworthy, but rather by Vyāsa, and by means of the Śruti, which is synonymous with the Veda.
This is even when there is a desire to know [the truth].

"From the sun rain is born, from that food, and from that living beings"—who would not trust such words of Vyāsa which reveal Kālindī’s status as the daughter of the Sun? Or who would lack faith in the Veda, the Śruti, which has this very meaning? Indeed, everyone trusts them, and everyone has faith in them.
And thus, it is indeed appropriate for the doe as well to have trust and faith there;
nevertheless, the innocent, deluded doe does not perceive water in the substrata that are the rays of the sun.

For by the statement "the pure water resides in the abode [of light]," it is established through both Vyāsa and the Śruti that water exists within the solar rays, making such a perception appropriate.
Locanā:
(lo, a) It is said that she is the Yamunā because she rains;
indeed, who other than Vyāsa—an authoritative person—could have stated that both rain and the Yamunā originate from the Sun?

But [it is said] by Vyāsa: "By the Veda, by tradition, and by the practice of the Vedas"—this refers to faith (*śraddhā*), which is firm conviction. This is a sarcastic statement uttered by a certain amorous woman under the pretext of sending a message through a female messenger to her lover.
In this matter, the point under discussion is even more excellent: that he is a city-dweller who speaks the truth; this is indeed authoritative.
It is therefore appropriate that you ladies, acting as his messengers, should have confidence in his truthfulness. But I alone am foolish, for I place my trust in falsehood.
Just as the perception of water arises for fawns in the mirages of the desert,
so too does my conviction arise regarding you.
Since the sun is the source of both the rain and the Yamunā, the water of those two is likewise of the nature of the sun.
And thus, while it is logical that the rays of the sun serve as the cause for the cognition of water,
nevertheless, because her perception of reality is deluded, the doe does not form the cognition of water there;
this point, though irrelevant to the present context, is difficult to understand.
And because the understanding of the subject matter under discussion is far removed [from us], there is the defect of "difficulty of meaning" (*kaṣṭārthatva*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
Here, in the word "here" (*atra*), he demonstrates that the intended meaning is difficult to comprehend.
The meaning is that "origin" refers to the progenitor, and for those two, it is water—meaning rain and the Yamunā river.
Since a river is filled precisely by rain produced by the sun, it is appropriate that the Yamunā serves as the cause for the cognition of being the producer of rain. This is the intended sense.
Because it is stated that the water exists within that [mirage],
and because it is an error, "therein" is used;

for since the Yamunā water is shown to originate from the sun's rays within the substratum of those mirages, one who is driven by thirst proceeds toward the Yamunā itself, and thus there is no cognition of water in that [mirage].
This is stated to demonstrate that one does not perceive [the water] because of the delusion of water in the rays of light; thus, this is a matter not under discussion [in the primary context].

For here, the ornament (alaṅkāra) named Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Praise of the Irrelevant) is present, consisting in the communication of the relevant subject through the description of something irrelevant.
In this context, the relevant [example] is the lack of conviction among deluded people even regarding a matter established by logic;
whereas the irrelevant one is the perception of water in a mirage.
"The sun always moves in the sky; the wind always blows."
Śeṣa always supports the earth; he is ever steadfast and free from boastfulness.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ka) He says "always" (*sadā*) to indicate that which has not been renewed; [the wise man] is steadfast and free from boastfulness.
There is an elision of the negative particle (*na*).
He states the distinction from this [type] regarding the aforementioned *pada* with the words "herein" (*atre*).
Following the interruption caused by a synonym of identical meaning, there is a distinction in the structural arrangement (*bhaṅgībheda*) based on the mode [of expression].

As for the phrase "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*): the meaning is that because there is no distinction in the structural arrangement based on the mode, it is precisely "unrenewed" (*anavīkṛta*). For example: "The sun always moves in the sky; the wind constantly blows."
The steadfast Śeṣa, who is free from boastfulness, always supports the earth without ceasing.
"In this context, the words *sadā* (always), *anitya* (not eternal), *sarvadā* (at all times), and *ajasram* (unceasingly) share the same meaning and possess the same mode (*samānaprakāratā*).

Regarding *bhānuḥ sadā* (the sun always): even for a king who lives on a sixth part [of the produce], the taking of that sixth part is his duty (*dharma*) consisting of the protection of the subjects; thus, the meaning is that this is *always* so.

Here, although the words *sadā* and *satatam* (continuously) have the same mode and the same meaning, in the case of *rātrindivam* (night and day), there is equality only in the sense, while there is a difference in the modes, namely the state of being night and the state of being day."
In this context, "always" (*sadā*) refers to the state of being unmodified.

Even if another synonym for this word were employed here, if there were no other interruption [of the flow], then this defect would still exist; thus, it differs from the fault of "repetition of a word" (*kathitapadatva*). — *Locanā*.
After "asya" (of this), the word "sadā" (always) is to be supplied;
this is expressed by another synonym, namely "sarvadā" (at all times), and so forth.
The state of being renewed is as follows:
“The sun thus proceeds day and night with its steeds yoked but once; the wind blows continuously;
Śeṣa perpetually supports the earth—this is the duty even for one who subsists on a sixth part [of the produce].”
"Thus [he spoke]:
'O Weapon, you were taken up by one who, out of fear of humiliation, would not take even what was improper; indeed, there was no one who was not within your reach due to his power.
Yet you were abandoned by him because of grief for his son, and not out of fear. Therefore, O Weapon, I shall release you.'"
Therefore, I too wish you well.
In this case, since no reason is stated for discharging the second weapon, there is the fault of being "without a reason" (*nirhetutva*).
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, kha) states: "It is without a reason"—namely, "it was seized. The essence [of this fault] is the failure to state a reason even when there is an expectancy for a reason.
This is the speech of Aśvatthāman, addressing the weapon being cast off due to Karṇa’s anger:
"O Weapon! You were taken up by my father—though it was improper for one of the Brāhmaṇa caste and even though it was unsuitable—from King Drupada out of fear of humiliation;
likewise, by the power of that same father of mine, there was indeed nothing that was not within your reach, meaning that even the Moon (Indu) became an object of your range."

Because my father heard that his son had been killed, he abandoned you out of grief for me and not out of fear, so that I too might release you; therefore, may it be well with you—this is the meaning.
"Herein"—that is, the second discharge of weapons by Aśvatthāman.
And in that context, the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "I also" (*aham api*) serves to arouse the expectation for a reason.
Locanā:
Regarding the phrase "the releasing of weapons," the word "Aśvatthāman" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
"O Prince, O lord of men,
may you attain prosperity!"—
here, because the contrary meaning "you shall die" is revealed, there is the fault of *prakāśitaviruddha* (contradiction by what is revealed).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ga) He states [the following] to clarify the contradictory meaning: "Your son" (*kumāras te*).
"Son" (*kumāra*) means a child.

In this case, the sense is that the son generally attains prosperity immediately after the death of his father. Regarding the verse, "O wise ones, tell me: should one serve the immovable mountains or the frail women?", there is ambiguity because, in the absence of a specific context, there is no certainty as to whether the speaker is a person of tranquil temperament or one characterized by passion.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, gha) He states the doubtful meaning with the words "acalā" (the immovable).

Regarding "here"—the meaning is that because there is no certainty in what has been said, there is doubt due to the absence of a definitive conclusion as to whether one should serve those who are "immovable" or indeed those who are "weak."
"One should not perform an action impulsively; lack of discernment is the gateway to supreme calamities.
For prosperity, being enamored of virtue, seeks out the one who acts with deliberation of its own accord."
In this second half [of the verse], since the meaning of the second line alone is expressed by way of contrast (*vyatireka*), there is tautology (*punaruktatā*).

*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ṅa) states the redundant meaning: "Impulsively" (*sahasā*) means lack of discernment (*aviveka*), which is acting without reflection; that, however, is the "footing of calamities," meaning it is the cause of the arising of misfortunes.
Since a cause with multiple factors pervades its effect, it has been shown that acting without deliberation pervades misfortune.
Through this positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyāpti*), he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*) that is thereby obtained: "For [the wise] choose...

He explains that the absence of acting without deliberation—which is the opposite of the pervader (acting without deliberation) whose nature is misfortune—pervades prosperity, which is the absence of the state of misfortune: "Those who are greedy for virtues..."
The meaning is that where there is acting with deliberation, there is prosperity.

Regarding the word "here" (*atrety*): by means of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) obtained from the second half [of the verse], and by means of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) obtained from the second quarter of that same second half, the meaning is precisely that of the positive concomitance established in the second quarter itself.
The meaning of the negative concomitance is ultimately resolved through the positive concomitance alone.
The meaning is that since the point has already been stated in the second half-verse by means of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*), it is therefore redundant.
An example of contradiction with common consensus (*prasiddhi-viruddhatā*) is as follows:
"And then, O hero, Hari, bearing a sharp trident, [stood] in the battle."
In this context, the trident of Hari is not well-known in the world;
for example: "From the blow of his foot, that Aśoka tree has produced sprouts and thorns."

In this case, it is well known that flowers alone grow on *aśoka* trees from the touch of a foot, and not sprouts; thus, there is a contradiction with the established conventions (*kavisamaya*) of poets.
“*Adhare karajakṣataṃ mṛgākṣyāḥ*” (The nail-marks upon the lower lip of the deer-eyed woman).
Here, [the context is] the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*).
Because it contradicts the treatises, it is contrary to knowledge;
likewise, it is also contrary to other treatises.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ca) He states [the fault of] contradiction with common renown (*prasiddhiviruddha*)—namely, "common renown" (*prasiddhi*).
Its essence is the state of being contradicted by the renown of poets.
However, contradiction with the renown of other people, such as in the description of the whiteness of fame (*kīrti*), is not a defect.
In that context:
"cold" means made thin by rubbing against cold stones;
"Hari" means Kṛṣṇa.
Regarding "here"—it means in this world, in the world of poets. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "from the blow of their feet."

Regarding the phrase "herein"—namely, "not even a sprout": one should not object by asking how a sprout is not well-known, given that even *dohada* (the longing of plants) is described in Kālidāsa’s poem, where it says, "and the flower was made to blossom by you. The meaning is that the fault lies in the fact that no poet has ever described a sprout; for "among poets, there is non-recognition even of what is real, and recognition even of what is unreal. Thus, the point is that the sprout is not established [by poetic convention].
But since the non-application of a word is not its meaning, there is no possibility of that [fault] here.
He states what is contrary to knowledge: "in the lower."
This is a science of knowledge (*vidyāśāstra*). Similarly, there is another [scripture], such as the *Dharmaśāstra*: "A wise person always bathes at night."
The statement that "a hero is victorious without strategy" contradicts the science of political ethics (*nītiśāstra*),
and the claim that "one suffering from fever ought to bathe" contradicts the science of medicine (*vaidyaśāstra*).
“How can Bhārgava now endure the breaking of such a bow, the exaltation of the Kṣatriyas, and the jewel among women?”
In this context, there is an expectancy regarding the phrase "to disregard the jewel among women. Vijñapriyā (vi,
cha) states the expectancy with the words "of the Lord" (*aiśasya*).

The defining characteristic [of the defect of *nyūnapada*] is being the object of a misconception regarding the connection of the meanings of words that have been expressed, while simultaneously possessing expectancy for the meaning of words not expressed.
The distinction [from *arthāntara*] is that in the case of *nyūnapada*, there is no such misconception. [The word] "of the Lord" (*aiśasya*)... [is used].
"How does he endure? How does he tolerate? How does he not feel aversion?"—this is the meaning.

Furthermore, this statement applies only to an object of aversion; since a "jewel among women" is not fit for aversion, it follows that indifference toward such a jewel is what is actually fit for aversion. Therefore, he says "he desires to be indifferent," [implying] that here, the particle *ca* following the direct object indicates that it shares a single action with something other than that object; consequently, there arises the delusion that even the "jewel among women" is connected to the action of enduring (*mṛṣyati*).

And in this context, the reading "Rāvaṇa" alone is appropriate, not "Bhārgava. For that [latter] one, who has conquered his senses, there is no hatred toward the neglect of women; thus, he is excused because of the absence of any desire for her. As it is said: "A virtuous man submerged in misfortune, a woman whose breasts have sagged, and a villain honored in an assembly—all these cause torment to my heart."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ja) He states the distinction from its associates with the words "a virtuous person" (*sajjana*). In the assembly (*samajyāyām*), that is, in the gathering (*samāje*).
The definition of *tattva* (the incongruous) is the description of two things, one superior and one inferior, as being connected by a single action.
Here, the virtuous man and the beautiful woman are both excellent, while their companion, the wicked man, is not; thus, there is a disparity between the companions (*sahacarabhinnatvam*).

“His command is cherished by the crest-jewel of Indra; the scriptures are his fresh eyes; devotion is his toward the Lord of Beings who wields the Pināka bow; and his abode is the divine city of Laṅkā.”
"His birth was in the lineage of Brahmā; oh, such a bridegroom as this is not easily found! Yet he would not be so if he were Rāvaṇa. Indeed, where can all virtues ever be found together?"

In this context, the matter is not concluded merely by the words "not Rāvaṇa. *Vijñapriyā* (vi, jha) states that this refers to being released at an improper place— the reality is that "being released" (*muktatā*) means completion at an inappropriate place, a location where completion is unsuitable.

"Ājñā" (the command)—this is the statement of Śatānanda, the priest of Janaka, expressing indifference toward Śauṣkala, the priest of Rāvaṇa, who had been sent by Rāvaṇa to request Sītā’s hand in marriage, following a prior praise of Rāvaṇa:
"Oh, what a marvel! Such a bridegroom as this is not found; for his command is cherished even by the crest-jewel of Indra."
The meaning is that even his command is worn on the crest by Śakra like a jewel.
Likewise, the scriptures themselves are a new, ever-fresh eye, because actions are performed solely through the vision of the scriptures.
And likewise, there is devotion toward the Lord of beings, the living creatures—the Great Lord who wields the Pināka bow.
Likewise, there is the divine city of Laṅkā as his place of residence;
likewise, there is his birth in the lineage and family of Druhiṇa (Brahmā).
All of these are indeed causes for excellence, provided that he were not Rāvaṇa by virtue of his wicked conduct.
The meaning is that if he were not one whose name is renowned for being helpful to the world and for causing cries of distress [to his enemies], then such a boon would not be obtained.
Therefore, the implication is that he must certainly be abandoned.
He asks again: "But where?
[The meaning is: "In all people, all qualities exist; but where indeed are the virtues? Is there not some quality that is also a fault? This is the sense.
And thus, the meaning is that for all [beings], qualities are indeed mixed with defects;
it does not mean that there exists a place where all qualities are present.

This is because the existence of all qualities has not been stated [in the text], and therefore it would be inappropriate to provide a justification for it; rather, having mentioned the existence of all qualities, it is precisely the existence of some defect that has been stated.
Regarding this:

[the objection] ending with "not Rāvaṇa" is because Rāvaṇa alone is worthy of being abandoned; whereas [the response] beginning with "But where indeed... is because he alone is worthy of being accepted.
Locanā:
(Lo, Ī) "Ājñāśaka" refers to Druhiṇa, that is, Brahmā.
A "vara" is a son-in-law or an excellent groom, distinguished by such qualities as those mentioned.
Rāvaṇa is the one who causes the world to cry out.
The meaning is this: all virtues reside in this ten-faced one;
causing the world to cry out is his sole defect.
And therefore, because the word *rāvaṇa* has shifted its meaning to another sense, it constitutes a defect precisely as a literal expression (*vācya*).
It would have been appropriate to conclude the sentence with this much alone.

As for what was further stated, beginning with "Where indeed... and so forth, by that [statement], the presentation of the meaning at the previous location was not abandoned; thus, this is the defect known as *apadokti* (improper phrasing).
Should it not be said that [the phrase] "nanu kva punaḥ" and so forth is a redundant repetition because it functions as a corroborative statement?
No, for this sentence is employed precisely to demonstrate the irrationality of Rāvaṇa’s position; thus, its use as a corroboration would be inappropriate.
If that were the case, a sentence intended to be stated as logical would have been stated as logical.
Regarding the phrase, “What can we describe of this ocean, a treasure-house of diamonds?”—
here, it would have been more appropriate to state it simply as “a treasure-house of jewels,” without such a specific qualification.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ña) Regarding the statement of distinction (*viśeṣokti*) where there is no distinction, he says: "of diamonds" (*hīrakāṇām*), etc.—herein.
For it is appropriate to speak of the indescribability [of excellence] due to the non-attainment of the highest degree of excellence (*utkarṣāparyāpti*).
The sense is that, however, when other jewels are absent, there is the cognition of the non-attainment of the highest degree of excellence regarding the object which is merely a diamond.
“The whirlpool itself is your navel, your eyes are blue lotuses, and the waves are your bracelets; therefore, you are a pond of the waters of loveliness.”
In this context, the restriction that "it must be a whirlpool" need not be stated.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ṭa): He states the formulation of a restriction where there is no restriction: "it must be a whirlpool."
*Valayaḥ* means a woman’s bracelet.

In this context, things such as the navel and so forth are to be predicated as having the nature of a *rūpaka* (poetic metaphor). Regarding the phrase "the navel itself is the *āvarta* (whirlpool)," the particle *eva* must be applied to exclude any other [feature] that might be fit for the metaphor of a whirlpool;
thus, it is "the *āvarta* itself."

Regarding the instrumental sense (*karaṇe*), however, he says "here" (*atrety*) because, since there is no other property in the navel that is capable of being represented as a pool to serve as a counter-correlate (*vyāvarttanīya*), the particle *eva* (only) used for the sake of such a restriction is not appropriate.

One should not suspect that the word *nābhiḥ* (navel) is a case of misplaced emphasis (*āvṛtti*), where the *eva*—which is properly placed after the word *nābhi*—is instead found after the subsequent word [i.e., *eva* is read as *nābhireva*].
This is because, due to the specific nature of its expression as a restrictive statement (*niyamokti*), the distinction between them must be incorporated therein.
"In the nights, women go to meet their lovers, veiled in blue garments.
Here, the specific nature of the night—namely, that it is dark—should have been expressed by the word *tamisrāsu* (in the dark nights).
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ṭha) He states a specific instance of contradiction (*viśeṣaviparyaya*): "They go," etc.—*nicola* means a garment.

Regarding the word "here"—since a blue garment is appropriate only for the *tamisrā* (the dark night), it is improper to speak of the night in its general sense as being characterized by moonlight, when it is more fitting to describe it specifically as *tamisrā*; this is the meaning. [As the saying goes: "What will those who are immersed in pleasures that are sweet at first sight not do?"
In this context, the restriction must be stated as "at the very outset.

*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ḍa) states the expression that reverses this restriction—namely, "at the very outset"—and explains: "O sir, what indeed do they not do? The meaning is: they certainly perform only what ought not to be done.

Regarding the word *atra* (here): since immersion [into the Self] is not something that should not be performed at all times (*sarvakāla-surasa-tve*), the meaning is that the restriction "only at the outset" (*āpātata eva*) must be stated in order to exclude [immersion] at all other times.
Now, if the expressed meaning were not stated, there would be an absence of the particle *api* in the passage beginning with "even a slight transgression" (*vyatikrama-lavam*).
And in this case, what is the difference between [the particle] *eva* and *iti*?
To this, [the author] says: “The very statement of a restriction (*niyama*) is the domain for the reversal of that restriction (*niyamaparivṛtti*). This is not so, according to the *Locanā*.

The meaning is that the very non-statement of a restrictive rule (*niyama*) constitutes its exception (*apavāda*). The underlying intention is that there is no evidence for [distinguishing them], as they belong to the same class (*ekajāti*).
This is because, even though both exist, there is no determining factor (*niyāmaka*) for assigning the status of being a verbal or a semantic defect to one over the other.

If it is asked, "What then is the distinction?"— the difference is that in cases such as "a slight transgression" (*vyatikramalava*), the perception of the fault occurs immediately after the utterance of the words, whereas here it occurs after the comprehension of the meaning.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ḍha) He raises a doubt regarding the distinction [of this case] because its expressed meaning has not been stated—namely, "But surely... Here, however, the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "but here, in the case of the letter *e*, there is an absence. Having shown that a resolution is possible here, he speaks in order to point out another defect: "In this case, of the restriction... In this context, the very non-statement of the restriction constitutes a distinct, specific instance that is the object of the reversal of the restriction.
This is the meaning.

And thus, according to the principle that a universal operates only by excluding particular objects, the meaning is that the non-denotation of an eternal, indivisible denotable object constitutes its [specific] purpose.

Since this resolution must be endured, he states another fault: "If it is argued..."—meaning, in the case where one is a verbal defect and the other is a semantic defect among the two, namely word and meaning.

In the phrase "due to the absence of a regulator" (*niyāmakābhāvāt*), it should be supplemented with the thought that "the very absence of a regulator is the fault. Regarding the question "What then is the way? (*tatkā gatiḥ*), the meaning is: "Therefore, what is the remedy?
He provides the answer: "In the passage beginning with 'even a slight transgression' (*vyatikramalavam*)," and so forth.
"Immediately after the utterance of the word":
the meaning is that, due to the expectation that there should not be even a moment's transgression [of the sequence], [the subsequent cognition] arises immediately after the utterance.
"But here," however...

The meaning is: "in the case of a statement that reverses the rule" such as "sweet at first sight" (*āpātasurasa*). "Immediately after the comprehension of the meaning" means that while being sweet at first sight is indeed perceived first, immediately thereafter there is always an exclusion of its being truly sweet; this is what is meant by the synthesis of the meaning.

Thus, although the distinction between defects of word and meaning was previously accepted by earlier authorities based on whether or not they tolerate the substitution of words, it ultimately results in this: a defect that cannot withstand the substitution of words is exclusively a defect of word;
and that which is to be understood prior to the comprehension of the syntactical connection of the word-meanings is also a defect of word.
And that which is to be understood immediately after the comprehension of the meaning is the "basis of the meaning" (*arthāśraya*).

Thus, one should understand that even in cases such as "irregularity of word-order" (*aniyamaparivṛtti*), there is a distinction [from other defects] because it constitutes an additional factor (*adhikapada*).

However, regarding "having another purpose that is not intended," as in the verse beginning with "by the arrow of Rāma-Manmatha," it is considered a defect of the sentence (*vākyadoṣa*) because it is intended to pervade the entire sentence by way of a restrictive rule (*niyama*).
However, in cases such as indecency (*aślīlatva*) and so forth, there is no necessary pervasion of the entire sentence.
*Vijñapriyā*:
This has been stated on the basis of experience.

In reality, however, in some cases, the author’s own intention is the sole determinant of whether a fault resides in the word or the meaning; otherwise, regarding both the *avimṛṣṭavidheyāṃśa* (failure to indicate the predicate) and the *duṣkrama* (bad order), since both depend equally on a reversal in the arrangement of words, what would be the criterion for deciding that one is a verbal fault while the other is a semantic fault?
Thus, although he himself stated that the determiner of what constitutes a defect in word and meaning applies universally, it is in some cases inconsistent.
This is because defects of word such as "unconventionality" (*aprayuktatva*) are understood immediately after the meaning is apprehended;

whereas a defect of meaning such as "harshness of sense" (*kaṣṭārthatva*) is not understood until the meaning has first been apprehended—since the cognition arises that the word itself is the conveyor of the meaning—and because it is understood only immediately after the word has been perceived.

Therefore, in order to state that there are only two kinds of restrictors (*niyāmaka*)—namely, that which was mentioned by the ancients as a restrictor in certain cases, and that which is a restrictor in our own statement—he says "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*).
This means that at the final conclusion of the restrictor honored by the predecessors, it results in this very way.
He states that same point which is about to be explained: "Accompanied by the function of words" (*śabdavṛttisahita*).
Here, the phrase "when the meaning is identical" is to be understood as an ellipsis.
For example, in the expression "pallavākṛtiraktoṣṭhī," even though *ākṛti* is used in the sense of *ākāra*, it remains a verbal fault.

However, because meaningless sounds, harsh syllables, and the like lack a corresponding meaning, they do not fall within the scope of this rule; rather, it is only that which is perceived immediately after the utterance of a word that falls within the scope of the aforementioned rule.

Thus, even in the case of an ineffective [word] such as "hanti," this very same rule applies. He demonstrates that very rule he has stated: "And that which [is perceived] immediately after the comprehension of the meaning."

The fault of meaning, such as *aniyama* (lack of restriction) and *parivṛtti* (inversion), and the fault of word, such as *adhikapada* (redundancy), [are distinct]. Even here, one should understand the distinction between them based on the very distinctions we have stated; thus he says, "And so" (*evaṃ ca*).
He states something else as the determinant for the fault of sentence, namely that the meaning of a word is unintended (*amatapadārthatva*); thus he says, "Unintended" (*amata*).
"Pervasiveness of the sentence" (*vākyavyāpitva*) means pervasion of the entire sentence in the form of a complete verse.

However, regarding the defect of indecorous meaning (*aślīlārthatva*), even though it pervades the sentence, it is classified as a "semantic defect" (*arthadoṣa*) because it follows the presence and absence of the semantic connection; with this in mind, he demonstrates its pervasiveness of the sentence by saying "in the case of indecorousness and so forth.
This means "in the case of semantic indecorousness and so forth."
Locanā:
(lo, ū) The phrase "by way of endurance and non-endurance" implies "immediately following [the previous discussion].

Regarding endurance under the substitution of words (*śabdaparivṛttisahatva*), examples include harshness of sound (*śrutikaṭutva*), deficiency, and the presence of discordant phonemes (*pratikūlavarṇatva*).
That which is to be understood prior to the cognition of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of word-meanings is, for example, the deficiency or redundancy of words and so forth;
in the verse beginning with *rāmamanmathaśareṇa*, etc., the phrase "even though it is to be understood immediately after the cognition of the meaning" is to be supplied as the remainder.

Regarding the phrase "due to vulgarity and so forth": the meaning is that since [such defects] can occur—whether they pervade the entire sentence, as in "hantumeva" (only to kill), or reside in a single word, as in "vivareṣiṇaḥ" (seeking an opening)—they are not necessarily defects of the sentence as a whole. For example: "Having gladdened his own side, he will destroy the opposing side.
Here, what is intended as the predicate (the thing to be enjoined) is: "Having destroyed the opposing side, he will gladden his own side."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ta) He states the lack of propriety regarding the injunction with the words "ānandita" etc.
The essential nature [of this fault] consists in the imposition of an intended meaning upon that which is unfit for the fulfillment of such an injunction.

The meaning here is that the propriety of the completion of the intended purpose lies solely in the act of bestowing joy upon one's own side immediately after the destruction of the opposing side, and not in the act of destroying the opposing side itself.

Nor should it be argued that there is a lack of clarity regarding the predicate (*vidheya*) here; for while the status of being a predicate is not perceived in the former case, it is indeed perceived as the predicate in this case.
This is because of the distinction that [the former] lacks the propriety of attaining the intended meaning (*tātparya*). "O Moon, the ornament upon the crest of Caṇḍīśa!"
O dispeller of the world's darkness!
O taker of the lives of those separated from their lovers! Do not torment me in vain.
In this statement by the lover separated from his beloved, the meaning of the third quarter is not to be restated. *Vijñapriyā* (vi, tha) states that restating it would be improper: "Caṇḍīśa," etc.
The essence [of this figure] is that the qualification of the subject (*anuvādya*) is in contradiction with the injunction (*vidhi*).
This is a statement by a woman separated from her lover addressed to the moon. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "O Moon, do not distress me in vain."
The three vocatives beginning with "Caṇḍīśa" are likewise [appropriate] because He, being of a single nature at that time, is addressed as such.
The first two qualifiers are intended to demonstrate His greatness.
The meaning of the third term, "prāṇa," and so forth, is that it is improper for Him to have a form that does not benefit Him.

“Just as you were firmly embraced here around the neck by one whose limbs were shrouded in passion with a sword-blade, and as you were seen falling even upon elephants from the hands of other men—he, being attached to her, cares for nothing else; let this be known to you. Therefore, by the command of Fortune, she has gone as if to the ocean to be proclaimed among the servants; so too has his fame departed.”
Here, although the statement was concluded with the words "let it be known to you," it is taken up again with the words "by him" and so forth.
Now, he states the defects of rasa:
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, da) He states the nature of "redundancy after completion" (*nirmukta-punarukta*)—namely, "the *lagna*," etc.—as follows: the nature of redundancy after completion refers to the restatement of a causal factor (*kāraka*) that has already been concluded.
The sense is that "completion followed by resumption" (*samāpta-punarāttatā*), however, consists essentially in the repetition of an adjective.
"The *lagna*," and so forth.

The meaning is that the fame of whichever king has reached the ocean—that is, extends as far as its shores—his fame is such. Here, a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is suggested: "By the command of Śrī. This implies that Śrī, the daughter of the ocean, has appointed her own servant, Fame, to report the transgression of her husband toward her father. Thus, there is an injunction for Fame to speak.
He states the *niyoga* (the specific application): "The ascendant" (*lagnam*), etc.
By that staff of youth—which, as the referent of a feminine noun, is presided over by a secondary woman—[the king's] enemy's throat alone was embraced. Of what sort [was that staff]?
Its limbs were covered by passion—that is, redness—and likewise by affection.

Likewise, here in this world, the elephant-goad (*yāsiyaṣṭi*)—falling upon the *mātaṅgas*, that is, the elephants themselves, as well as upon the *mātaṅgas*, that is, the *ṣiḍgas* (outcaste lovers)—is seen by the "enemy-men," that is, by other men who are indeed "excellent men" (*prakṛṣṭapuruṣa*).
By this, witnesshood is demonstrated.
Let it be known to my father, the Ocean: "My husband, being attached to such an unworthy woman, does not consider anything good or bad regarding the King."
The meaning is: "I was given to the servants by him, as if to say, 'By this reckoning of the auspicious and inauspicious.
This is a praise, for by disregarding fear of enemies through the assistance of his sword-blade, even the servants were made prosperous.
Here, the word *iti* is not intended to express the case-role (kāraka) of the object; rather, everything up to the end is to be understood as the object-kāraka (*vedanīyaṃ karmakārakam*).
