And that [fact] has been concluded with the words, "let it be known to you.
Furthermore, the phrase "by him I was given" is employed again as the agent of the karma to be experienced.
— Locanā:
Regarding the term *lagna*: *rāga* means redness, crimson, and passion;
*mātaṅgas* refers to elephants and also to Cāṇḍālas.
The expression of rasa by its own name [as if it were] something superior or distinct from others applies equally to the permanent (sthāyin) and transitory (saṃcārī) emotions. (VisSd 7.12)

The inclusion of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth that constitute the essence of the obstacle, as well as the difficult, inferred implication of the ensuants (*anubhāva*) and excitants, [is the function of suggestion]. (VisSd 7.13)

Untimely expansion and contraction, as well as repeated flashes of light, failure to maintain the focus on the primary subject, and the description of what is not a constituent part [of the visualization]. (VisSd 7.14)

Excessive expansion of the constituent parts (*aṅga*), the inversion of the primary elements (*prakṛti*), impropriety of meaning, and other such factors are considered defects pertaining to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, dha) He states the defects of rasa with the words "of rasa" (*rasasya*).
The connection here is that the term "even for the permanent and transitory emotions" (*sthāyisaṃcāriṇor api*) also implies expression by its own name.
"Obstructive" (*paripanthī*) means the mention of excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth belonging to a rasa that is antagonistic [to the intended one].
Regarding "suggestion" (*ākṣepa*):

the meaning is that suggestion—namely, the complete and intense contemplation of the ensuants (*anubhāva*) and the determinants (*vibhāva*)—is stated to be a defect [if it occurs] as a mere cognition.
"At the wrong time" means at an inappropriate moment; "expansion and interruption" refers to the expansion and abandonment of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). This is the sense.

Regarding "inappropriateness of meaning" (*arthānaucitya*)— which refers to that which is devoid of aesthetic emotion (*anaṅga*), whose essence is not the *rasa*, and which does not contribute [to it]— the phrase "other than what has been stated" means that the inappropriateness of meaning consists in something other than what was previously mentioned.
"The word for *rasa*" (*rasasya svaśabdaḥ*) refers both to the word *rasa* itself and to words such as *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) and so forth.
For example, in sequence:
"Upon beholding that fawn-eyed woman, an indescribable emotion arose within us," and "Having gazed upon the orb of the moon, my inner self was immersed in love."
An example of the permanent emotion (sthāyibhāva) being expressed by its own word is as follows: “When you came within the range of her vision, delight was born in her.
(Vijñapriyā)

Regarding the phrase "having observed her" (*tām udīkṣya*): here, in the first half [of the verse], the word *rasa* is the expressive term, while in the second half, the word *śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment) is the expressive term.

Now, one might object: "The aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) arises for the listener alone from hearing the poem, and not for the speaker because of his own love and so forth; so how can the 'speaker's flavor' (*vaktṛ-rasa*) be said to be the expressed meaning here? If this is raised, we say no. This is because in the expression *rasasya*, the meaning is "of the stable emotional state" (*sthāyibhāvasya*). Thus, it refers to the speaker’s underlying emotion.
Nor should it be argued that such a distinction is untenable because the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) cannot be spoken of separately from what is denoted by its own specific term;

for the separate mention is made precisely due to the difference in the expressive words, since the permanent emotion itself is expressed here by the word *rasa*—which denotes the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and so forth—as well as by the term *sthāyibhāva*.
Therefore, in this context, it is the permanent emotion alone that is expressed by the word *rasa*.
"Furthermore, the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* has written that an object characterized by rasa and so forth is not to be expressed even in a dream;
yet [the author] states that it is expressible by means of a word denoting a permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), as in the word ‘was born’ (*ajāyata*).
An example of the expressibility of a transitory emotion (*vyabhicārin*) by its own specific term is as follows:"
“*The innocent girl became bashful during the kissing of her beloved.*” Here,

in the first quarter, the reading “*āsīnmukulitākṣī sā*” (she had her eyes closed like buds) would have been more appropriate, as it describes bashfulness by way of its external manifestation (*anubhāva*).
*Vijñapriyā:*
Regarding the term "transitory" (*vyabhicārin*): the ellipsis is to be supplied as "of that which is capable of attaining the status of a *bhāva*.
And its attainment occurs only when it is suggested by a sentence that is free of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*).
In this case, since the enjoined quality of "possessing shame" is understood through a sentence free of expectancy, it certainly possesses the capacity to attain the status of a *bhāva*.
However, there is a fault [only] when that [feeling] is expressed by its own specific word [as a subordinate element].

When it is understood through a sentence possessing expectancy (*sākāṅkṣa*), there is no fault in expressing it by its own word provided it has not yet attained the state of being a fully manifested emotion (*bhāvatāprāpti*). For example: "The young girl, her face bowed with shame, was kissed for a long time by her laughing lover..."—here, the mention of "shame" by its own word is not a fault, as it has not yet reached the state of being a fully manifested emotion (*bhāva*) as a qualifier of the object to be described.
[This is] a fault.
Locanā:

(lo, ṝ) Regarding the statement "by way of the manifestations"—for it is the transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*), manifested through their respective physical and verbal expressions (*anubhāva*), that are to be relished by sensitive connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*).
And here, where there is a description of several transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*) through their effects (*anubhāva*) in one place, whereas they are expressed by their own words elsewhere,
there is not merely a defect of rasa and so forth;
rather, there is also a sentence-level defect known as "redundant word" (*adhikapada*).
For example: "The young girl, her face bowed with shame, was kissed for a long time by her laughing lover. And: "Do not be angry, O slender-limbed one;
know that youth is unstable."

In this context, the description of the instability of youth is an *aṅga* (subordinate element) of the *śāntarasa* (the sentiment of tranquility), which acts as an antagonist to the *śṛṅgārarasa* (the erotic sentiment), and it serves as the *vibhāva* (determinant cause) for that very *śāntarasa*. Therefore, its inclusion within the *śṛṅgāra* is not appropriate.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, pha) He states the inclusion of the *vibhāva* that is an *aṅga* of a sentiment acting as an antagonist: "Pride" (*māna*).

The meaning is this: when a particular stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) residing in the spectator attains the state of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), the communication—by that very same speaker—of the excitants (*vibhāva*) of another flavor that obstructs the intended flavor is a defect.

In the example "Do not practice pride" (*mānaṃ mā kuru*), the stable emotion of love (*rati*), which is attaining the state of *rasa* in the spectator, resides in the speaker; however, the excitant of its opposite, the flavor of tranquility (*śāntarasa*), is "instability in youth," and this has been stated by that very same person. Thus he says: "In this case...
And so: "Abandon pride, enough with battles; youth once gone does not return again."

In the verse from the *Raghuvamśa*: "When it was as if announced by the cuckoos, 'The mind of Smara [Kāma] delights in this,' the beloved companions rejoiced," the description of the instability of youth is not a defect;
for here, the very emotion (*bhāva*) of intense passion residing in the beloved companions attains the status of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) within the audience.

It is not that the instability of youth was mentioned by her beloved friends; rather, it was mentioned by the cuckoos, so there is no fault. In this very context, the expression of the instability of youth itself should be understood as a counter-emotion (*paripanthyanubhāva*), even though it was not explicitly stated by the author.
— *Locanā*:
(lo, ḷ) The meaning is that [the emotion] is contrary to the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*).
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "of the determinants (*vibhāva*) etc.," the consequents (*anubhāva*) and transitory states (*sañcārin*) are included.
Among these, an example of the inclusion of a contrary consequent is as follows: "Seeing a traveler on the road eager for sexual union, the fawn-eyed woman..."
Having abandoned all sensory objects, she departed for another forest.
In this case, going to the forest because of having renounced all sense objects is an ensuant (anubhāva) of the sentiment of tranquility (śāntarasa).
Otherwise, however, going to the forest is sometimes a subordinate element (guṇa) [of another rasa], such as in the context of a secret tryst (abhisāra) and so forth.
The same applies to the transitory mental states (vyabhicāribhāvas) as well.
"While the cool-rayed moon whitens the surface of the world and gladdens the eyes of the people, let that slender maiden with her smiling face, who has cast but a slight sidelong glance, be beheld."

In this case, since the [poetic figures] result in the excitant (*uddīpana*) and the objective determinants (*ālambana-vibhāva*) of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), they involve a strained interpretation.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi,
ba) states, "It makes white," thereby clarifying [the point] through a strained interpretation of the ensuant (*anubhāva*).
"Beheld" means by the man;
the "excitant" is the moon.
The object is the heroine.
The meaning is that the two [the eyes] are indicators of the experience—which culminates in the widening of the eyes with joy—precisely through the excellence of their aspiration;
for if the beholder were in a state of tranquility, it would be possible even for the eyes to close due to dispassion.
However, through the sequence of connecting the context, there is the manifestation of the described emotional states (*anubhāva*).
Locanā (*Lo*, *e*): "They culminate in the emotional states."
If there were a culmination in rasa (aesthetic flavor), it would be clearly evident that the casting of glances and so forth function as *anubhāvas* (consequent effects).

However, in this case, the casting of glances and other such acts are merely the effects of her love directed toward the hero; they have arisen here in conjunction with something else, because they cause an immediate perception that is not yet certain.

Alternatively, the meaning is that since the physical form (*rūpa*) of a certain hero being gazed upon has not become an *anubhāva* that awakens her love, there is no culmination in the *śṛṅgāra-rasa* (erotic sentiment) due to the presence of the *vibhāvas* (determinants) such as the casting and scattering of glances.
“He abandons his delight, his intellect is shattered, he stumbles excessively, and repeatedly reels about;
alas, such a dire state violently overcomes his body—what can we do in this matter?”

In this context, since the avoidance of pleasure and so forth can also occur in [the experience of] compassion and other [emotions], the excitant (*vibhāva*) in the form of a beloved woman must be inferred with difficulty. *Vijñapriyā* (vi, bha) states that the excitant is to be conceived with difficulty: "she avoids," etc.
In all instances such as "pariharati" (he avoids), the augment *mum* is applied by the agent.
The word "bata" expresses lamentation; its syntactical connection is: "Alas, his body is afflicted by these uneven [strokes].
"Prasabham" means by force.
Regarding "herein"—this too is to be understood with difficulty through the connection to the context.

An example of untimely expansion (*akāṇḍaprathana*) is as follows: in the second act of the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*, while many heroes are being slaughtered, there is the untimely expansion of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) between Duryodhana and Bhānumatī. An example of interruption (*cheda*) is as follows: in the *Vīracarita*, when the mutual fury between Rāghava and Bhārgava has reached its peak, Rāghava says, "I am going to remove my marriage bracelet."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ma) Kaṅkaṇamocana is a specific auspicious rite performed after the wedding. It is a repeated wearing [of ornaments], as for example in the lamentation of Rati in the Kumārasambhava.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ya) Regarding the "lamentation of passion": "Then she, once again overwhelmed, her breasts grey from embracing the earth, with her hair disheveled, lamented as if making the very ground share in her sorrow."

Having begun thus, while the continuous flow of the pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa-rasa*) was proceeding and spring was being beheld— “Beholding him, she wept bitterly and struck her chest, which was pressed by her breasts”—
having expanded [the description] in this way, there is again a contraction:
Locanā.

(Lo, Ai) Regarding *rativilāpa* (lamentation over love): through the passage beginning with "then, being devoted to delusion," even though the sentiment of compassion (*karuṇa*) had reached full development, the passage "then she again became overwhelmed" creates a sense of distaste, like giving food once more to one whose throat is already filled with food. An example of the failure to maintain the primary subject (*aṅgin*) is found in the fourth act of the *Ratnāvalī*, where Sāgarikā is forgotten upon the arrival of Bābhravya.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ra) "The forgetfulness regarding Sāgarikā"—Sāgarikā is Ratnāvalī; she is the heroine in that drama.

The glorification of the non-essential (anaṅga) is, for example, when in the *Karpūramañjarī*, having disregarded the description of spring composed by the king and the heroine themselves, there is instead the praising of that described by the bard. The excessive expansion of the essential (aṅga) is, for example, the amorous dalliances of celestial nymphs and so forth in the *Kirātārjunīya*. *Vijñapriyā*: [This is the commentary on the above.]
Regarding "of the bodiless one" (anaṅgasya)—the meaning is: of that which does not assist the rasa under discussion.
Regarding "described by bards"—the word "by the king" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
In Bhāravi’s *Kirātārjunīya*,
there are characters who are divine, non-divine, and both divine and non-divine;
these possess the qualities of the *dhīrodātta* (noble and self-controlled) and other types of heroes.
These [types of *prakṛtis*] also possess the qualities of being superior, inferior, or middling.
Locanā:
[The author] explains the fault called "deviation from the *prakṛti*" with the words beginning "the *prakṛtis*," and so forth.
The divine are Mahendra and others, as well as Śrī Kṛṣṇa and others;
the non-divine are Duṣyanta and others;
the divine-and-non-divine are Śrī Rāmacandra and others—this and so forth has already been stated previously.

Although it is possible for [the hero] to take on any one of the types such as the *dhīrodātta* (noble and self-controlled), he is generally characterized primarily by *vīra* (heroic) and other such rasas.
Their definitions have been stated.
Among these, when someone is described in a manner contrary to how they actually are, that is the fault known as *prakṛtiviparyaya* (inversion of nature).
For example, the slaying of Vālin by Rāma—who is *dhīrodātta* (noble and self-controlled)—under the pretext of being *dhīroddhata* (bold and haughty);

or as in the *Kumārasambhava*, the description of the erotic sentiment (*saṃbhoga-śṛṅgāra*) between the two supreme deities, Pārvatī and Parameśvara. Regarding this, some say: "This description of the sexual union of the parents is utterly improper."
Vijñapriyā:
In [the verse beginning with] "divyā" and so forth, the meaning is "of the divine and other heroines.
"Divine" refers to the gods; "non-divine" refers to humans.
"Divine and non-divine" refers to those who are incarnations of gods or humans; the meaning is that they are his very own natures (*prakṛti*).
He demonstrates what was stated [in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*] as "another [type of] impropriety of meaning":
Locanā:
(Lo, Au) Regarding what was stated—that it is improper to describe the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) in relation to supreme deities—the intention is this:

those secret matters that manifest the erotic sentiment and are unfit to be described concerning one's parents should not be described when they pertain to supreme deities; otherwise, [one would have to describe them] as in the *Raghuvamśa*, regarding Rāmacandra after he had regained his own kingdom following the slaying of Rāvaṇa.
A description of Sītā’s conversation, or anything else of that nature composed by a great poet, would be improper;
indeed, such descriptions in various ways throughout the works of all great poets would be inconsistent.
Likewise, [improper would be] the going of non-divine beings to heaven or the netherworld, the leaping across the ocean, and so forth.
This matter—the account of Kuvalayāśva and others of great majesty, which is well-known from the Itihāsas and other sources—is indeed fit for description;
otherwise, such a description would itself be a source of defect.
In this way, the description of any other improper action should be understood as the defect known as *prakṛtiviparyaya* (inversion of the natural order).
Another form of impropriety (*anaucitya*) consists in the description of place, time, and so forth in a manner contrary to reality;
for if that were the case, the possibility of turning disciples toward the teachings would be lost due to the appearance of unreality in the poetry.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, śa) Another form of impropriety is "inappropriateness regarding place and time.
Describing human speech in heaven is inappropriate with respect to place;
describing the characteristics of one season during another season is inappropriate with respect to time.
Locanā:

(lo, a) She points out another impropriety with the word "another" (*anyat*), meaning [impropriety regarding] place, time, and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), she includes the heroine’s kicking with her foot and the like, as well as the hero’s anger.
The boldness of a young girl; the excessive modesty of a mature courtesan;
and the noble lineage of the rival hero.

And so it has been said: "Even when describing the lineage, valor, learning, and other qualities of an enemy, it truly delights us when the excellence of the hero is proclaimed through his victory over him."
Thus,
while the description of the limbs of the deities begins with the head,
when the head itself is to be worshipped, the description is intended to begin from the feet.

For humans, it is not desired that description begins with the feet; rather, it is intended that description begins from the head. In this same manner, all instances of impropriety—which cause the disruption of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)—should be diligently avoided by good poets. As stated by the author of the *Dhvanyāloka*: "There is no cause for the disruption of *rasa* other than impropriety."
The application of propriety (*aucitya*), however, is the supreme secret (*upaniṣad*) of rasa;
apart from these [factors], there is no possibility of figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) or defects (*doṣa*). (7.15)
Regarding these aforementioned defects:

after stating the defects [beginning with] *vijñapriyā* (*vi*, *ṣa*), [the author] says "separate from these" (*ebhyaḥ pṛthak*) to indicate that even the defects of ornamentation (*alaṅkāradoṣa*) are included within these very same [categories].
Locanā:
(Lo, Ā) [Objection: "If these alone are the defects, then why are the defects of figures of speech mentioned by the ancients [separately]?
To this, he says: "From these," and so forth.
How is it that [the defect of] "non-distinctness" (*apṛthak*) does not apply to them?

He says: For instance, in a simile (*upamā*), there is "unfitness of meaning" (*anucitārthatva*) in cases of dissimilarity (*asādṛśya*) and impossibility (*asaṃbhava*), as well as when the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) possesses a lower or higher number of properties (*jāti*, *pramāṇa*, *gata*, *nyūnatva*, *adhikatva*); likewise, in a corroboration by a different matter (*arthāntaranyāsa*) and in the substantiation of a matter imagined (*utprekṣita-artha-samarthana*). *Vijñapriyā*: [This refers to the following examples: "The moon is like a lotus," where there is dissimilarity; "The sky is like a tortoise," where there is impossibility; "The face is like the moon," where the standard of comparison has fewer properties; "The face is like the moon," where it has more properties; and so forth. In a *arthāntaranyāsa*, such as "The earth is supported by the mountain-king; likewise, a noble person is supported by his own character," there is unfitness of meaning if the illustration is inappropriate. Similarly, in the substantiation of an imagined matter, such as "The moon is as if a thief of the night-lotuses," there is unfitness of meaning if the basis for the imagination is unsuitable. Thus, these defects do not apply to those [other figures].
(vi, sa) Regarding this, he states where each specific defect of ornamentation is subsumed: "In the case of simile (*upamā*)," etc.

"Lack of similarity" (*asādṛśya*) refers to the absence of resemblance between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*). "Impossibility" (*asambhava*) refers to the non-establishment of the object of comparison.
Regarding the term *jātipramāṇa*: *pramāṇa* here means measure (*parimāṇa*).

The meaning is that it constitutes an improper sense when, in relation to the genus of the object of comparison (*upameya*), the genus of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is either excessively deficient or excessive; and likewise, when, in relation to the measure of the object of comparison, the measure of the standard of comparison is either excessively deficient or excessive.

Thus, when an imagined object is supported by a corroborative instance (*arthāntaranyāsa*), the defect occurs at that very moment; the meaning is that this constitutes "inappropriateness of sense" (*anucitārthatva*).

Now, one might object: in the phrase "beasts in the sacrifice of battle," the revelation of the cowardice of heroes implies a censure of them, and this has been shown to be "inappropriateness of sense. However, when an imagined object is supported despite a lack of similarity or impossibility, such a form of impropriety does not exist; rather, the impropriety must be stated as the falsity of the matter being presented. If so, how can impropriety be common to both cases?

If it is argued that "the absence of propriety" (*aucityābhāva*) is precisely what constitutes this [defect], then since all defects are inherently improper, it would follow that this cannot be established as a specific variety of defect; this is true.
However, its defining characteristic is the absence of propriety itself, provided that it is not already subsumed under the definitions of other defects.
Examples in order:
“I weave the moon of poetry, which has the rays of extensive meaning.
Locanā:
(lo, i) Regarding the phrase “for instance”—here, there is no similarity between the poem and the moon.
“Your arrows fall like streams of blazing water.
Regarding the phrase "in succession" (*krameṇa*) in the commentary *Vijñapriyā*: there is a lack of similarity (*asādṛśya*) between this and the expression "I compose" (*grathnāmi*).
"Poetry is like the moon" is a simile (*upamā*).

Even if this were treated as a metaphor (*rūpaka*), the same fault would apply, because that too is rooted in similarity; for when a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is impossible—as in the case of "flaming"—flaming streams of water are not well-known.
If it is argued that this might instead be a "hyperbolic simile" (*abhūtopamā*), we say no.
Since the status of being an "unreal simile" (abhūtopamā) applies only where the well-known status of the object of comparison (*upamāna*) is established even through mere possibility,
as for example: "Your face shines forth like the essence of the luster of all lotuses gathered together somewhere"— the wise know this to be an unreal simile.

In this passage, by first presenting the possibility that Daṇḍin might somehow steal away the splendor of all lotuses from the Creator (Brahmā) through the word "anywhere" (*kvacit*), an "unreal simile" (*abhūtopamā*) is shown by means of such a comparison.

For this very reason, even in the phrase "like a creeper with the power of a sprout of young coral," since a creeper is seen upon the branches of trees such as the *vaṭa*, one conceives of a creeper upon the coral sprout and thus constructs that comparison.
However, in the present case, because fire in water is entirely contradicted by experience, it is impossible to conceive of a blazing stream of water.
Locanā:
(lo, ī) The blazing of streams of water is impossible.
“Like a caṇḍāla, this king is exceedingly reckless in battle.”
“The orb of the moon shines like a piece of camphor.

*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ka): He states that the genus of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is extremely inferior to the genus of the object of comparison (*upameya*), as in the example "like a Caṇḍāla."
In this case, there is an absolute inferiority of the *caṇḍāla* caste in comparison to the royal caste.

He provides an example of the absolute inferiority of the standard of comparison (*upamāna-parimāṇa*) in relation to the standard of comparison itself: "Like Śiva, this peacock shines with a blue throat. (*karpūra* etc.).
"This peacock shines like Śiva, having a blue throat. (*haravannīlakaṇṭho 'yaṃ virājati śikhāvalaḥ*).
“Your breasts are like mountains.
Vijñapriyā:
Thus he also speaks of the excessiveness of their genus and size, [saying] "like Śiva."
And [the word] "breasts" [is used].
A peacock is a "crest-strong" one (*śikhābala*).

Since the body of Hara possesses multiple individualities due to the difference in its states, "Hara-ness" (*haratva*) is also a genus (*jāti*), which is more extensive than "crest-strong-ness" (*śikhābhalatva*).
Locanā:
(lo, u) By the outcaste for the king;
by a piece of camphor for the moon.
There is a similarity between her throat and that of Hara (Śiva), and between her breasts and a mountain:
"He who protects the darkness hidden in his caves during the day, as if it were afraid of the sun."
"Even toward a lowly being who has sought refuge, those of lofty mind indeed feel an exceedingly great sense of 'mine'."
In such cases, it is entirely inappropriate to justify the appearance of an imagined object by treating its very nature as being non-existent; thus,
he provides a justification for the imagined object through the figure of *arthāntaranyāsa* [corroboration by a different fact], beginning with the words "from the sun" (*divākarāt*).
The Himalaya protects the darkness hidden in its caves from the sun;
here, it is poetically imagined (utprekṣate) that he does so "as if out of fear.
In this regard, he states a corroborative generalization (arthāntaranyāsa): "even one who is small..."

"By the greatness of those with high heads" means, by implication, of the great ones who possess lofty crowns, as well as of those with high peaks. Here, he points out the fault [in such cases] with the words "in instances such as these.
"Justification" (samarthanam) means establishing [the meaning] as being true.
The meaning is: since the fear of darkness is in every respect a false imagination, how can it be established as true by means of an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general proposition)?
Thus says Locanā.

In the section beginning with "divākarādau" (in the case of the sun and so forth), he demonstrates the impropriety in supporting a matter that has been conceived through poetic fancy (*utprekṣita*). The phrase "of the matter conceived through poetic fancy" and so on means that it appears precisely as something non-existent,
because it is the object of a mere possibility (*sambhāvanā*).
The owl is "fearful by day" (*divābhīta*).
Alternatively, "fearful by day" (*divā bhītam*) may be an adjective qualifying "darkness," meaning that which is afraid of the day. Such is the Himālaya.
*Śiras*, *śṛṅga*, or *mūrdhan* [are synonyms for "head"].
It is a fault when a word occurring in three quarters of a verse is not employed [in the other quarters],
as for example:
“At nightfall, that beautiful woman comes together with her affectionate kinsmen to the bower-mansion.”
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, gha) "Suddenly"—the meaning is that the heroine Sundarī, accompanied by her affectionate female companions, suddenly and with a smile, goes at that very moment to the bower-mansion when the lord of the night has risen.
Locanā:
Accompanied by her friends, suddenly, with speed, and together with laughter;
in this case of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), the word *yathā* is considered non-expressive (*avācaka*) because it serves as the concluding marker of the fancy.
— *Locanā*:
(lo, ṝ) For the word *yathā*, like words such as *iva* and others, is not a direct denoter (*vācaka*) of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
As in:
"This king protects the earth just as Dharma incarnate [protects it]."
Vijñapriyā:
Regarding "the state of indicating *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy)"—this means being employed for the purpose of expressing *utprekṣā*.
"This" refers to [the particle *iva*].

*Dharma* here means merit (*puṇya*); because it lacks a physical form, there is a poetic imagination (*utprekṣā*) of it as such, but it is not a comparison with a deity having a physical form, for in that case, the qualifying attribute "having a physical form" would result in redundancy.
Likewise, in alliteration (*anuprāsa*), "discordant phonemes" refers to those that contradict the prevailing *vṛtti*.
For example: "ovaṭṭai ullaṭṭai," and so forth.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ca) "Thus" means:
a contradiction of the style (*vṛtti*) is the presence of phonemes that are incompatible with its aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
“Ovaṭṭa” and so forth have been explained previously.
Locanā:
(lo, ḷ) Vṛtti is the operation directed toward rasa, which resides in specific phonemes.

And in the case of a simile (*upamā*), when there is an excess or deficiency of the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*), there is respectively the fault of "superfluous words" (*adhikapadatva*) and "deficient words" (*nyūnapadatva*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
[Regarding the phrase] "of the common property."

*Adhikatva* (excess) is the mention of a common attribute in the object of comparison (*upamāna*) that was not mentioned in the subject of comparison (*upameya*). *Nyūnatva* (deficiency) is the non-mention of a common attribute in the object of comparison that was mentioned in the subject of comparison.
Examples in order:
“Śambhu, whose splendor is white as snow, shines with the light of his eye like an autumnal cloud illuminated by lightning, appearing like a fragment of a dark rain-cloud.”
In this case, because the Lord's state of having a blue throat (*nīlakaṇṭha*) is not established, the fourth quarter [of the verse] is redundant.
*Vijñapriyā*:
Regarding "with the light of his eyes"—here, Śambhu is the object of comparison (*upameya*).
The autumn cloud is the point of comparison, and the lightning is the light of the eyes;
furthermore, there is indeed a mention of the two common properties: whiteness through ashes and the acquired brightness of the autumnal season.

However, because the blue-throated nature (*nīlakaṇṭhatva*) of Śambhu, the object of comparison (*upameya*), is not mentioned, there is a superiority in the autumnal cloud, the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), which possesses a similar attribute such as being dark-blue (*nīla*). This is what [the author] expresses with the word "here" (*atra*).
This rule applies specifically to a common attribute (*samānadharma*); but when another attribute is mentioned, there is no such restriction.
Just as in this very [verse], when the fourth quarter is formulated as "in the center of the circle of the sky" (*nabhomaṇḍalamadhyama*), Locanā says: "(Lo,
E) the state of being accompanied by *sa* and *ba* must be stated."
“Embraced by Kamalā, wearing a radiant pearl necklace, and the enemy of Mura, he shines like a dark cloud adorned with lightning.”
In this context, the deficiency of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) must be stated.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi,
jha) states its inferiority with the word "lotus" (*kamala*).
Embraced by Kamalā (Lakṣmī) and wearing a radiant necklace, the enemy of Mura shines like a dark rain cloud adorned with lightning; such is the meaning.

Here, he demonstrates by way of a stylistic turn (*bhaṅgyā*) that lightning, which occupies the place of Lakṣmī, is inferior to the girl who occupies the place of the pearl necklace—this is indicated by the phrase "here" (*atra*).
Locanā:
This is because the object of comparison (*upameya*), namely the pearl necklace, is explicitly mentioned.

In this very context, there is a breach of uniformity (*bhagnaprakrama*) regarding the difference in gender and number between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), as well as differences in tense, person, mood, and so forth.
The examples follow in order:
“The moon is pure like nectar.”; “sudheva vimalaścandraḥ” (the moon is pure like nectar).
“Her fame is white like moonlight.
Vijñapriyā:
[This refers] to this very same [verse]. (vi, ña)
The meaning is: "only in the case of simile. Regarding "the violation of the established order" (*bhagnaprakramatva*):

when the description of the object of comparison (*upameya*) begins with a certain gender and a specific number—such as singular, dual, or plural—and the description of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is expected to follow with that same gender and number, the violation of the order occurs if it is not stated accordingly. This is the meaning.
The meaning is that there is a break in the sequence (*bhagnaprakrama*) regarding the distinction between the present time and so forth,
because [the subject] is not expressed in the form required by the context.
Furthermore, in the phrase "sudheva," there is a difference in gender between feminine and masculine.
In the phrase "like moonlight" (*jyotsnā iva*), there is a difference in grammatical number:
"A certain indescribable splendor belonged to the two of them as they traveled in pure attire,
like the sky at the conjunction of the variegated moon and the sun when freed from frost."
In this case, the splendor of the moon and the painting as they truly are did not indeed exist [only then];
rather, it exists at all times.
— Locanā:
In this simile, by the phrase "it always occurs," there is a difference in time between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*).
In the example, "O slender one, you shine like a creeper," the creeper shines [at its own time], while you shine [now].
But you shine.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṭa) He states the difference in time with the words "some indescribable splendor" (kāpyabhikhyā).
The splendor (*abhikhyā*) or beauty of those two, Dilīpa and Sudakṣiṇā, was like the conjunction of the moon with the Citrā constellation in the month of Caitra;
indeed, it did not exist [otherwise], because while their beauty was constant, there is no intention to speak of it as being past.
Thus, in the phrase "at eva" (only thus), there is a distinction of persons.
Because the expression "the creeper shines" is possible;
and in the phrase, "May your son live long, like the sage Mārkaṇḍeya," the sage Mārkaṇḍeya is indeed still living.
Indeed, this is not to be enjoined by the word "may he live" (*jīvatu*).
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ṭha): There is a difference in the nature of the injunction between [the phrase] "may he live long" (*ciraṃ jīvatv*) and this.
And this is indeed a very minor fault, because the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is possible through transposition.
For this very reason, such usage occurs everywhere in poetry.
However, in this context, there is no fault where, despite a difference in gender or number, the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharmma*) does not undergo alteration.
The examples in order:
"The face shines like the moon. — *Locanā*.

Regarding the phrase "But here" (*iha tu*): this is the meaning. For in cases where, despite a difference in gender and so forth, a common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharmā*) establishes a connection for both the simile-source (*upamāna*) and the simile-target (*upameya*) as being non-different, there the cognition is not obstructed. In the example "The face... (*mukham*), the intended object to be established (*sādhya*) is the common sense-object consisting of the face and the moon, both of which appear (*bhāti*).
This same point applies further on as well:
"Clad in that attire, which was unlike that of other women and filled with sweetness,
he possessed a supreme splendor, like her own graceful charms."
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ḍa) When there is a difference in gender or number, the fact that the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) does not connect with both [the subject and the object] in its stated form is the seed of the fault.
However, if it is possible for it to connect with both in its stated form itself, then there is no fault; thus he says: "And here, [regarding] gender and number... etc.
Regarding the example "The face is like the moon":
here, the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is indeed identical in form in both cases, yet the two genders (*liṅga*) differ.
Regarding the difference in number (*vacana*), he says: "In that dress" (*tadveśa*).

Filled with sweetness and loveliness, her possession (āveśa) bears—meaning, it assumes—the highest beauty; this is the singular form of the root *dhṛ* (to hold/bear). Of what nature is it? It is unlike other women, being uncommon to any other woman (*anyastry-asādhāraṇa*).
This is the form of the root *dṛś* ending in the suffix *ṭak*.
These are like its delusions—for they too possess supreme beauty.
This is the form of the root *dhā* in the plural.

Thus, *madhuratābhṛtaḥ* means "possessing sweetness"; this is the form derived from the root *bhṛ* with the suffix *kvip*. Similarly, in the word *asadṛśaḥ*, this is also the form derived from [the root *sadṛś*] with the suffix *kvip*.

It has been stated that the violation of uniformity (*prakramabhanga*) in cases of differences in gender (*liṅga*) and so forth is included within other defects; the author now causes that [point] to be understood—by the phrase "in the previous examples.
This means: in examples such as "the moon is stainless like nectar" (*sudheva vimalaś candraḥ*), and so on.
*Locanā*.
In the phrase "sadṛśa" (lo, a), when it functions as an adjective qualifying the subject (*uddeśya*), the word *sadṛśa* ends in the singular;

in the alternative case, [the phrase] "filled with sweetness" (*madhuratayā bhṛta*) is also in the singular. When it functions as an adjective qualifying the confusion (*vibhrama*), the word *sadṛk* ends in the plural.
"Dadhati" is the singular form of the root *dhā*,
and [the other forms] are verbal forms (*tiṅanta*) of the root *dhā* in the plural.

In the previously cited examples, because the connection of only one of the two— the object of comparison (*upamāna*) or the subject of comparison (*upameya*)— with the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is established, there is a clear failure to carry through the intended meaning that was begun.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ḍha) "Of one alone" means that because the connection [of the simile] is established through a common property such as stainlessness and so forth for a single object of comparison (*upameya*) by virtue of having the same gender and so on, the connection cannot be established with a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) that possesses a different gender. This is the meaning.
Regarding the phrase "of that which has been introduced"—the meaning is "of that which was commenced" due to the requirement for connection with both [parts].
Thus, in the case of *anuprāsa* (alliteration), its futility constitutes the fault of "lack of significance" (*apuṣṭārthatva*).
For example: "anaṇuraṇanmaṇimekhalamaviralaśiñjānamañjumañjīram... [etc.]
The red-footed partridge,
as it wanders about, produces groundless anxiety.
Vijñapriyā:
"Thus" (evam)—the meaning is: regarding that fruitlessness which belongs to the qualifier employed for the sake of alliteration;
[the prefix] *anu* [is used].
This is the speech of a tranquil man upon seeing a courtesan walking with graceful charm: "O lady with ruddy feet!
Your wandering—that is, your movement—is the agent [of this action]."
The meaning is that, for men, it causes groundless longing—that is, it generates thoughts of love. Of what nature is this wandering?
It is such that there the jeweled girdle, strung with gems, resounds loudly—that is, not faintly.

"Wherein the anklets (*mañjīra*) and foot-ornaments (*nūpura*) jingle incessantly and sweetly"—in this case, because the speaker is tranquil, these specific qualifiers describing a movement that excites passion constitute "lack of purposeful meaning" (*apuṣṭārthatva*). Their inclusion is solely for the sake of alliteration (*anuprāsa*). Furthermore, although those qualifiers may be useful for the poet's own creative fancy (*kāmacintā*) despite being redundant, they lack relevance to the intended *śāntarasa* (the sentiment of tranquility), and thus there is "lack of purposeful meaning."
Locanā:

(Lo, Ā) The meaning is that [the word *lo*] is both useless and redundant (*apuṣṭārthatva*), because it serves no purpose for the subject matter (*prakṛta*) by virtue of its being composed of variegated colors (*citravarṇa*).

Thus, in the case of *samāsokti*, although the secondary object is understood through the power of common adjectives (*sādhāraṇaviśeṣaṇa*), its explicit mention again by means of a word [is redundant]; likewise, in the case of *aprastutapraśaṃsā*...

Since the intended meaning is understood through the mere suggestion (*vyañjanā*) alone, the verbal expression of that same meaning would be redundant. *Vijñapriyā* explains: "In this way, it is [redundant] in the case of *samāsokti*."
*Samāsokti* (Condensed Expression) is the suggestion of the non-contextual through the description of the contextual;
*Aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Praise of the Irrelevant) is the suggestion of the contextual through the description of the non-contextual.

In these two figures of speech, although the non-contextual and contextual meanings are suggested (*vyaṅgya*), the fact that they are nevertheless expressed by words (*śabdena tadupādānam*) constitutes nothing other than tautology (*punaruktatvam*). This is the meaning.
The examples in order are as follows:
“Though possessing passion for her eyes and a body that brings comfort and dispels heat,
the sun was driven out from his abode in the sky by the courtesan Night, who was devoid of wealth.”
In this context, her status as a courtesan is understood by the mere phrase "the western direction.
Regarding that, *Vijñapriyā* (vi, tha) states that there is redundancy in the *samāsokti* (condensed metaphor) [if one were to add the word "passion"], saying: "anurāga... (passion...).
A courtesan from the western direction drove out the sun from his dwelling in the sky; that is, she caused him to depart.
Of what sort was he? He was "apetavasu," meaning one whose wealth (or rays) had departed.

Although there are other qualifying attributes that could have served as reasons for his expulsion, the author states that she drove him out because he was "apetaraśmi" (devoid of rays), adding the word "anurāga" (affection/attachment).

The meaning is: following after day (*anu divasasya*), he possesses passion (*rāgavantam*)—that is, redness (*raktimāvantam*)—and for that very reason, he bears a body that is pleasant (*sukham*) to the eyes, meaning it produces comfort and is not hot.

Here, by virtue of this punning contradiction (*śliṣṭavirodha*), the expulsion from her own home—which is her dwelling—from the courtesan is suggested through implication (*vyañjanā*) regarding a hero who possesses passion, whose body produces pleasure for the eyes and is very cool, yet who is devoid of wealth (*vasu*, i.e., riches).
And in that case, just as the penniless leader is suggested through the power of the closely connected qualifiers, it is equally appropriate that the courtesan also be suggested;
for if she were expressed directly, there would be redundancy—thus he says: "In this case, it is only the other direction [that is intended]."
Locanā:
(lo, i) "Anugata" means redness, which is passion, as well as love;
by the word "vasu," rays and riches are meant.
The meaning is that *ālaya* signifies a support (*āśraya*) and a dwelling (*gṛha*),
and thus it is understood as "prostitution";
furthermore, by employing the word itself [again], it results in redundancy.
“When birds are summoned, the mosquito is not barred from coming forward; whether dwelling in the midst or at the head, a glass trinket assumes the rank of jewels.
Even a firefly does not hesitate to move among the luminous; fie on this commonality of the mindless, which, like a master who has not discerned the inner truth, fails to distinguish between them!”
Locanā:
(lo, ī) A "grass-gem" (*tṛṇamaṇi*) is a particular kind of gem used for clearing away grass;

it is that by which, being neither greater nor smaller [than the object], the distinction between things—whether large or small—is not revealed when they have not been examined according to their true nature.

The meaning is that "universal" (*sāmānya*) refers to the genus (*jāti*), because a universal remains in a single form across all case-endings (*vibhakti*). Furthermore, it is inappropriate [to express this] by means of *vyañjanā* (suggestive power), since the intended sense is already conveyed by the fact that it produces an excellence of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*).
In this context, it is inappropriate to mention a master who lacks consciousness.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, da) He states the redundancy [of this] with *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise): "When summoned," etc.—"Fie upon the common person! because he is insentient, being devoid of the consciousness of what is auspicious or inauspicious.
One whose inner mind (*antara-manas*) is such that it has not touched upon or contemplated reality—such a person is like a lord.

[The author] demonstrates the insentience of the universal (*sāmānya*): when birds are called and people are traveling through the sky, even a mosquito coming forward before them is not warded off, because they are moving through the air.
Only the warding off [of obstacles] ceases;
here, it should be understood that movement alone is the enjoined object, since it is precisely that which makes possible the demonstration of sentience in general.

Likewise, the *tṛṇamaṇi* (grass-gem) is a gem that attracts grass and is of little value; whether situated at the front or in the middle, it bears the burden of those highly valuable gems that create the splendor of the chariot—the burden consisting in the production of the chariot’s beauty.
It imposes a burden.
The lexicon states: "The word *dhūḥ* is feminine or neuter, meaning the front of a vehicle.
A *yāna* is a chariot.
In the phrase "in the middle," because [the vehicle] is present [in the context], the word "of the vehicle" (*yānasya*) is understood.

Regarding the phrase "dwelling in the middle," there is a variant reading in some places: "dwelling in the midst of the ocean" (*madhyevāridhi*). In that case, the meaning is "dwelling in the middle of the ocean" or "dwelling repeatedly in the middle."
Because of the commonality with the dust of water (vāridhvāsa) in the case of gems, the "burden" (dhuram)—meaning the weight—consists of being counted as a gem among great-value jewels.
The word "even" (api) connects with the term "among the radiant.
Therefore, the meaning is: "Fie upon the ordinary person," because of such improper conduct.
In this context:
the insentient Lord is the subject under discussion (*prākaraṇika*),
while mosquitoes and the like are not the subject under discussion (*aprākaraṇika*).

The meaning is that since those [qualities] are already obtained through the power of the names themselves by means of suggestion (*vyañjanā*) from the insentient Lord, their explicit mention would be redundant.
Thus, in the case of alliteration (*anuprāsa*), there is a contradiction with what is well-known (*khyātaviruddhatva*) due to the absence of established usage.
