“The wielder of the discus bestowed upon that king the status of being presided over by the Discus, the lineage of the Discus-wielder, the exalted clan of the Discus-piercer, the Bull, and the Bull-banner.”
Vijñapriyā:

"(vi, dha) 'Because of the absence of common usage'—this means that there is an absence of common usage for the word-meaning intended [by the author] in the specified object of the action (*karman*). [The word] *cakra*..."
Viṣṇu, the wielder of the discus, bestowed upon this king the status of being presided over by the discus—that is, his conquest of the circle of kings.
Likewise, Indra, the breaker of mountain peaks, elevated his lineage;
and Maheśa, whose banner is the bull, [bestowed] Dharma, the bull.
In this regard, there is no established status as the agent for these [poets] in the acts of seeing; rather, it was stated in that manner solely for the sake of alliteration.
Locanā:
(Lo, u)—the intended meaning of "cakā" is as follows:
Furthermore, the praise of [the wheels] beginning with the *cakra* merely on the grounds of their being presided over by the *cakra* is certainly not well-known;
rather, it is composed solely for the sake of alliteration (*anuprāsa*).
And regarding the faults mentioned, he states that they are sometimes not faults and sometimes even virtues:
Vijñapriyā:
"Of the aforementioned defects" means of those beginning with being unpleasant to hear (*duḥśravatva*).
When the speaker is possessed by anger, and likewise when the subject matter is highly agitated;
However, in sentiments such as the Furious (raudra), extreme harshness of sound may indeed become a poetic quality.
Locanā:
(lo, ū) Now, regarding these faults which have been divided into five types based on their location within the words, she states that in certain instances some of them may appear differently:
here, "anger" (*krodha*) is intended as not having attained the state of the Furious Sentiment (*raudra-rasa*).
Because that has been mentioned separately;
"in a sublimated object" means one endowed with the quality of perfect sublimation;
by the word "etcetera," the loathsome is included.

And in these cases, because they consist of the nature of relish (*āsvāda*) and poison respectively, and because they assist through the excellence of their primary qualities, the designation "quality" (*guṇa*) is used figuratively.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, pa) Regarding the expression "in the speaker"—it means in one who is elevated, fierce, that is to say, terrifying.
The syntactical connection is that [harshness] is an absolute excellence in sentiments such as the Furious (raudra).

Now, one might object: "If sweetness and the like alone are the excellences (guṇas), then how can qualities such as being difficult to hear be considered excellences? To this, he says: "And among these...
Sweetness and the other [excellences] are the primary excellences, consisting of specific aspects of the nature of aesthetic relish (āsvāda).

The meaning is that because they perform that metaphorical application which consists of their excellence, it is appropriate to designate them by the term "qualities" (*guṇa*) in a metaphorical sense (*aupacārika*).
Locanā:
(lo, ṛ) The primary quality is that which consists of the very nature of the sun, such as sweetness (*mādhurya*) and so forth.
The figurative (bhākta) is the metaphorical (aupacārika).
In order, for example:

"For me, who am emaciated by the severance of that [love], whose life-breaths are gasping in my throat, the cruel five-arrowed god mercilessly pierces my heart to its depths with arrows sharpened on stone."
May he, who was once made terrifying by the mass of flames from the fire of his fierce eye, now remain with his entire being subject to the compassion of Śambhu for all living beings.
In this context, the speaker is angry regarding the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).

*Vijñapriyā* (vi, pha): Regarding the speaker here who is joined with anger, he states the quality of being "unpleasant to hear" (*duḥśravatva*)—namely, "the interruption of that" (*tadviccheda*), etc.
While my body was emaciated by the interruption of that [union] and my life-breath was choked in my throat,
let the cruel five-arrowed god, piercing me mercilessly with his exceedingly sharp shafts,
be rendered formidable by the all-consuming flame of the fierce fire from the eye of Śambhu.

Regarding the question, "How will Śambhu do this?", he says: "Out of compassion for me, a supplicant being. That is, he will act in this way solely out of pity for me, who am a petitioner. As for the word "anna": [it means] food.
In cases such as the interruption of the throat or the stumbling of sounds, letters like *cha* and *ṭha* are difficult to hear; these are the qualities of a speaker who is ill-behaved.

"May the dance of Śambhu bestow auspiciousness upon you—[the dance] which, under the guise of the spray of water tossed up by the mass of restless waves of the celestial river as it roars while being shaken against the vault of heaven, forcibly casts the constellations into the sky; and [the dance] in which the fragments of the cosmic egg whirl about due to the force of the wind arising from the momentum of the rotation of his staff-like feet raised upwards."
In this context, a bold *tāṇḍava* dance should be expressed.

These two verses are my own. Even when the sentiment (*rasa*) is the Furious (*raudra*) or others, the extreme harshness of sound, despite being disregarded by those [who favor other sentiments], is an absolute merit.
For example:
"Having cut again and again the skin... and so forth.
Here, the sentiment (rasa) is the loathsome (bībhatsa).
Vijñapriyā:
Regarding the term *uddhata* (exalted), he says "on the head" (*mūrdhni*).
May the Śāmbhava *tāṇḍava* dance bestow auspiciousness upon you all.

What kind of *tāṇḍava* dance was it? It was one in which, by the pretext (*dambhāt*) of the water-sprays (*ambhaḥ-kṣodānām*)—that is, droplets of water—suddenly and violently tossed up (*uddhūtānām*) by the tossing mass of surging waves (*lolena kallola-jālena*) of the celestial river Gaṅgā as she flowed with her head shaken; [the dance was performed] under that guise.
It was such that hundreds of thousands of stars were cast up to the sky as far as the navel;
furthermore,

it was such that the fragments of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍakhaṇḍa) were whirled about by the force of the two winds suddenly surging upward with impetuosity due to the excessive whirling of the two staff-like legs placed above.
"Where such [is found]";
"herein" means that in passages such as "having cut out the arrogant and terrifying [flesh]," there is the *bībhatsa* (disgust) sentiment.
Locanā:
(lo, ṝ) [The *ṛ* sound] removes arrogance.

In the Furious (*raudra*) sentiment, there is harshness of sound, as in my father’s words: "Having suddenly pulverized these eight principal mountain ranges into fragments with the blow of a clearly manifest, formidable slap..."
Then, with the whistling of the wind as vast as the gale at the end of an aeon, I shall toss the ocean from shore to shore with my spreading blasts.

In the context of a conversation beginning with amorous advances and the like, the quality of indecorum (*aślīlatva*) is, on the contrary, a merit. For example: “...and again, and again. [In such cases, it is a virtue. As for instance:
“When the hand has entered the narrow space and stirred within, the male organ, approaching,
shines forth through the means of its own accomplishment.”

For in this context of a gathering at the commencement of amorous play, the established rule of the *Kāmaśāstra* states: "One should dismiss a female companion by means of offering betel, and one should hint at secret matters through words with double meanings.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it should be understood that this applies to storytelling for tranquility (*śama-kathā*) and other such occasions.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, bha) "In sexual union" (*surata*) means in such gatherings as those where the commencement of sexual union occurs;
[the phrase] "by the trunk of an elephant" (*karihastena*) [is used].
This is a suggestion of a means for sexual union with a young girl through words with double meaning (*dvayarthapada*).

For instance, a man's banner or flag shines as it enters and moves forward within the army—that is, the interior of the host. What kind of place is the interior of the army? It is "obstructed" (*sambādhe*), being crowded and enclosed.

To the question, "In that case, how does the entry occur?", he says: "By the trunk of an elephant. This means [the entry occurs] when [the place] has been stirred up by the trunk—the proboscis—of elephants (kariṇām).
Here, the phrase with its double meaning (*dvyarthapada*) indicates the method of sexual union for young girls.
For instance, when it has entered within the narrow and contracted birth-canal (*yoni*) of the means [of union] and moves back and forth, the male member (*dhvaja*, *liṅga*) shines forth.
He states the method for entry: "by the hand of an elephant.
[This refers to the position where] the middle finger is outside, joined with the index and ring fingers.
This is known as the *karihasta* (elephant-hand) gesture by those expert in the treatises on erotics (*kāmaśāstra*).
"Thus" means: when stirred by those three fingers.
"In this case" means: [as follows].

The meaning is that one should reveal or indicate secret matters—that is, hidden things—in such contexts as a social gathering (*goṣṭhī*) and so forth. By the phrase "and so forth," he indicates what is included: "talk of tranquility" (*śamakathā*).
For example: “In [the face] resembling the swollen belly of an upturned, bloated frog...”
Who would feel attachment for a woman’s wound that is oozing and infested with worms?
“In this instance, there is the *jugupsā-ślīla* (the offensive due to disgust).
That which is to be understood by the speaker as having an inauspicious intention is to be grasped through words such as ‘and so forth’ (*prabhṛti*).
For example: ‘May the sons of Pāṇḍu, who have extinguished the fire of enmity through the pacification of their enemies, rejoice together with Mādhava!’”
May the sons of the Kuru king, along with their servants, having adorned the earth with blood and having their bodies wounded, become well again.
In this context, there is an indication of an impending inauspicious event for the Kurus through an improper word (*aślīla*).
Locanā:
(lo, ḷ) *kariṇaḥ* means "of the elephant" (*gajasya*); *hastaḥ* means "the trunk" (*sthūlahastaḥ*).
"When the index and ring fingers are joined and the middle finger is on the outside"—
this is the form well-known in the treatises on erotics (*śṛṅgāraśāstra*), which drives away the female vulva, has the shape of a penis, and is called the "elephant trunk" (*karikara*).
In a narrow or confined space.

The banner, the means such as horses and so forth, and the female organ should be indicated or alluded to in a discourse on tranquility through vulgar language, as for example: "Who, other than a worm, would feel attachment to a woman's wound—which resembles the split belly of a frog swollen from a blow and is dripping with moisture?"
Thus,
in cases such as *śleṣa* (paronomasia), the faults of "meaningless" (*nihatārtha*) and "unemployed" (*aprayukta*) may not be considered defects.

For example: "Falling [into the ocean], it was saluted like Hari, like Hari, like Hari—the water of the celestial river, which cleaves the mountains, is purifying, victorious, highly esteemed by Naraka, and deep."
In the Indra-pakṣa, the word *pavitra* has its primary meaning suppressed;
in the Siṃha-pakṣa, the word *mataṅga* is not used in the sense of an outcaste (*mātaṅga*).
Vijñapriyā:
"May they be"—by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of *yamaka* (paranomasia) and *citra* (puzzle-poetry) is intended.

Among those [faults], since both *nihatārtha* (having a hidden meaning) and *aprayukta* (unconventional usage) are not faults in the case of *śleṣa* (punning), he provides a single example for it: "O you who split the mountains, purifier...
[The verse continues: "...I bow to the water of the celestial river Gaṅgā as it flows down."
In this context, providing three examples based on the distinction of qualifiers, he states the qualifiers—beginning with "mountain"—as follows:
"What kind of water is it? It is that which cleaves the mountain and is pure.
Here, the example is "like Indra [cleaving] Hari."

For he too protects—meaning the gods—with the mountain-shattering thunderbolt (*vajra*); as for the water, it is "conquering" (*jaitra*), meaning the destroyer of *naraka*, that is, the torment born of sin. Here, the simile is "like Viṣṇu in the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa," for he too was the conqueror of *naraka*, namely the demon Naraka-āsura.

What kind of water is it? It is "highly esteemed" (bahumata), meaning approved by many people, and "dense" (gahana), meaning thick due to the excessive force of its current. Here, the simile is that of a lion (*hari*);
for he too is the slayer of many deer (*mataṅga*).
He points out two defects [in the comparison] with the word "here" (*atra*).

Nor should it be said that in this instance, in the phrase "only Hari" (*harimeva*), there is the fault of *anavīkṛtatva* (lack of freshness) or *kathitapadatva* (repetition of words). For making several things expressed by a single word the subject of a comparison constitutes a specific kind of poetic charm (*vaicitrya-viśeṣa*); since it produces that charm, it is not a fault. — *Locanā*.
Regarding "parvata" and so forth: in the sense of the Ganges water, it refers to that which has the nature (*śīla*) of piercing the mountain (*parvata*).
"Vapitram" and "pūtam" are two words. In the sense of Indra, it means one who protects (*trāyate*) by means of the *pavitra*—the thunderbolt (*vajra*)—which pierces mountains (*parvatabhedin*).

In the interpretation as *jala* (water), it consists of two words: *bahūnām* (of many) and *mataṃ sammataṃ gahanaṃ ca* (the accepted, dense [forest]). In the interpretation as *siṃha* (lion), it is a single word: *bahūnāṃ mātaṅgānāṃ hantāram* (the slayer of many elephants).
The excellence would consist in the fact that the speaker and the subject matter are both knowledgeable [of the truth],
as for example:
"They declare you to be Primordial Matter (prakṛti) which sets in motion the goals of the Spirit (puruṣa)."
They know you alone to be that Puruṣa who beholds me and remains indifferent.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ya) It would be a quality (*guṇa*). "Knowledge" (*jñatva*) means being learned (*paṇḍitatva*).

They address you thus: they address you as Brahmā, the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) that sets in motion the human goals—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; for according to the Sāṃkhya tenet, primordial nature is the state of equilibrium among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and from that alone arises the production of all things.
The meaning is: "you who are of such a nature in that state.
And thus they know you alone as the Puruṣa, the Puruṣa who is the creator of all.
To the question, "What is the proof for that? he says: "taddarśinam"—one whose vision, that is, knowledge, is derived from that very [state].
Because he knows it through the Veda composed by him and through inference from the mountains, oceans, and so forth created by him;
because he is indifferent toward the production of all effects due to the absence of any self-interest;
here, Brahmā is the one to be denoted.
The speakers are Indra and others;
all of them are indeed learned.
Since terms such as *prakṛti* and so forth are unfamiliar [to common people], their status as a merit arises from the manifestation of learning.
Locanā:
(lo, ai) You, whose form is perceived through mere vision of that [one], possess the capacity to manifest the word "pratīta" (perceived).
Primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is the state of equilibrium among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
The *puruṣa* is the immutable one whose nature is consciousness (*cit*). That which has the disposition to act for his sake is [Prakṛti].
As it is said: "All actions whatsoever are performed by the qualities (*guṇas*) of Prakṛti."
One whose self is deluded by egoism thinks, "I am the doer."
Its "manifestation" (darśana) means its illumination; for primordial matter (prakṛti), which is insentient by nature, possesses causal efficiency only through the transfer of consciousness (cit).
Here, the term *prakṛti* and others are well-known from the Sāṃkhya treatises.
Or, it may also refer to self-reflection (*parāmarśa*).
The phrase "unfamiliarity is a merit" is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].

For example: "I meditate upon that moon of the Self, which is pure and the support for the supportless state—that which is joined with the digits for the increase of the darknesses, and which wanes through them for their destruction."
Vijñapriyā:
Regarding the line from the verse, *svayaṃ vāpi parāmarśe*, she connects what was stated previously—that unfamiliarity is a merit—by saying "unfamiliarity.
The phrase "endowed with digits" means that I constantly study and meditate upon that moon which is the very nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
The meaning is that he is distinct from the moon.
He describes his distinction from other moons with the word "endowed" (yukta).

Being distinguished by the *kalās*—that is, by the attributes (*dharmas*) consisting of the desire to assume a body which appear dark—he exists for the sake of increasing the *tamases*, which are delusions (*mohas*) consisting of the lack of awareness regarding the non-difference between the body and the self, just as...
When Rāma assumes a physical body,
the other moon, being endowed with its sixteen digits (*kalās*), serves only for the destruction of darkness and obscurity;
likewise, when deprived of those digits, it serves for the destruction of that very same darkness.
Because there is an absence of such delusion due to the fact that [the moon] has not assumed a physical body,

whereas the other moon, being devoid of its digits (*kalā*), serves only to increase darkness. Since it lacks the digits that destroy darkness, it possesses the nature of a cause for the increase of darkness, according to the principle that "that which exists when the other exists, and which does not exist when the other does not exist, is the cause of that."
Likewise, suchness is pure,
whereas the moon possesses a mark;
likewise, it rests upon the supportless state of emptiness, whereas the moon rests upon the circle of lights.

In this context, although the two categories *kalā* and *tamas* are not explicitly mentioned, they are themselves included in the reflection (*parāmarśa*) because they are intended as objects of reference due to their being perceived by others.
Locanā:
(lo, o) "By the sixteen *kalās*."
And these are the eleven organs and the five subtle elements (tanmātras).
In the lunar sense, "kalās" refers to the digits or constituent parts.
*Tamāṃsi* refers to ignorances and darknesses;
[the phrase] "by those parts" means by those portions of these darknesses.
The term *nirālamba-pada* (the supportless state) refers to the side of the Self (*ātman*), because there is no further substratum for it;
on the side of the Moon, it refers to the sky.
Here, the meaning of the word *kalā* is well-known only from the Yoga scriptures, as it is said: "The Puruṣa consists of sixteen parts."
And the state has been explained once again.
When that which has been prescribed is restated for the sake of expressing dejection, wonder, anger, wretchedness, or in the case of *lāṭānuprāsa*, compassion, or conciliation; (VisSd 7.19)
In the case of *arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya*, when joy is present, the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) is indeed a poetic quality (*guṇa*). For example:
“Ruddy the sun rises,” and so forth;
herein there is a restatement of what has been enjoined.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, la) Regarding the phrase "of that which has been prescribed": therein, he provides an example of a restatement of what has been prescribed—namely, "it rises.
As for the word "herein":

The meaning is that there is an *anuvāda* (reiteration) in the form of a restatement, wherein the "copperiness" predicated with reference to the rising sun is subsequently referred to as being predicated with reference to the setting sun as well:
"Alas! Alas!
My beloved has gone away in spring, O friend; he has not returned."
Here there is despondency: “It is strange, it is strange! How is there a moon with a beautiful face in the skyless [space]?
Here there is astonishment.
Locanā:
(vi, va) "In the non-ether" means: in you, who are distinct from ether. [She says:
"O fair-eyed one, fix your gaze!"

Here there is *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration). In such passages as "his eyes and [the god] Nayaṇa," there is *dhvani* (suggestion) in which the expressed meaning is transferred (*arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya*).
The same applies elsewhere as well.
*Vijñapriyā*:
Alliteration (*lāṭānuprāsa*) occurs both within compounds and outside of compounds.
Yamaka (chiasmus) occurs through identity of meaning.

Regarding the phrase "his very eyes"—here, the second occurrence of the word *nayana* (eye) has its literal sense transferred (*saṃkramitavācya*) to another meaning, namely "superior form. The same applies to other instances; for example, in that [verse], "Go, go, do not stay here" is used in the sense of anger.
"Alas, I am ruined! expresses dejection; "Come, come, my child!
expresses compassion.
"Release, release your anger! is used for conciliation; "Tell me, tell me the news! is used for joy;
"This one, this one is the hero! is used for emphasis.
Likewise, if there is ambiguity, it results in what is known as "disguised praise" (vyājastuti).
An example of this very [figure of] *guṇa* is as follows:
"O King, now our two residences are equal: yours, with its vessels of broad gold and its retinue adorned to the utmost; mine, dense with sporting female elephants."
Vijñapriyā:
"The state of being doubtful" means that which is fit for doubt.

Its fitness [for doubt] arises from having two referents; however, there is indeed certainty because of the two meanings in the two qualificands. Thus he states the meaning of the word: "only a quality."
The meaning is that it is a "quality" (guṇa) by virtue of certainty.
Regarding the phrase "pṛthukārtta": this is a statement made by a poor man to a king. "Our dwelling is now equal."

The implication is that if you obtain wealth from him, it will not be equal to what you have already received. A royal palace is one where there are large vessels (*pātrāṇi*) of *kārttasvara*—that is, gold;
whereas the abode of the poor is a vessel for the distressed cries (*ārttasvarasya pātram*) of many children (*pṛthukānām*), due to the lack of food.
A royal palace is such that it is adorned with gold and other ornaments, and its entire retinue resides there;
whereas a poor man's dwelling is such that its entire retinue sleeps upon the ground, being deprived of beds.
A royal palace is dense with trumpeting female elephants and male tuskers.
The dwelling of the poor man is dense with the dust of mice, ants, and other creatures that reside within its crumbling walls.
Here, by means of the pretext of comparing his own home [to the king's], the king’s superior wealth is described; thus, there is *vyājastuti* (ironical praise).
Note that *vyājastuti* is used here as an illustration [of a broader category].

In examples such as "parvatabhedi pavitram" (the mountain-splitting, purifying [thunderbolt]), it should be understood that the same principle applies even in cases of simile (*upamā*), pun (*śleṣa*), and so forth.
Locanā:
(lo, au)—"pṛthu" means a vessel or locus for the cries of distress of the *pṛthuka* [children] or the *balas*.
Where there were broad and vast vessels of refined gold, golden bowls;
where those who dwell upon the earth are adorned and embellished;
and where, as they remain sporting, gleaming particles of dust arise.
The playful female elephants and male elephants;
however, when a preeminent grammarian is the subject or the speaker,
there is "difficulty," meaning either harshness or unpleasantness to the ear.
It is simply called a *guṇa*.
For example:
"There is a certain [root] similar to *dīdhī*, *vevī*, and *iṭ* which is not a recipient of *guṇa* or *vṛddhi*."
There is something resembling the *kvip* suffix, in the presence of which you do not exist.
In this matter, the meaning is difficult;
moreover, the speaker is a grammarian.
[Vijñapriyā:]
"Foremost among grammarians" means one who is preeminent in grammar. "Difficulty" refers to the state of having a difficult meaning.

The term *dīdhī-vevīṅ* refers to a certain person who is not a recipient of *guṇa* or *vṛddhi*, meaning he is devoid of both *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. This is because, in the case of the two roots *dīdhī* and *vevī* as well as the augment *iṭ*, there is an absence of *guṇa* and the *vṛddhi* that would otherwise supersede it.
Likewise, a certain person is like the *kvip* suffix.
When a person is present, even for that which is proximate to them, there is no *guṇa* or *vṛddhi*;
for even when a verbal root is proximate to the *kvip* suffix, there is an absence of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*.
— Locanā:
(lo, a) *dīdhī-vevīṅ* refers to a certain enemy; *guṇa* refers to qualities such as valor and the like.
In one alternative, there is the substitution of *i* for the vowels beginning with *ī*, such as the substitution of *e* (*etva*) and so forth;
[in the other] there is *vṛddhi*, which is "increase" (*samṛddhi*).

In the alternative case, there is the substitution of *a* (*aitva*) and so forth for the vowels beginning with *ī*, because of the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* in the case of the roots *dīdhī* and *vevī*.
The suffix *kvip* is like a thief who carries away everything; thus, through its elision, there is the total destruction of the enemy.
Here, it is not merely a matter of being unpleasant to hear or difficult to pronounce, even though such qualities belong to this [word].
"In this [sentence], 'I never forgot you, my teacher,' there is the quality of being unpleasant to hear; a grammarian is the intended speaker."
Thus, even regarding his being a speaker;
Vijñapriyā:
"Thus" means as follows.
He demonstrates this to the grammarian: "In this [verse], 'O Teacher!
here in this world, I have never at any time failed to satisfy you.'"
"Thus" means that,
in the case of this grammarian's mode of speaking, even the quality of being "difficult" (kaṣṭatva)— that is, being hard to hear— is actually a merit (*guṇa*).
This is because his manner of speaking and his difficulty have both been illustrated [in the preceding examples].
Vulgarity occurs in low expressions. (VisSd 7.21)
It is simply a quality (*guṇa*). As in my own verse:
"This orb of the moon appears here like a mass of *heṅga* grass."
These people, deluded by their breath, fall upon their hopes like a difficult-to-hold stream of milk.
This is the statement of Vidūṣaka.
Vijñapriyā:
[It refers to] "in my own statements" (vi, ka).
The word "guṇa" (quality) is to be supplied [from the previous verse].
Regarding the word "eso" (this):
"This orb of the moon is seen like a lump of fresh butter."
And these rays of his fall upon the quarters like streams of milk.
(Thus the Sanskrit paraphrase) (vi, ka):

"Haiyaṅgavīna" is clarified butter produced from yesterday's milking; in the speech of one greedy for food, this is an example of a foodstuff, and here it constitutes the rustic quality (*grāmya-guṇa*).
Locanā:
(Low characters such as the Vidūṣaka and others:
"This—'This orb of the moon is seen like a lump of fresh butter;
and these rays of it fall upon the quarters like streams of milk.'"
However, the lack of a causal basis for what is conventionally known does not constitute a defect in meaning;
for example: “Now, at the time of twilight, it causes pairs of wheels to separate.
When something is well-known in the convention of poets, even if it contradicts [actual] renown, it is a merit. (VisSd 7.22)
And those things well-known by poetic convention:
darkness is described in the sky and in sin; whiteness is described in fame, laughter, and glory; and redness in anger and passion.

The lotuses, blue water-lilies, and other such flowers found in rivers and oceans spread throughout every body of water; flocks of birds such as swans disperse across them; the moonlight is drunk by the *cakra* birds; and during the rainy season, the swans depart for Lake Mānasa.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, kha) Regarding "samprati"—since it is well-known that the time of twilight causes the separation of pairs of *cakravāka* birds, there is no need for a further reason here.
He shows what is well-known according to poetic convention (*kavisamaya*) and so forth with the words "mālinyam" (darkness).
The meaning is "in evil.
Fame arises from virtuous action, while glory arises from giving; such is the distinction between glory (*yaśas*) and fame (*kīrti*).
The swan is a *marāla*;

the *aśoka* tree blossoms from the kick of a woman's foot; the *bakula* blooms with the wine from the mouths of women; necklaces rest upon the limbs of youths; and the heart bursts open from the torments of separation.

The bowstring is a garland of *rolamba* bees, and the arrows are made of flowers; the heart of a young man would be pierced by these shafts of the Flower-Arrowed God (Kāma) just as it is by the side-long glance of a woman.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ga) The grammatical construction is: "The face of women [blooms] with wines, just as the *vakula* tree blooms.
Locanā:
The connection is that "the necklace and the heart burst.
"Young people" refers to both young men and young women;
it is specifically the young men who [are struck] by the side-glances of women.
The lotus blooms by day, the night-lily blossoms at night,
moonlight appears in the bright fortnight, peacocks dance amidst the rumbling of clouds, and fruit does not grow upon the *aśoka* tree.

There would be no jasmine in spring, nor would there be flowers and fruits on trees whose essence is fragrance; other such [conventions] found in the poetic tradition should be inferred from the compositions of great poets. (VisSd 7.25)

The examples for these are clear in the original treatises (*ākara*). In words such as *dhanurjyā* ("bow-string"), the words "bow" (*dhanus*) and so forth are used for the purpose of conveying the state of being strung and the like.
For example: “When heaven and earth were filled with sounds arising from the twanging of the bowstring.
Here, although the meaning is already conveyed by the word *jyā* (bowstring), the inclusion of the word *dhanus* (bow) indicates that the string is dependent upon the bow.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [other examples are implied].
“Your ear-ornament shines.
Here, the word *karṇa* (ear) is used to convey the fact that it is situated on the ear. — Locanā:
(Lo, ī) Even by the employment of words such as "ear-ornament" (*avataṃsa*) and so forth, there is redundancy because the meaning of "ear" is already understood;
for instance, words denoting "ear" convey the ear of the subject at hand by excluding other ears,
and the beauty and so forth of those [earrings] have their own causes.
However, the sense is that it ultimately culminates in being caused by the heroine who is the subject of the context.
In this same manner, [the description] begins with the earrings on the ears, the crest-jewel on the head, and so forth.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, gha) Regarding "bow" (*dhanuḥ*) and "being mounted upon" (*ārūḍhatva*): the cognition of that [bow] arises from the word "bow" and so forth; and "being mounted upon" is either indicated (*lakṣaṇayā*) by the word "bow" through the cause of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), or it is "being mounted upon" with the genitive sense (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*) elided.

Regarding the phrase "even though the meaning has already been conveyed": it should not be argued that the meaning of the word *jyā* (bowstring) is simply a specific universal (*jāti*) manifested by a particular configuration (*saṃsthāna-viśeṣa*), namely the state of being a bowstring belonging to a bow.
For even if *jyātva* were a universal, since the bow—which is related to it—is recalled as something that must be bent, the bow is obtained through that very [recollection];
thus, the objection that the word *dhanuḥ* (bow) would be redundant is set aside by the fact that it serves to convey the state of being "mounted" (*ārūḍhatva*).

In this case, even though [the earring] is already situated on the ear, the possibility of tautology is indeed avoided because the term *karṇāvataṃsa* (ear-ornament) has as its referent the same thing as the word *savataṃsa* (possessing an ornament).
Nor should it be argued that, even if there is a secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) for "situated on the ear," tautology would still occur by conveying the sense "an ear-ornament situated on the ear";
for since the word *avataṃsa* signifies an ornament suitable for the ear, there is no tautology in the expression "an ornament suitable for the ear, situated on the ear."

Regarding the phrase "in this way, upon hearing": in these two cases, there is indeed the application of an additional word because the states of being a "bracelet" (*kuṇḍalatva*) and being a "crown" (*kirīṭatva*) are universals (*jāti*) manifested by configuration (*saṃsthāna*). Thus, although it is established that the word *mālā* (garland) without a qualifying prefix denotes only a string of flowers, in the expression "The flower-garland shines for you," the word *puṣpa* (flower) is used for the purpose of increasing the excellence of the flowers.
Thus, in the expression "pearl necklace" (*muktāhāra*), the word "pearl" (*muktā*) indicates that it is unmixed with other gems; as stated in the *Vijñapriyā*:
"(vi, ṅa) It denotes only a garland of flowers."

And thus, here too, there would result the very same charge of tautology. The meaning is that for the sake of establishing "excellent flowers," the portion consisting of flowers is already the meaning of the word *mālā* (garland), while the word *puṣpa* (flower) functions as an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the sense of "excellence. This is the case in the expression *muktāhāra* (pearl necklace) as well.
According to the *Kośa*, "necklace" (*hāra*) refers to a pearl necklace (*muktagraiveyaka*);
since even a single pearl is included within the denotation of the word "necklace," the fault of tautology (*punarukti*) would likewise apply here.
However, the quality of being unmixed with other gems is understood through the secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word "pearl."
These should be employed as they stand [in the ritual]. (VisSd 7.26)
The bowstring and such [ornaments] should be depicted only as they exist in fine poetry,
and not those that do not so exist, such as the waist-belt, the hand-anklet, or the bracelet.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ca) "They exist only in fine poetry"—the logical connection (*anvaya*) is that because they exist in fine poetry, they must necessarily be composed [therein].
Thus, it is shown here that the basis for this figurative usage (*lakṣaṇā*) is its conventional rootedness (*rūḍhi*).
The point is that, however, such conventional rootedness does not exist in the case of the girdle on the hips and so forth.
In the case of [the description of] one immersed in bliss and so forth, the deficiency of words may be a merit.
For example:
“Her breasts were made small by a firm embrace, while the thrill of horripilation broke forth; her beautiful lower garment slipped away due to the excess of the essence of intense affection.”
"Do not, do not, O giver of honor!
Is she sleeping, or has she died, or is she dissolved within my mind, or has she vanished?"—thus she spoke with fainting words.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, cha) "In the statement" means in the utterance of words such as "immersed in bliss.
"Deep embrace" refers to this speech of a female friend directed toward her male friend.

The compound is: "she whose breasts were made small by a tight embrace and who had horripilation breaking forth. This is not a compound [of *kuca* and *romodgama*] because it would be inappropriate to describe the color of the hair on the breasts.

My heroine, possessing those two aforementioned attributes—namely, one whose garment was slipping from her beautiful hips due to the excess of the sentiment of intense affection—[says: "O giver of honor (*mānada*), [please] press me," as implied by the ellipsis.
The meaning is that she became the object of the fourfold set of conjectures, beginning with "Is she asleep? and so forth, while she was uttering indistinct syllables such as "mā mā mā mā.
She was "asleep" (suptā), meaning she was slumbering because of her lack of movement; from her extreme lack of movement, there arose the conjecture of death.

Because [the sound] was within the mind, there arose the conjecture of dissolution into the mind (layavitarka); and because the two minds had not yet emerged externally, there arose the conjecture of total dissolution (vilaya), which consists of an absolute merging.
Locanā:
(lo, u) "gāḍheti"—here, by the words "asleep" and so forth, there is an increasing degree of immobility in successive stages.
What [is it]? My beloved, of the aforementioned form, is as if asleep within my mind.
Because she remains steadfast;
fearing that she might even rise again after having fallen asleep, he asks, "Is she dead?
Since she too could be cast out by others, he says, "She has dissolved."

The distinction is that they are like lac and wood. Even if it were of such a nature, one might think it could be separated by someone; therefore, he says "melted"—the sense being that, like milk and water, there is an absolute absence of the perception of difference.
Then, with the words "therefore me," there is a general refutation of the subject under discussion.
In the phrase "māti mām" (she crushes me), the verbal form "pīḍaya" (crush) is deficient.
This deficiency is a merit (*guṇa*), as it reveals the heroine’s state of being rendered motionless by intense bliss, such that she lacks the capacity even to utter a coherent sentence.
Here, "pīḍaya" is the missing word.
In some cases, there is neither a fault nor a merit—
namely, the deficiency of words (*nyūnapadatva*).
For example:
"She might remain hidden by her power due to the force of her anger, yet she does not stay angry for long; her heart is moist with affection for me, and she would even ascend to heaven for my sake.
Even the enemies of the gods would not have been able to carry her off while she stood before me; yet she has become utterly beyond the range of my eyes—what manner of fate is this?"
Vijñapriyā:

"(Vi, Ja) *tiṣṭhet kopa*—" This is Purūravas’s reflection upon not having found Urvaśī. Reflecting that "she, Urvaśī, remains hidden by her own power and invisible," he says, "She is not far away. Reflecting thus, "for the sake of heaven," he says, "But [if she were] with me..."
He states that the possibility of her being abducted by an asura is inconceivable, saying: "To abduct her...
The reason for this is given by the phrase "standing before me.
Therefore, because there is no cause for her not being seen, he says "And she..."—meaning she has gone to, or reached, a state beyond the range of perception (*agocara*).
In this context, after the phrase "it would be as if concealed by power," the words "for this is not so" (*naitadyataḥ*) are deficient.

Even though these words are missing, it is not a merit [of the verse], because they fail to heighten the transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) called "reflection" (*vitarka*), which is suggested by this sentence.

Furthermore, there is no fault, because the cognition of the meaning of the sentence beginning with "he should remain" (*tiṣṭhet*) is clearly manifested through the understanding produced by the sentence beginning with "not for long" (*dīrghaṃ na se*).
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, jha) The meaning here is that [the lengthening of the vowel] and the phrase "not she" (*na sā*) serve as reasons specifically for the negation of what was stated previously, and not for the cognition of the previous [state].
[Objection: Granted that it may not be a poetic excellence (*guṇa*), since it does not produce any excellence (*utkarṣa*).
But since it might be argued that this constitutes a fault, he says: "It is not long," and so forth.
The sublation (*bādha*) is indeed manifest—because there is a rule that the opposing statement of another is necessarily of such a nature.

And thus, the point is that even the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of the words "This is not [the case], because... by virtue of the requirement of syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) does not constitute a fault.
Locanā:
"Tiṣṭhet" and so forth;
she is concealed by divine splendor.
That Urvaśī is invisible; by means of realization— that is, by knowledge—
the later realization sublates the earlier realization.
Wherever there is an additional word, it is a fault. VisSd 7.27.
For example:
"I do not know why a wicked person acts so rashly toward matters that are beyond even the range of the mind; yet I do know this: he does not touch upon actual cruelty."
In this context, "not not knowing" (*na na jāna*) expresses the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*).
Locanā:
The exclusion of non-connection takes the form, "I do indeed know."

In the second [verse], by the word "knowing" (*jāna*), there is a specific excellence of exclusion (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*) through the exclusion of connection with others, in the sense that "I alone know.
*Vijñapriyā*:
"A quality exists somewhere"—the meaning is: where an additional word has a different meaning through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) or indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

"He practices" (ācāratīti)—the meaning is that I am not unaware of what a wicked person suddenly practices, namely, harmful and unreal matters that are beyond even the range of the mind; rather, I know them very well.
However, the meaning is that my heart does not touch upon such cruelty at all.
*Vicchitti* (distinction) is a stylistic turn (*bhaṅgi*) consisting of a particular mode of cognition.
"In this context"—the two cases of the arising and non-arising of expectancy constitute the seed for what is neither a defect nor a merit.
In some instances, the repetition of what has already been concluded is neither a defect nor a merit.
For example: “anyāstā guṇaratna-” and so forth.
Here, although the sentence is completed by the first half, the sentence of the second half is taken up again.

Thus, it should be understood that when only a qualifier is taken up again, this constitutes the fault of *samāptapunarāttatva* (resuming what was already finished), but not when an entire different sentence is resumed.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ṭa) Regarding the phrase "anyastā," although the sentence is completed by the first half-verse, there is no fault because the expectation arises as to how the excellence of the producing qualities, such as the jewels and so forth, is distinct here.
He determines whether the fault of "resuming what has already been concluded" (samāptapunarāttatva) is indeed a fault or not by stating "evañca" (and thus).

In the phrase "of the mere qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇamātrasya*), it should be understood that "that which is not required" (*anākāṅkṣitasya*) is meant; for it has already been shown previously that there is no fault when there is a requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*) for the qualifier. Thus, it is the requirement itself that acts as the regulator.

Regarding the statement "not [due to] the qualifiers 'sentence-ness' and 'being a qualifier'," the phrase "of another sentence" was said with the intention that expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) necessarily persists in another sentence.
Locanā:
(Lo, ṝ) The second half of the verse begins with "O illustrious Kānti," and so forth.
And thus— "of the mere qualifier" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).
By this, other words such as the agent, the object, and so forth, are also included when they complete the sentence,
as illustrated by examples such as "The Sun is Hari," and so on.
In some cases, being "pregnant" (garbhitatva) is a merit—as for example:
"The earth, with its four boundaries demarcated by the temples of the world-elephants, is being conquered; yet even as we speak, it is already won. Behold! We are covered in horripilation."
What more need be said? Homage to that Rāma, for whom this wondrous narrative was composed as a gift for the Brahmin, and from whom it arose, and in whom its meaning finds its final rest.
In this context, the sentence beginning with "vadanta eva" and so forth nourishes an excellence of aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) by means of the insertion of one sentence into another.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ṭha) "The herd of elephants of the quarters... [and so on].
The word *āghāṭa* means a boundary.
Thus, by Rāma, that very earth whose four boundaries were demarcated by the herds of elephants of the [four] quarters—
earth which was accomplished and brought under his own control through a proof free from contradiction— is now being bestowed upon the Brahmin.
"What more shall we say? is the ellipsis.
"To that Rāma, let this be a salutation"—meaning, to him from whom this wonderful tale emerged, since it could not have arisen from any other cause;
and into whom alone it has gone to its end.
The meaning is: "Even as we were saying that it had set because someone else had caused it to do so for some time, we were actually thrilled with horripilation; look at this!
The particle *hi* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).
The word *atra* means "in this [instance]."
Because astonishment is evoked precisely when the sentence has not yet reached its conclusion.
*Locanā*:
(Lo, Ḷ) The phrase beginning with "diṅbhātaṅga" means "bounded by the four oceans."
Likewise, there is the state of excellence that is falling away.
In some cases, "thus" (*tathā*) constitutes a merit (*guṇa*).
For example: “*cañcadbhuja-*,” etc.
Here, in the fourth quarter, the abandonment of verbal bombast due to the delicacy of the meaning is a merit.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ḍa) Regarding the fourth quarter here:
"O Queen, she will braid your hair."

In the verse beginning with "bhīma," the meaning is that there is a quality of delicacy (*sukumāratā*) both in the phonemes and in the absence of compound words. In certain instances, there is no fault in expressing a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) by its own name, provided that the composition does not involve the [standard] excitants (*vibhāva*) and ensuants (*anubhāva*). (VisSd 7.29)
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ḍha) "In some cases, when stated" means that there is no fault in some instances when the deviation is stated by its own word.
Regarding the question "Where is there no fault?", he says: "anubhāva," etc. *Racanā* means presentation.
He explains those two types of *anaucitya* (inappropriateness) with the verses beginning with "yatra," and so forth.

Where there is no clear comprehension through presentation by way of the ensuants (*anubhāva*) and determinants (*vibhāva*), and where the absence of nourishment provided by the determinants and ensuants is itself appropriate—
this is the *Vijñapriyā*.

(vi, ṇa) "Produced by the determinants and consequents"—the meaning is that the absence of the nourishment of the transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*), which consists in its being manifested by its own determinants (*vibhāva*) and consequents (*anubhāva*).
In this regard, there is no fault if the transitory emotion is expressed by its own word.
For example:

“May Gaurī bring you auspiciousness—she who, at their first union, was made to cry out by her innate longing, who turned away again and again out of modesty but was drawn back toward him by the various words of her female kinswomen; she who, seeing her husband before her, was filled with the essence of trepidation, and who, her hair standing on end with thrill, was embraced by the laughing Hara.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ta) He provides a single example for both [types]: "autsukyena" (with eagerness).

On the first day of her new union, Gaurī, having turned away due to the eagerness caused by the desire for proximity to Hara, and subsequently due to the innate shame that arises simultaneously with it, [acts] as described in the passage beginning with "tataśca taistaiḥ" (and then by those various...).

Then, having seen her husband Hara before her, she experienced a state of intense trepidation; thereafter, being embraced by the laughing Hara, her hair stood on end with thrill—may she, the Goddess Śivā, be thus for your welfare.
—Locanā.

To the question "Why is there no fault?", he says: "By the [vibhāva] called *anubhāva*," and "by eagerness (*autsukya*)," meaning by the concomitant haste (*tvarā*) that arises immediately thereafter.

The meaning is that she acted with haste out of fear, because of the possibility of confusion. Similarly, in other instances, just as these states such as longing (*autsukya*) are conveyed through the medium of their physical manifestations (*anubhāva*), such as turning away— as in the verse beginning "From afar [she was] longing, upon his arrival, she turned back"— so too is longing conveyed through the manifestation of a sudden stretching forth.
The point is that since there is no clear comprehension [of the intended meaning], it is more appropriate to express the transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) by its own name.

In this case, if longing (*autsukya*) were presented through its effect (*anubhāva*), namely haste (*tvarā*), there would be no immediate understanding of the "union" (*saṅgama*), because haste can also arise from fear and other causes.
Since shame (*hrī*) and its manifestation can occur through anger and the like when it is being turned away,

and since the full development of fear (*sādhvasa*) and laughter (*hāsa*) would generally be contrary to the primary rasa under discussion, it is proper that these [emotions] be expressed by their own specific names.
*Vijñapriyā*:
Regarding this, [the phrase] "by way of the face" means that the effect (*anubhāva*) of eagerness (*autsukya*), which consists in haste, is manifested through the face.
He states the reason why there is no immediate comprehension: "because haste can also arise from fear and so forth."

Thus, because the manifestation of shame (*hrī*) is also withdrawn, there is no immediate perception of it; therefore, he states that there is no fault in the word "shame" being the denotation [of that state]. He says: "And of the manifestation of shame," thereby showing the absence of nourishment produced by the excitants (*vibhāva*) and ensuants (*anubhāva*). Regarding "fear and laughter": fear is terror, and laughter is the expansion of the mind caused by something laughable, as shown in the definition of the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*).

And those two—the permanent moods (*sthāyibhāva*) of the terrifying (*bhayānaka*) and the comic (*hāsya*) sentiments—are here [in this context] transitory moods (*vyabhicāribhāva*) within the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) of Gaurī and Maheśa;
the meaning is that the nourishment (*paripoṣa*) of those two by their respective determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth would be largely incompatible with the primary erotic sentiment at hand.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the term *vibhāvādi*, the consequents (*anubhāva*) are included.

For instance, trembling (*kampas*) is first of all the *anubhāva* (consequent emotion) of fear (*sādhvasa*), while the laughter of Maheśa is the *uddīpanavibhāva* (excitant cause). Therefore, if the phrase "trembling" were employed without taking into account fear and laughter, then [the trembling] would be attributed to fear from seeing the serpent on his body and to disgust from seeing the moist elephant hide and skull— both of which are contrary to the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).

The meaning is that because they arise from its trembling, there would be no suggestion (*vyañjanā*) of only fear (*sādhvasa*) and laughter (*hāsa*), which are transitory states (*vyabhicārin*) of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), since suggestion is impossible for fear and joy. Therefore, these—eagerness, shame, fear, and laughter—are expressed by their own words. It is stated "because of predominance" because even in the case of fear and laughter, suggestion is possible; thus, there is not absolute opposition.
The statement of a contradictory element, such as a transition (*sañcārin*), by virtue of its being sublated, is a poetic excellence (*guṇa*).
Locanā:
"Contradictory" means opposed to the intended *rasa* and so forth.
For example: “Where is the improper act [of the hare-marked moon], and where is his lineage? and so forth.

Here, the suppression of the factors of *praśama* (tranquility)—namely *vitarka*, *mati*, *śaṅkā*, and *dhṛti*—by the factors of *abhilāṣa* (longing), namely *autsukya*, *smṛti*, *dainya*, and *cintā*, ultimately brings forth the excellence of aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*) dominated by *cintā*. Thus says the *Vijñapriyā*.
Regarding the phrase "of the transitory emotion (*sañcārī*) and so forth": *sañcārī* means a transitory emotion (*vyabhicārī*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the ensuants (*anubhāva*) and the determinants (*vibhāva*) are also included.

Even when that [transitory emotion] belongs to a conflicting rasa, its description as being sublated by a more powerful [emotion]—by virtue of its being sublated—is a merit (*guṇa*) insofar as it serves to ensure the victory of the rival [rasa].

Regarding the phrase "of the limbs of tranquility" (*praśamāṅgānām*): tranquility (*praśama*) is the state of being overwhelmed by the aesthetic flavor of peace (*śānta-rasa*). The meaning is "of its [the tranquility's] constituent parts" (*tadaṅgānām*), that is, of those belonging to it.
Regarding the term "limb of longing" (*abhilāṣāṅga*): it means longing is passion (*rati*), [and the limb consists] in the eagerness for that and so forth.
Regarding the term "limit" (*paryanta*): [it refers to the culmination].
"Who indeed is the fortunate youth who shall drink this lower lip?"—this is the implied meaning (*vyaṅgya*).
Even for one who has transgressed, there may be remembrance through similarity, whether in speech or in action. (VisSd 7.30)
There would be no mutual contradiction between two elements that have attained the status of the primary and the subordinate.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, dha):

Regarding the phrase "even though they are contradictory"—even when there is a mention of a contradictory rasa, such as a transitory emotion (*sañcārībhāva*) and the like, whether it is being remembered or is manifested through recollection, or even when it is expressed with equality alongside the primary rasa...
There would be no contradiction;

the meaning is that there is no mutual contradiction between being the possessor of a limb (aṅgin) and being a limb (aṅga). Furthermore, the word "and" (ca) should be supplied here in the phrase "between being the possessor of a limb and being a limb."
For example, in sequence: “This is that [man] with the excellence of his tongue,” and so forth.

Here, when the object of focus has vanished, because the *rasa* (sentiment) of love (*rati*) has ceased to exist, the limbs of that [love] being remembered serve to intensify the sorrow, thereby becoming conducive to the *karuṇa* (pathetic) sentiment.
*Vijñapriyā*:
"This is he," and so forth, is clear.
Here, the lifting of the tongue and other such factors are the excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) when being remembered; they are manifested (*vyaṅgya*) by that [remembrance].
The erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is also being remembered; even though it is manifested, it is characterized as "being remembered" because it has passed into the past.
Locanā: (Lo, O) the object of focus,
the subduing of battle.

“With sweat-drops of perspiration flowing from passion, with the broad surface of their thighs resounding from the blows of their hands, and with their lips repeatedly bitten by their teeth, the kings were possessed by wrath as if by a most beloved woman.”
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
pa) Regarding the statement "with passion" (*sarāgayā*),
he says this in order to describe the anger of kings seated on their thrones for the purpose of preparing for war.

The kings, out of anger, resorted to [the earth] as if they had approached their most beloved wives; that is to say, they submitted to the wrath of the angry Earth, who is naturally fond of anger. He states her epithets: "full of passion" (sarāgayā).
The description of wrath as being red in color is established by the tradition of poets.
But in the alternative view, [the earth] was one filled with passion because of her being most beloved,
and possessing a redness caused by anger;
for from her flowed— meaning trickled out— the thick sweat-water of kings.
By such a fury—
that is, by her most beloved wife from whose body thick sweat had flowed out—
[she was struck] with a blow of the hand. Thus [it is said].
The striking of the throne with the hand by kings, performed out of anger,
refers to the breadth— the width— and the height— the loftiness— of the throne.
But by the striking of her own hand, the beloved caused the throne in the form of Pṛthu’s own thighs to resound. "Repeatedly" refers to the biting of the lips by the king, performed out of anger.
But for the beloved, it is performed by herself.
Locanā:
(lo, au) *Rāga* means redness and love.

In this context, the erotic sentiment of enjoyment (*sambhoga-śṛṅgāra*) is intended [as the primary rasa], while the transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) of heroism (*vīra*)—namely, anger—is indicated through the similarity of its physical manifestations (*anubhāva*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
"In this context" (*atrety*).

The meaning is as follows: since even a permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) belonging to one rasa can serve as a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) for another rasa, here anger—the permanent emotion of the *raudra* (furious) rasa—is a transitory emotion for the *vīra* (heroic) rasa that has been introduced. Through its manifestation, the *sambhoga-śṛṅgāra* (erotic love-in-enjoyment) is intended to be suggested here by way of similarity with the contextual *vīra* rasa.
Thus, the suggested sense is [the hero's] being full of passion and so forth.

Now, one might object: by the expression "as if by the most beloved," it is the most beloved woman herself who is intended through the comparison, and not the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*). To this, he replies: "by the similarity of the manifesting emotions" (*anubhāva*).
For both the heroic (*vīra*) and the erotic sentiments possess such manifesting emotions as passion (*sarāgatva*) and so forth.

The meaning is that if there is a similarity between them in terms of being denotable by the same word and in their form and flavor (*rasa*), then there is also a similarity between the two emotions (*rasa*)—the Furious and the Erotic—that are suggested by them.
Although it has been stated: "When two amorous persons, mutually favorable, engage in looking, touching, and so forth, that is illustrated as *sambhoga* (enjoyment)."
"Thus, the characteristic of *sambhoga* has been described.

Nevertheless, because there is indeed conformity [to the aesthetic sentiment] even when observing anger dependent on intoxication (*pramada*) and so forth, this is precisely *sambhoga-śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment of union)."

“May the three eyes of Śambhu protect you during his time of meditative absorption—the first, almost closed like a bud from the closing of his meditation; the second, languid with the sentiment of sexual union upon the lotus-face and full breasts of Pārvatī; and the third, inflamed by the fire of wrath as he draws his bow far back.”
Here, there is the *rati* (devotional attachment) directed toward the Blessed One, nourished by the sentiments (*rasa*) of tranquility (*śānta*), the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), and the furious (*raudra*).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ba) He states the lack of contradiction between two elements that have attained the status of being subordinate (*aṅga*) to the principal element (*aṅgin*)—namely, "one" (*ekam*).
May the three eyes of Śambhu protect you—eyes which possess distinct flavors at the time of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
He demonstrates their state of having distinct flavors there by saying: "by the closing of meditation, they are almost like buds.
In some places, however, the reading is: "due to the closing of meditation, they are almost bud-like."

Then, by the suffix *kta* applied to the word *mukula*, "mukulitam" means resembling a bud; however, because it is preceded by the prefix *pra*, it refers to a slightly opened bud. This is the *anubhāva* (consequent emotion) of tranquility (*śānta*).
Regarding the word "second":
in the phrase "the face-lotus and the weight of the breasts," because these are parts of a living being (*prāṇyaṅga*), it is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*).
This is an ensuant emotion (*anubhāva*) of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).
"Another [meaning]" means:
regarding that Madana who has drawn his bow far back, it is "kindled by the fire of anger"; this is the sense.

Here, although anger—the *sthāyibhāva* of the *raudra-rasa* (furious sentiment)—is directly expressed (*vācya*), it is further suggested (*vyañjanā*) through its excitants (*uddīpana*) and consequents (*anubhāva*), yet it remains subordinate to another [element]. Thus he says: "here."
In this context, the term "peaceful" (*śānta*) and so forth refers to the stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*).

He states "here" (*atra*) to explain that there is no contradiction because those aforementioned opposing emotions—which are suggested by the described external manifestations (*anubhāva*)—do not function as subordinate elements (*aparāṅga*) to one another.
*Locanā*.

(Lo, a) Here, regarding the term "peaceful" (*śānta*): the meaning is that there is no mutual contradiction between the peaceful and other sentiments—even though they are opposed—because they exist as subordinate elements (*aṅga*) to the dominant sentiment (*aṅgin*) of love directed toward the Blessed One.

Or, for example: “Seized by the hand, he was cast off; forcibly struck, he still clung to the hem of her garment; grasping her hair, he was pushed away; falling at her feet, he was not even looked upon in her agitation.”

May that fire of Śambhu’s arrow burn away your misfortunes—that fire which, like a lover who has recently offended his mistress, was embraced by the young women of Tripura with their lotus-eyes filled with tears, as they were cast down [by the arrow].
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, bha) Having thus demonstrated the non-contradiction among mutually contradictory factors within a single subject (*aṅgin*), he states the non-contradiction of such factors through both direct and indirect means—as for example: "May that fire of Śambhu’s arrow, famous for its burning of Tripura, burn away your misfortune. (*kṣipta iti*) [The verse continues: "May that fire of Śambhu’s arrow, famous for its burning of Tripura, burn away your misfortune. (*tripurudāhe sa prasiddhaḥ śāmbhavaḥ śarāgnir vo duritaṃ dahatu*).

Of what sort was he? Like a lover who, having committed an offense, is cast off by the young women of Tripura with lotus-eyes full of tears as he clings to their hands; even so, though he was seizing the hem of the garment, he was struck down.
For the particle *api* is used here out of its natural order;
likewise, while grasping at her hair, he was repelled.

In the case of the lover (*kāmipakṣe*): she grasped his hair for the sake of a kiss; likewise, due to her agitation and fear, the fire [that had been kindled] by the falling of his feet was not looked upon.
However, as for the lover who had fallen at her feet, the act of looking at him with agitation—that is, with reverence—was not performed [by her].
"Embracing" is clear.
In the case of Agni, the tears arise from fear; in the case of the lover, they arise from anger.

Here, the primary element is the poet’s *rati* (devotional love) directed toward the Blessed Lord. Since the Blessed Lord’s *utsāha* (enthusiasm) regarding the destruction of Tripura serves as a nourisher (*paripoṣaka*) of that *rati*, and because it has not reached the status of a *rasa* due to its lack of full development—remaining merely a *bhāva* (transitory emotion)—the *karuṇa* (pathetic) rasa is subordinate (*aṅga*) to it.

And because the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) has arrived through the force of similarity with "like a lover" (*kāmīva*), and because it does not constitute a state of final repose, it likewise serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa*). Thus, since both the pathetic and the erotic sentiments simultaneously serve to intensify the savoring of the aesthetic emotion (*bhāva*)— which is love directed toward the Lord and nourished by His heroic energy (*utsāha*)—
there is no contradiction between them in their capacity as subordinate elements.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ma) The primary [element] is that which resides in the poet and culminates in the poet, because [the phrase] "may he burn" and so forth is suggested by a sentence that is complete in itself; and [this applies] to that [suggestion].
In this regard, the Lord’s energy (*utsāha*)—manifested through the employment of the fiery weapon (*āgneyāstra*) against Tripura—is the predominant [sentiment] (*pradhāna*).

And that energy, by indicating its own greatness, serves as a nourisher (*puṣṭikāraka*) of the sentiment of love (*rati-bhāva*) directed toward Him, in the form of an intensification; thus he says: "by way of being a nourisher. The meaning is that energy is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the sentiment of love.
The grammatical connection is that compassion (*karuṇa*) is a constituent element (*aṅga*) of that energy (*utsāha*).

Now, one might object: "Energy is the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*), and since it is what is suggested (*vyaṅgya*) here, the heroic sentiment itself must be the primary element in this case."
To the question, "In that case, how is the predominance of the state of *rati* (love) asserted? he replies: "And because of its lack of full development.

This means that because that *utsāha* (energy) is suggested by a sentence containing an expectancy (*sākāṅkṣa*), whereas the *kavi-bhāva* (poetic sentiment) is suggested by a sentence free of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*), it lacks predominance in the form of being underdeveloped; thus, by not having reached the status of *rasa*, it remains merely a *bhāva*, which is to say, a *sthāyibhāva* (permanent emotion).

Regarding the term "karuṇa" (the pathetic sentiment): it means that the pathetic sentiment, which is suggested by the pitiable state of the young women of Tripura, is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) that serves to nourish [the primary sentiment]. Regarding the phrase "of that" (*tasya*):...
The meaning is "of this *karuṇa* (pathetic sentiment)";

the syntactical connection is that "the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) is a subordinate element" (*aṅga*). And its status as a subordinate element arises from the intensification of the standard of comparison and the object compared.

Thus, he demonstrates that the *karaṇa* (instrumental) and *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) sentiments—though they are by nature antagonistic—are not contradictory when they serve as subordinate elements (*aṅga*) to the *vibhāva* (excitant) directed toward the Lord, which is nourished by the Lord’s own enthusiasm; this is shown by the phrase "and thus, without rest" (*evam cāviśrānti*).
This is because [the subordinate sentiment] does not find its final repose (*aviśrāntidhāmatayā*), but rather possesses expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatā*) by virtue of being its substratum (*āśrayatayā*).
This means "by way of requiring a substratum" (*aṅgin*).

As for the Lord’s enthusiasm (*bhagavad-utsāha*), although it is indeed a constituent part (*aṅga*), because it is not in contradiction with the emotion (*bhāva*), its contradiction has not been shown.
Now, one might object: even in the case of rasa, which is suggested by the remembered excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, [is there not a contradiction?]

It has been stated that even though there is the possibility of a contradiction with Aṅgiras regarding the similarity of the *vibhāvas* and so forth being remembered— which is a similarity intended by the speaker's intention— there is nonetheless no contradiction;
[the author] raises the doubt that there is no possibility of a contradiction with Aṅgiras at all— *Locanā*.

(Lo, ā) The meaning is: "by means of [factors] such as *vibhāva* due to being un-nourished. The reason for the phrase "of mere emotion" (*bhāvamātrasya*) is that it has not yet reached the state of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), because it is merely a subordinate element (*aṅga*).
"Attained through the power of similarity" means attained by the force of similar qualifiers.
Regarding the phrase "of compassion":

the meaning is that although compassion is the primary element (*aṅgin*) in relation to the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), it is nevertheless subordinate (*aṅga*) to the Blessed One’s passion and energy. Furthermore, in this case...

There is no contradiction in the manifestation of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*) even as a constituent part through its being remembered in the manner previously described, such as "This is that excellence of taste... and so forth.
For instance, there were those young women of Tripura for whom the lover, in order to dispel their jealous anger, performed the act of rejecting the grasping of his hands.

In those very same pitiless women, the Śāmbhava fire of arrows acted in such a manner that, through the perception of similarity, the *karuṇa* (pathetic) rasa—being recollected by means of the *īrṣyā-vipralambha* (love-in-separation characterized by jealousy)—is, on the contrary, nourished.
And by that, the aesthetic emotion (*bhāva*) of love directed toward him, which is already fully nourished by the extraordinary power of the Enemy of Tripura, is brought to its ultimate perfection.
Now, one might ask: how can a contradiction be conceived between such a rasa, which consists of a dense, full-blown bliss based on a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*), and another rasa?
Because there is no possibility of mutual exclusion due to the absence of simultaneity—given that [the two] exist through their inclusion and manifestation within a single sentence.
Vijñapriyā:
"Now, [it may be argued]... (vi, ya).

Regarding the term *samūhālambana* (having a collective substratum): it refers to how the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), which is being relished according to the analogy of the juice of a refreshing drink (*prapānaka-rasa*), is described as consisting of a collective substratum of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth.

Since this [flavor] is suggested by a syntactically complete sentence (*nirākāṅkṣa-vākya-vyaṅgya*), it is "full" through the fulfillment of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā-pūrti*). It is "dense" because it does not grasp other objects, and it is "compact" because its nature is bliss (*ānanda*).
How can such a flavor be compared with another flavor that is being recollected or that possesses a desired similarity?
The meaning is that a contradiction is to be expected.
He states the reason for this impossibility with the words "in a single sentence.
For [the injunction] of Aṅgiras arises from a sentence whose prescribed content is already complete and free of expectancy.

The meaning is that, since the two sentences containing the remembered [object] and the standard of comparison appear as syntactically expectant subject-sentences, there is an absence of simultaneity in the form of appearing as a single sentence; consequently, it is impossible for them to mutually sublate one another.

The point is that, due to the lack of equal strength, the primary, self-contained prescriptive sentence—which is the principal element—sublates the two remembered standards of comparison by virtue of its status as the predominant suggested meaning.

Nor should it be said that this erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is being remembered through sentences already devoid of expectancy, such as "this hand, which was the height of aesthetic relish," and so forth;
for [the sentence] "this hand, which produced the height of relish, has fallen" possesses an expectancy precisely for the predicate of falling.

However, their falling—which serves to manifest the pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa*)—is merely metaphorically termed "being remembered" because, even though the erotic sentiment is suggested (*vyaṅgya*), it is [now] remote. This is how it should be understood.
Nor is there a relationship of part and whole,
because both rest in their fullness and independence.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(Vi, Ra) Having thus demonstrated that there is no possibility of conflict between the two objects of comparison when they are being recollected, he raises the doubt that there can be no relation of principal and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) even between those two which have attained the status of principal and subordinate—stating, "nor is there a relation of principal and subordinate," meaning "between both of them.
The meaning is: between the *śṛṅgāra* and *karuṇa* rasas, which are mutually opposed.

"Independently" means that because the sentences beginning with "despised" (*kṣipta*) and the sentence beginning with "like a lustful man" (*kāmīva*) are self-sufficient (*nirākāṅkṣa*), they are not suggested by the latter;
independence itself is fullness (*pūrṇatā*).
Because the longing is fulfilled,
Locanā says:
"Now, regarding the passage beginning with 'samūha'— if there were a contradiction between two aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*),..."
Or perhaps there might be a relationship of part and whole;
however, neither of these two modes is possible between two *rasas*.
To the question of how contradiction is not possible, he says: "Because mutual sublation is untenable."

He asks how it is that mutual exclusion is untenable, and says: "In the case of a single sentence..."—the meaning is this: because there is an absence of simultaneity caused by the mention in a single sentence regarding the manifestation [of the two rasas], for simultaneity is possible only through mention in a single sentence;
however, that is not possible for the two rasas.
The reason for this is "the collection" (*samūha*).
The meaning is as follows: because it has as its objective support (*ālambana*) the collection of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, according to the manner of the double statement.
Indeed, the totality of the determinants and so forth constitutes the meaning of a single sentence.
And how could there be a single causal complex for two things that are mutually contradictory?
How could there be completeness based on a single sentence as the cause?
For the term "dense" (*ghana*) refers to a flow that is uninterrupted by heterogeneous elements.
He states the reason for the impossibility of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal (aṅgāṅgibhāva) with the words "nor even" (nāpi).
The relationship between the subordinate and the principal consists in being the beneficiary and the benefactor (upakāryopakāritva).
It is true that this has been stated.

For this very reason, because these other rasas lack repose in independence and consist merely of portions of the full rasa, the ancients designated them by the name *saṃcārī-rasa* (transitory rasa) due to their distinct nature. However, according to the venerable Śrī Caṇḍīdāsa—the foremost among learned poets and the younger brother of my grandfather—they are called *khaṇḍa-rasa* (fragmentary rasa). *Vijñapriyā*: [Commentary]...
